Title: Identification of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus within the Nation’s Veterans Affairs Medical Centers using natural language processing
Journal_Source: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: VA Informatics and Computing Infrastructure (VINCI) (VA HSR HIR 08-204); Consortium for Healthcare Informatics Research (CHIR) (VA HSR HIR 08-374); Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Prevention Epicenters Program (5U01CI000334, 07FED706504)
Population_Description: Nationwide patient-level, free-text microbiology reports from all VA VistA systems, 1990-2009: 33,024,796 unique records from 128 VistA sites representing 152 currently active acute care hospitals (170 total over the period); reference comparisons used data from eleven VA sites, VISN 4 (ten hospitals) and VA Salt Lake City
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Laboratory information system
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Infection prevention and control team; Surveillance analyst / public health; Researcher
All_Models_Evaluated: Single rule-based NLP information extraction system (Apache UIMA pipeline: section identification, organism detection, susceptibility detection, MRSA inference). Training set: S. aureus sensitivity 99.6%, specificity 99.9%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 99.6%; methicillin resistance sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 99.9%, PPV 99.7%, NPV 99.9%. Validation set vs 5,927 electronic records: S. aureus 100%/99.9%/99.9%/100%; methicillin resistance 100%/99.9%/99.9%/100%. Validation set vs 3,092 expert-reviewed records: S. aureus 98.3%/99.7%/99.6%/98.6%; methicillin resistance 99.2%/99.4%/97.9%/99.8%. Separate MRSA-surveillance-screen string-searching algorithm: sensitivity 99.4%, specificity 97.9%.
Best_Performing_Model: Rule-based NLP information extraction system (Apache UIMA pipeline) - the only system developed and evaluated; no model comparison was performed, so there is no higher-scoring alternative
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Validation set - S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference compared with electronic (data warehouse) records; expert-reviewed comparison gave 98.3% (S. aureus) and 99.2% (methicillin resistance)
Specificity_Population_Set: Validation set - S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference compared with electronic (data warehouse) records; expert-reviewed comparison gave 99.7% (S. aureus) and 99.4% (methicillin resistance)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Validation set - S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference compared with electronic (data warehouse) records; expert-reviewed comparison gave 99.6% (S. aureus) and 97.9% (methicillin resistance)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Training and test sets were created by randomly splitting the expert-annotated sample rather than separating sites or time periods; independently derived electronic data and expert annotation served as comparison standards rather than as separate external validation cohorts, and no prospective or site-level accuracy validation is reported.
Reported_Limitations: No valid reference standard exists; limited accessible electronic data for comparison; a random sample from more facilities would have improved the completeness analysis but was logistically infeasible; per-site samples were small so no VA site-specific accuracy estimates could be reported; completeness cannot be confirmed for unsampled VA sites.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Systematic biases can be introduced when data are derived from or processed electronically; microbiology data may be systematically or sporadically entered in the wrong place in VistA, and report-format variation across sites and years could affect extraction.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not discussed; accuracy could not be reported by VA site, so variation in performance across facilities or patient groups is unaddressed.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: No governance risk raised; the study used existing VA microbiology records with approval from the VA Salt Lake City Health Care System Research Review Committee and the University of Utah Institutional Review Board.
Reviewer_Notes: Single-country (USA) national VA retrospective data-validation study of one rule-based NLP information extraction system. No model comparison: the NLP pipeline is the only system evaluated, so it is the unit of analysis for the metric fields. Absence-required Yes/No fields answered 'No'/'NR' where the text layer reports no such item; quotes given are the metrics/assessment sentences that demonstrate the absence. Not a predictive model, so predictor/feature-importance fields follow the system's rule inputs (text, organism, susceptibility, metadata terms).
Unresolved_Items: The paper reports accuracy against two reference sets (independently derived electronic data and expert-reviewed annotation) and at two levels (S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference); it does not state which is primary, and the values differ. Whether the multi-site, multi-year VA comparison constitutes external validation is also a judgement call.
Sample_Size: 33,024,796 unique microbiology records from 128 VistA sites (152 currently active acute care hospitals; 170 total hospitals over 1990-2009); validation comparisons used 5,927 electronic and 3,092 expert-reviewed records
Conflicts_of_Interest: None of the authors have received reimbursements, fees, funding, or salary from an organization that may gain or lose financially from this publication; there are no outstanding patents; all authors have affiliations with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Inclusion_Criteria: Microbiology documents containing the strings “staph”, “coag”, “mrsa”, “orsa”, “oxacillin” or “aureus” (10,000 randomly selected records) queued for expert review; VISN 4 and Salt Lake City microbiology data that had already been annotated; PCS microbiology records collected from all VistA systems, 1990-2009
Exclusion_Criteria: MRSA surveillance screens were removed before information extraction: 4,002 records identified as screens in the expert-reviewed data set were removed, and screening studies were identified by reviewers but removed during evaluation of information extraction accuracy
Data_Types_Used: Free text / clinical notes; AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables
Data_Source_Name: VA Patient Care Services (PCS) microbiology data extracted from VistA; VISN 4 data warehouse; VA Salt Lake City Health Care System (VA SLC HCS) data warehouse
Dataset_Size: 33,024,796 unique microbiology records from 128 VistA sites; expert-annotation sample of 10,000 records; validation comparisons of 5,927 electronic and 3,092 expert-reviewed records
Missing_Data_Method: Completeness estimated by matching microbiology accession numbers against independently derived data warehouse records (98.5%, 95% CI 98.5-98.6%) and by analysing gaps in sequentially ordered accession numbers, which yields a lower bound because gaps also arise from non-patient samples
Geographic_Representativeness: Nationwide VA microbiology data from 128 VistA sites representing 152 currently active acute care hospitals; comparison data came from eleven VA sites, VISN 4 (ten hospitals) and VA SLC, plus ten randomly sampled hospitals for sequence-gap analysis; no site-specific accuracy estimates could be reported
Specimen_Type_Detail: All cultured sample and specimen types appearing in microbiology reports (11,596 unique types reviewed); MRSA surveillance tests from the anterior nares were filtered out before extraction
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance inferred for cultures in which S. aureus was detected (i.e. MRSA), together with identification of S. aureus itself, extracted from free-text microbiology reports and validated against independently derived electronic data and expert annotation
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) and coagulase-positive S. aureus
Drug_Classes: Antimicrobials recorded in susceptibility testing: penicillinase-resistant penicillins (oxacillin, nafcillin, methicillin) and cephalosporins (cefoxitin, cefazolin, cephalothin), plus mecA / penicillin binding protein 2A testing
Specific_Antibiotics: oxacillin; cefoxitin; cefazolin; cephalothin; nafcillin; methicillin (resistance); penicillin binding protein 2A / mecA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: A culture was positive for methicillin resistance when S. aureus was detected and the detected susceptibilities indicated resistance; susceptibility terms were mapped to resistant, susceptible or indeterminate, and resistance could be evidenced by oxacillin, cefoxitin, penicillin binding protein 2A or mecA testing, or by resistance to cefazolin, cephalothin, nafcillin, or a simple statement of methicillin resistance
AI_Purpose: Apply NLP information extraction to nationwide VA free-text microbiology reports to extract organisms and antibiotic susceptibilities and infer MRSA, then validate the extraction against independently derived electronic data and expert annotation
Num_Models_Compared: 0 - no models compared; a single rule-based NLP information extraction system was developed and assessed against two independent reference standards (electronic data warehouse and expert annotation)
Feature_Engineering: Hand-crafted rules exploiting the semi-structured report templates (section identification, organism detection, susceptibility detection, MRSA inference); descriptor terms for quantity, concentration and resistance were stripped to leave the organism name, which was then mapped to SNOMED-CT; susceptibility terms were mapped to resistant/susceptible/indeterminate
Feature_Selection_Method: Iterative manual rule and term-list development on training reports with detailed failure analysis after each iteration
Software_Libraries: Apache Unstructured Information Management Architecture (UIMA); MUMPS (VistA database language); SQL relational database
Other_Metrics: MRSA surveillance-screen filter: sensitivity 99.4%, specificity 97.9%; data completeness 98.5% (95% CI 98.5-98.6%); NPV 100% against electronic data and 98.6% (S. aureus) / 99.8% (methicillin resistance) against expert-reviewed data
Internal_Validation: Random split of the expert-annotated sample into training and test sets (half in each; all Salt Lake City data used for training), with a second comparison set of 5,927 electronic and 3,092 expert-reviewed records
Train_Test_Split: Half of the expert-annotated records for training and half for the test set; the validation comparison used a second set of 5,927 electronic and 3,092 expert-reviewed records
Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Decision rules / surrogate tree
Clinical_Insights: Clinical experts were involved in developing the NLP tools and inference algorithms; clinical nurses experienced in reading microbiology reports annotated S. aureus status, methicillin resistance and surveillance-test status, and discordant records were re-reviewed by a domain expert
Generalisability_Details: Authors state the NLP methods are robust and should serve well against other organisms, but caution that report-format variation may be greater when combining data from disparate non-VA health systems, and they could not report VA site-specific accuracy
Maturity_Evidence: Rule-based NLP system developed on VA microbiology data and evaluated against two independent reference standards using a random training/test split; the extraction runs as a background data-collection service on VINCI but has not been evaluated prospectively or in routine clinical decision-making
Integration_Point: Background data-extraction process that pulls microbiology reports from VistA at each medical centre through RPCs/VistaWeb into a secure SQL database, with NLP applied on the VINCI computing environment before use in surveillance analyses
End_User_Described: Infection-control programmes and surveillance analysts / researchers - for example the VA Inpatient Evaluation Center, which gathered the data to evaluate the National MRSA Prevention Initiative
Barriers_List: Differing data models between systems; messaging strategies; security issues; microbiology data siloed at each hospital; loss of standardised structured fields in the free-text format; report-format variation between centres and over years; MUMPS has only one data type so there are no data type checks; data may be entered in the wrong place in VistA
Facilitators_List: Reuse of existing, reliable VA data processes (RPCs and VistaWeb) that require no independent maintenance and can run as a background process; semi-structured report templates that support rule-based extraction; expert annotation and clinical expert involvement; availability of independent reference data sets
Future_Directions: Contribute the dataset and methods to a comprehensive infectious disease surveillance system; validate routine data warehouse pulls for completeness and concordance; extend the NLP methods to other organisms; combine data across non-VA health systems
Limitation_Categories: Reference standard and data access: no valid reference standard exists; limited accessible electronic data for comparison; only a sample of facilities could be studied; no VA site-specific accuracy estimates; small per-site samples; report-format variation across sites and over time
Data_Quality_Concerns: MUMPS has only one data type so there are no data type checks; data may be systematically or sporadically entered in the wrong place in VistA; microbiology report formats changed over the years and varied between centres; sequence gaps in accession numbers at about half the sites examined

Title: Epidemiology and prediction of multidrug-resistant bacteria based on hospital level
Funder_Names: China Postdoctoral Science Foundation (No. 2021M693593); GuangDong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (No. 2021A1515111146)
Population_Description: Patients with bacterial infection detected at a large teaching hospital (the Eighth Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University, Shenzhen, China) between October 2010 and October 2020; only the first result of multiple tests in the same patient was included
Data_Source_Other: Monthly hospital reports (39 hospital-level indicators: hospital operation volume, nosocomial infection, antibacterial drug use, outdoor temperature, incidence of nosocomial infections)
Top_Predictive_Features: Ranked by random forest IncNodePurity: (1) number of hospital operations; (2) number of type I incision operations; (3) number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues; (4) number of discharged patients; (5) average hospital stay (days); (6) average rate of unreasonable outpatient and emergency prescriptions; (7) rate of antibiotics use in discharged patients
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Infection prevention and control team; Programme manager / policymaker
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest (RF) model for variable-importance ranking (IncNodePurity) - no performance metric reported; regression tree (rpart/CART) prediction model with thresholds (hospitalised emergency rescues 314; hospital operations 1333; clinical pathway rate 9.3) and estimated case counts (about 14 vs as high as 77) - no accuracy, AUC or error metric reported
Best_Performing_Model: Regression tree (rpart/CART) - the model the paper uses to establish the prediction (early-warning) model for the number of patients with MDRB infection; no comparative performance metric is reported for it against the random forest
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The regression tree was fitted to the whole 10-year single-hospital dataset to derive thresholds; no internal validation (cross-validation or train/test split), external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment is reported
Reported_Limitations: Data came from monthly hospital reports over 10 years, so the machine learning model could only produce monthly rather than weekly or daily estimates for real-time prediction; the ecological research design cannot demonstrate causality; the model was built on one hospital, so indicator thresholds may not be generalisable to other hospitals owing to differences in hospital volume
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not discussed; the paper reports only age and sex distributions of infected patients (Supplementary Fig. S1) and performs no equity or fairness analysis
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethics approval is stated as not applicable; no other ethical or governance issues are discussed
Sample_Size: Monthly hospital-level data for October 2010 to October 2020 (39 indicators per month); the number of patients or isolates is not reported in the text
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients detected with bacterial infection by the hospital laboratory information system between October 2010 and October 2020; only the first result of multiple tests in the same patient was included
Exclusion_Criteria: Not otherwise specified; only the first results of multiple tests in the same patient were included
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: The Eighth Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University laboratory information system (LIS); monthly hospital reports
Dataset_Size: Monthly database of 39 hospital-level variables from October 2010 to October 2020
Geographic_Representativeness: One large teaching hospital in the central urban area of Shenzhen, a megacity in southern China with a permanent resident population of 13.43 million
Primary_AMR_Outcome: The number of patients with multidrug-resistant bacteria (MDRB) infection per month (variable c4) at hospital level, modelled from 39 hospital-level indicator variables; five MDRB categories analysed: ESBL-producing Escherichia coli, MRSA, ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii and carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (E. coli), Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), Klebsiella Pneumonia (K. pneumoniae), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Haemophilus influenzae; the five MDRB analysed are ESBL-producing E. coli, MRSA, ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa
Num_Pathogens: 7 named species (E. coli, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa, N. gonorrhoeae, A. baumannii, H. influenzae); five MDRB categories analysed in detail
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems (carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa); beta-lactams (ESBL-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae); methicillin (MRSA)
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDRB infection is counted as the number of patients with multidrug-resistant bacteria infection (dependent variable c4), predicted from 39 hospital-level predictor variables using real-world monthly data
AI_Purpose: Use a random forest model and cross-correlation analysis to explore hospital-level factors affecting MDRB infections and their predictive power, and build a regression tree model to predict the number of hospitalised patients with MDRB infection in order to build an early-warning platform for drug resistance
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (random forest for variable importance; regression tree/CART for prediction); no head-to-head performance metric is reported
Feature_Engineering: 39 factors collected in five groups (hospital operation volume x1-x15, nosocomial infection g1-g8, antibacterial drug use y1-y10, outdoor temperature, incidence of nosocomial infections c1-c3); all variables organised on a monthly basis to build a database; average daily, daily maximum and daily minimum temperature used to adjust for seasonal influence
Feature_Selection_Method: Random forest multivariate importance using increases in node purity (IncNodePurity), with the loss function selected through the best segmentation; the highest-ranked variables were carried into cross-correlation and regression tree analysis
Num_Features_Total: 39 independent variables
Num_Features_Selected: Not stated numerically; the highest-importance variables were selected for cross-correlation and regression tree analysis (number of hospital operations, number of type I incision operations, number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues, number of discharged patients, average hospital stay, rate of unreasonable outpatient and emergency prescriptions, rate of antibiotics use in discharged patients)
Software_Libraries: pheatmap, randomForest, rpart, rpart.plot, ggplot2 (R version 4.0.3); IBM SPSS version 25.0 for cross-correlation
Other_Metrics: Regression tree thresholds and predicted case counts: emergency rescues <314, hospital operations <1333 and clinical pathway rate >9.3 give an estimated 14 MDRB patients in the hospital in the current month; emergency rescues >314 gives an estimate as high as 77
Overfitting_Method: Random forest selected partly because it prevents overfitting; no cross-validation or train/test split is reported
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Surgical, emergency and hospitalised rescue patients showed the highest risk of MDRB infection; more rational perioperative antibiotic use and a higher clinical pathway rate are linked to fewer patients with MDRB infection, while excessive surgical volume and inappropriate antibiotic use in emergency patients may increase MDRB numbers
Generalisability_Details: The model was built on data from one hospital, so the threshold values of the indicators may not be generalisable to other hospitals because of differences in hospital volume
Maturity_Evidence: Model developed on 10 years of monthly hospital-level data from a single hospital; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment is reported
Integration_Point: Hospital-level monthly drug-resistance early-warning platform; not integrated into clinical or laboratory systems
End_User_Described: Not explicitly described; the model is intended for hospital-level monitoring and early warning of MDRB infection
Barriers_List: Monthly (not weekly or daily) resolution of the data limits real-time prediction; the ecological design cannot demonstrate causality; the single-hospital model means indicator thresholds may not transfer to hospitals of a different volume
Future_Directions: Improving the accuracy of the data without changing the methods, and wider validation of indicator thresholds across hospitals with different volumes
Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 groups of variables / 39 variables in total
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest IncNodePurity (increases in node purity) plus multivariate importance by removing predictor variables from each single tree in the forest
Novel_Predictors_Details: Hospital-management indicators highlighted as influential, including the number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues, the rate of rational perioperative antimicrobial drug use in type I and II incision operations, and the rate of clinical pathways
Limitation_Categories: Data granularity (monthly only), ecological design (no causality), and generalisability (single hospital, hospital-volume-dependent thresholds)
Data_Quality_Concerns: Data collected from monthly hospital reports over 10 years, so only monthly estimates could be produced
Reporting_Clarity: No predictive performance metric (accuracy, AUC or error) is reported for the random forest or the regression tree; results are descriptive (importance rankings, cross-correlation lags, regression tree thresholds)

Title: Moving from predicting hospital deaths by antibiotic-resistant bloodstream bacteremia toward actionable risk reduction using machine learning on electronic health records
Funder_Names: UF Informatics Institute; National Institutes of Health - National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIH/NIAID) grant #R01AI141810
Population_Description: Adult patients with Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infection (BSI-KP): 1,398 patients (1,271 inpatient, 118 outpatient); median Charlson comorbidity index 4.00; 50.7% of inpatients transferred to ICU
Top_Predictive_Features: Boosted logistic regression effect sizes (expert-chosen set, ICU population): Betalactam resistance in Klebsiella before or upon the infection (OR 10.12); HIV/AIDS (2.83); Amikacin use upon the infection (2.63); Tobramycin use upon the infection (2.34); Carbapenem resistance in Klebsiella upon the infection (2.23); Ethnicity group - not hispanic (2.06); Infection source - throat/lung (1.78); Vancomycin use upon the infection (1.76); Carbapenem resistance in non-Klebsiella organisms before or upon the infection (1.74); Fluoroquinolone resistance in Klebsiella upon the infection (1.68)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: qPitt score: AUROC 0.631 (whole population), 0.589 (ICU). Expert-chosen input set - LASSO 0.778, decision tree 0.684, decision tree depth=6 0.686, random forest 0.761, boosted logistic regression 0.801 (best; sensitivity 0.750, specificity 0.740; ICU 0.726/0.689/0.684), support vector machine 0.623. Full input set - LASSO 0.856, decision tree 0.791, decision tree depth=6 0.792, random forest 0.881, boosted logistic regression 0.885 (best; sensitivity 0.809, specificity 0.849; ICU 0.854/0.810/0.810), support vector machine 0.724. Emulated external validation (boosted logistic regression): AUROC 0.888, sensitivity 0.741, specificity 0.901; ICU 0.922/0.773/0.969
Best_Performing_Model: Boosted logistic regression (BLR)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: All patients (N=1,389); 30-day mortality=15.8% (189/1,389)
Specificity_Population_Set: All patients (N=1,389); 30-day mortality=15.8% (189/1,389)
AUROC_Population_Set: All patients (N=1,389); 30-day mortality=15.8% (189/1,389)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Emulated external validation is reported: clinics in the 322 zip code (Duval County) were held out of training and used for testing, with results reported for the whole and ICU populations; the authors note the model is not yet deployed in clinical care
Reported_Limitations: No data available outside Florida (mitigated by emulated external validation in the Duval/Jacksonville area); all ICD-10 codes converted to ICD-9, an often ambiguous conversion that can introduce measurement error; the prediction model is not causal by design and may retain colliders and confounding bias, so counterfactuals cannot be used seamlessly for interventions
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Counterfactual use of the model is flagged as unsafe: risk recalculation by changing variables (e.g. using a different antibiotic) is not guaranteed to be correct, so counterfactuals cannot be used seamlessly for interventions
Sample_Size: 1,398 adult patients with BSI-KP
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared.
Inclusion_Criteria: UF Health adult patients (18+ years) admitted at inpatient or outpatient clinics with BSI diagnosis (ICD-9 790.7, 995.91, 995.92, 038.xx); at least two years of medical history; antibiogram result within 7 days of BSI-KP diagnosis
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: University of Florida (UF) Integrated Data Repository (IDR)
Dataset_Size: 1,398 patients in the study population (1,271 inpatient / 118 outpatient); model analysis set n=1,389; 266 distinct diagnostic codes above the set frequency
Ethnicity_Details: Race - White 806 (63.4%) / Black-Other 465 (36.6%) inpatient; 77 (65.3%) / 41 (34.8%) outpatient; ethnicity group (not hispanic) used as a model variable
Geographic_Representativeness: Single health system in Florida; no data outside Florida; external validation emulated on clinics in one zip code area (322, Duval County, Jacksonville)
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood; urine
Primary_AMR_Outcome: 30-day mortality following BSI-KP diagnosis; antimicrobial resistance profiles (betalactam, carbapenem, aminoglycoside, fluoroquinolone, sulfonamide resistance in Klebsiella) are predictors, not outcomes
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP); other members of the Enterobacteriaceae family
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycosides; Betalactams; Carbapenems; Fluoroquinolones; Sulfonamides
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin; Carbapenem; Cefazolin; Ceftriaxone; Piperacillin; Amikacin; Tobramycin; Trimethoprim; Ceftazidime
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Antibiotic resistance and multi-drug resistance (MDR) prevalence estimated from the antibiogram test performed before or upon BSI-KP diagnosis, stratified by Klebsiella species and other organisms
AI_Purpose: Develop a machine learning prediction model of BSI-KP 30-day mortality from EHR data for general wards and the ICU, to improve on the qPitt score and support clinical decision-making
Num_Models_Compared: 7 (qPitt score baseline plus 6 machine learning models: LASSO, decision tree, decision tree depth=6, random forest, boosted logistic regression, support vector machine)
Feature_Engineering: All ICD codes at five-digit granularity present with at least 10% frequency; antibiogram results; medication prescriptions; comorbidities
Feature_Selection_Method: Expert-chosen variable selection (selected by the co-authors, supported by literature evidence); full set of ICD codes present with at least 10% frequency
Num_Features_Total: 266 distinct diagnostic codes above the set frequency
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search within the bootstrapping on cost (0.001-10) and gamma (2^-8 to 2^4)
Other_Metrics: AUROC, sensitivity and specificity (out-of-bag bootstrapping, 25 samples), compared with Bengio's and Nadeau's corrected t-test; odds ratios with 95% CI for predictors
Baseline_Method: qPitt bacteremia score embedded in a logistic regression
Baseline_Performance: AUROC 0.631 in the whole study population, 0.589 in the ICU stays
Internal_Validation: Out-of-bag bootstrapping (25 samples)
Train_Test_Split: Emulated external validation: 19.4% of data points (269/1,389) held out by clinic zip code area (322)
CV_Folds: 25 out-of-bag bootstrap samples (no k-fold cross-validation reported)
External_Validation_Description: Emulated external validation: data from clinics in the 322 zip code (Duval County, Jacksonville metropolitan area) removed from training and saved for testing (269/1,389 data points, 19.4%); boosted logistic regression AUROC 0.888, sensitivity 0.741, specificity 0.901 in the whole population and AUROC 0.922, sensitivity 0.773, specificity 0.969 in the ICU population
Overfitting_Method: Out-of-bag bootstrapping (25 samples); emulated external validation
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Decision rules / surrogate tree; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Beta-lactamase resistance in Klebsiella before/upon infection was the strongest predictor of 30-day mortality (OR 10.12, CI 3.28-40.39); the qPitt score (OR 1.53), infection source of throat/lung (OR 1.78) and resistance to other antibiotics also predicted death; in the full ICD code model, do-not-resuscitate status was the strongest predictor (OR 17.01)
Generalisability_Details: Models generalize well in the emulated external validation across clinics in other zip-code areas, with putative covariate and outcome distribution shifts; data were not available outside Florida
Maturity_Evidence: Emulated external validation on held-out clinics (322 zip code, Duval County): boosted logistic regression AUROC 0.888 / sensitivity 0.741 / specificity 0.901; ICU AUROC 0.922 / sensitivity 0.773 / specificity 0.969
Integration_Point: At BSI-KP diagnosis for adult inpatients/ICU patients, to compute 30-day mortality risk and support judicious prescribing of last-resort antibiotics
End_User_Described: clinicians
Barriers_List: Model is not causal by design; counterfactual risk recalculation not guaranteed correct; residual confounding and collider bias; data only from Florida; ICD-10 to ICD-9 conversion measurement error
Facilitators_List: Interpretable model usable in routine clinical settings
Future_Directions: Attach a more solid causal structure to the machine learning to develop an interventional model and optimize patient survival
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Boosted logistic regression effect sizes (odds ratios)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Beta-lactam resistance in Klebsiella before or upon infection (OR 10.12) and the do-not-resuscitate ICD-9-CM V49.86 code (OR 17.01) were the strongest predictors; acetaminophen use was associated with decreased risk
Limitation_Categories: Geographic generalisability (data only from Florida); ontology conversion / measurement error; non-causal model with residual confounding and collider bias
Data_Quality_Concerns: ICD ontology conversion (ICD-10 to ICD-9) is often ambiguous and can affect modelling, introducing measurement errors
Reporting_Clarity: Clear metrics reporting (AUROC, sensitivity, specificity with SDs from 25 bootstrap samples); confidence intervals given only for model odds ratios; no code or data availability statement

Title: PhageLeads: Rapid Assessment of Phage Therapeutic Suitability Using an Ensemble Machine Learning Approach
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Ministry of Higher Education of Malaysia (Program Konsortium Kecemerlangan Penyelidikan)
Population_Description: Phage protein sequences from NCBI RefSeq: 188,080 protein sequences from 7686 phage genomes for training (from 8368 phage GenBank files, 772,938 CDS); 45,231 protein sequences from 63 phage genomes (dated after March 2018) for validation; 423 phages (240 temperate, 183 lytic) in the lifestyle dataset. No human/patient subjects.
Data_Source_Other: NCBI RefSeq public database (phage complete genomes in GenBank format)
Top_Predictive_Features: Reduced tripeptide frequencies (50.32% of total features), dipeptide frequencies (33.54%), reduced dipeptide frequencies (9.58%), generic protein features (6.56%). Ranking by feature importance calculated from the XGBoost module.
All_Models_Evaluated: Five temperate-marker XGBoost predictors within the PhageLeads ensemble — validation MCC (accuracy, F1): integrase 0.92 (0.99, 0.92), Cro/CI 0.71 (0.99, 0.71), immunity repressor 0.87 (0.99, 0.86), ParA 0.76 (0.99, 0.75), antirepressor 0.92 (0.99, 0.92). Integrated lifestyle classification on the 423-phage lifestyle dataset: MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1-score 0.95 (16 mispredictions: 7 FP, 9 FN). Baseline BACPHLIP: 7 erroneous predictions on the same dataset. Random 10-fold CV MCCs: integrase 0.97, Cro/CI 0.91, immunity 0.96, ParA 0.90, antirepressor 0.94; clustered CV: 0.81, 0.16, 0.58, 0.44, 0.64 respectively.
Best_Performing_Model: PhageLeads ensemble lifestyle classification (XGBoost temperate-marker predictors) — highest on the review's primary metric (MCC): 0.92 on the phage lifestyle dataset (accuracy 0.96, F1-score 0.95)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Phage lifestyle dataset (423 phages: 240 temperate, 183 lytic), compiled by Mavrich and Hatfull
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation via 10-fold cross-validation plus validation on an independent external dataset (423-phage lifestyle dataset compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull, not used in training): MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95. This independent external validation supports level 3.
Reported_Limitations: Ambiguously annotated proteins in databases (some Cro/CI annotated as 'transcriptional regulators' or 'repressor', integrases as 'DNA-binding protein'/'recombinase', ParA as 'Chromosome partitioning protein'), some protein classes removed due to consistent misannotation; lifestyle information from literature reviews not completely dependable and may bias models (hence no lifestyle info used in training); clustered 10-fold CV revealed low conservation for ParA (0.44) and Cro/CI (0.16) markers.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Lytic phages found to carry AMR or virulence genes are unsuitable for therapeutic use: five of 183 lytic phages encoded virulence proteins (increased serum survival proteins ISS, Type III secretion system effectors, Cytolethal distending toxins, Shiga toxins, NleG effectors), one encoded both chloramphenicol resistance (CatA1) and ISS, posing risk of adverse effects / gene transduction into host genomes.
Reviewer_Notes: Phage genomics/bioinformatics study developing the PhageLeads ensemble XGBoost tool to predict phage temperate markers and screen for AMR/virulence genes (via ABRicate) for therapeutic phage selection. Best model = PhageLeads lifestyle classification (MCC 0.92, acc 0.96, F1 0.95) validated on the external 423-phage lifestyle dataset. No patient/clinical data; AMR aspect is detection of AMR/virulence genes in phage genomes. Data from NCBI RefSeq (training 188,080 proteins/7686 genomes; validation 45,231 proteins/63 genomes). Web-deployed (www.phageleads.dk).
Unresolved_Items: Best_Performing_Model unit: the paper's best model on its primary (training) dataset would be the individual temperate-marker predictors (integrase/antirepressor MCC 0.92), but the paper's headline application and its reported lifestyle accuracy are for the integrated ensemble lifestyle classifier; I coded the ensemble lifestyle classification (MCC 0.92, acc 0.96, F1 0.95) as the best-performing model. Clinical_Maturity_Level 3 rests on the independent external lifestyle dataset.
Sample_Size: Training dataset: 188,080 protein sequences from 7686 phage genomes (genomes, not patients)
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared — 'The authors declare that there are no conﬂicts of interest.'
Exclusion_Criteria: Data-level exclusions: proteins <30 amino acids removed; hypothetical proteins and proteins with unclear annotations removed; ambiguously annotated proteins (e.g. DNA binding protein, transcription regulator, repressors, DNA partitioning proteins without subunits) removed from respective datasets.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype
Data_Source_Name: NCBI RefSeq (phage complete genomes)
Dataset_Size: Training: 188,080 protein sequences from 7686 phage genomes; Validation: 45,231 protein sequences from 63 phage genomes; Lifestyle dataset: 423 phages
Geographic_Representativeness: Global public repository data: 8368 phage genomes from 17 families used to train PhageLeads; no geographic framing reported.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Presence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes and virulence genes in therapeutic phage genomes, detected via the ABRicate tool; and classification of phage lifestyle (temperate vs lytic) based on predicted presence of temperate markers (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor).
Pathogens: None as study target — the subjects are bacteriophages (therapeutic phage candidates); no specific bacterial pathogen is the outcome organism
Drug_Classes: Phenicols (chloramphenicol resistance gene detected)
Specific_Antibiotics: Chloramphenicol (resistance gene CatA1, chloramphenicol O-acetyltransferase, detected in Stx2 converting phage vB_EcoP_24B)
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Presence/absence of AMR genes (detected by ABRicate comparing predicted ORFs against NCBI, CARD, ARG-ANNOT, Resfinder, MEGARES, EcOH, PlasmidFinder, Ecoli_VF and VFDB databases) and presence/absence of temperate markers (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor) — gene-presence labels, not clinical MIC/phenotype thresholds.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To develop an online single-step tool (PhageLeads) using an ensemble of extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) predictors to determine the presence of temperate markers in phage candidates and, with ABRicate, screen for AMR and virulence genes, in order to rapidly select safe therapeutic phages.
Num_Models_Compared: 5 temperate-marker predictors within the PhageLeads ensemble (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor) plus the integrated lifestyle classification, compared against baseline BACPHLIP
Feature_Engineering: 1576 protein features extracted from protein sequences using custom scripts (per [26]): 400 dipeptide frequency, 100 reduced amino acid dipeptide frequency, 1000 reduced amino acid tripeptide frequency, 34 PROSITE domain features, and 42 generic protein features from the BioPython SeqUtils ProteinAnalysis module.
Feature_Selection_Method: Iterative feature reduction: for each round the 50 least-contributing features were removed until the minimal number was reached; final features selected based on Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) scores from testing each model on the test dataset. Overall selection driven by feature importance computed by the XGBoost module.
Num_Features_Selected: 626 unique features used for the final predictors (171 integrase, 90 Cro/CI, 59 immunity repressor, 18 ParA, 71 antirepressor; 1576 reduced per predictor to 350, 251, 142, 74, 201 respectively)
Class_Imbalance_Method: XGBoost 'scale positive weight' parameter (set = number of negative data / number of positive data) to compensate for unbalanced classes
Hyperparameter_Method: Prediction threshold tuning: iterating through incremental threshold values and selecting the threshold with the highest MCC on the training dataset (e.g. 0.252 integrase, 0.363 Cro/CI, 0.472 immunity, 0.03 ParA, 0.389 antirepressor)
Software_Libraries: XGBoost, scikit-learn (StratifiedKFold), python networkx, BioPython SeqUtils ProteinAnalysis, DIAMOND, cd-hit, ABRicate
Other_Metrics: Confusion matrix on lifestyle dataset (Lytic 177/7, Temperate 9/231); random 10-fold CV MCCs (integrase 0.97, Cro/CI 0.91, immunity 0.96, ParA 0.90, antirepressor 0.94); clustered 10-fold CV MCCs (integrase 0.81, antirepressor 0.64, immunity 0.58, ParA 0.44, Cro/CI 0.16); prediction speed 1.6 s/phage for PhageLeads, 8.1 s for gene detection, 2.3 s for BACPHLIP.
Baseline_Method: BACPHLIP (random forest-based phage lifestyle predictor using presence of 206 lysogeny markers via HMM sequence similarity)
Baseline_Performance: BACPHLIP made 7 erroneous predictions on the lifestyle dataset (vs PhageLeads' 16 mispredictions, 7 FP + 9 FN); authors attribute BACPHLIP's higher accuracy to its smaller training data (634 genomes, 5 families)
Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross-validation (two variants: generic random via scikit-learn StratifiedKFold, and clustered using cd-hit at 60% identity where proteins from the same clusters stay in the same bins)
External_Validation_Description: Independent external dataset: the 423-phage lifestyle dataset (240 temperate, 183 lytic) originally compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull [50], on which PhageLeads achieved MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95. Also a temporal hold-out validation set of 63 phage genomes dated after March 2018 (45,231 proteins).
Overfitting_Method: Feature reduction — iteratively removing the 50 least-contributing features per round to minimize overfitting probability and prediction time
Generalisability_Details: Clustered 10-fold cross-validation (cd-hit at 60% similarity, proteins from same clusters kept in same bins) assessed prediction of unseen protein clusters; clustered CV MCCs were lower (integrase 0.81, antirepressor 0.64, immunity 0.58, ParA 0.44, Cro/CI 0.16), indicating lower conservation for ParA and Cro/CI and the value of large training datasets.
Maturity_Evidence: Independent external validation on the 423-phage lifestyle dataset (compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull) achieving MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95 — evidence of external validation, hence level 3.
End_User_Described: Researchers / laboratory scientists assessing the therapeutic suitability of phages
Barriers_List: Ambiguously annotated proteins in databases; removal of some protein classes due to consistent misannotation; lifestyle information from literature reviews not completely dependable; low sequence conservation for ParA and Cro/CI markers limiting clustered-CV performance.
Future_Directions: Exploration of three-dimensional protein structures to resolve misannotations, in order to further improve PhageLeads performance; also applicable to predicting lysogenic markers for metagenomic contigs.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance scores calculated from the XGBoost module (used to select final features per predictor)
Limitation_Categories: Ambiguous protein annotations/misannotation; unreliable lifestyle labels from literature; low sequence conservation of specific markers (ParA, Cro/CI); false-positive temperate predictions in lytic phages.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Authors removed proteins <30 amino acids, hypothetical proteins, proteins with unclear annotations, and ambiguously annotated proteins (e.g. DNA binding protein, transcription regulator, repressors, DNA partitioning proteins without subunits) to reduce misclassification.

Title: Rapid, label-free pathogen identification system for multidrug-resistant bacterial wound infection detection on military members in the battlefield
Country_Countries: United States of America (Optowares, Inc., Woburn, Massachusetts; US military members)
AI_Application_Type: AI Signal Processing; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Funder_Names: DHA SBIR Program; U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command (USAMRDC); U.S. Air Force Material Command
Population_Description: 12 bacterial strains - six multidrug-resistant (MDR) and six antimicrobial-susceptible strains representing six species of the ESKAPEE group (Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter cloacae, Escherichia coli); all obtained from ATCC and cultured in a BSL-2 facility; bacteria spiked into wound-like samples; no human subjects / patient data
Data_Source_Other: In-house ATR-FTIR spectral data generated from cultured ATCC bacterial strains (six MDR and six susceptible) spiked into wound-like samples under laboratory conditions
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: SVMDA (sum vector machine discriminant analysis) classification model: >95% averaged analytical sensitivity and specificity for the six bacterial species (Fig 6A); 100% accuracy in classifying species identity in four unknown samples (Fig 6B). A PLSDA (partial least square discriminant analysis) pre-model was built first to check class boundaries, but SVMDA is the reported classification model
Best_Performing_Model: SVMDA (sum vector machine discriminant analysis) - the only classification model reported; >95% averaged analytical sensitivity and specificity; 100% accuracy on four unknown samples (metric used: analytical sensitivity/specificity and species classification accuracy)
Accuracy_Value: 100% (species identity classification in four unknown samples)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Four unknown samples (spectra from samples including those shown in Fig 3)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Six bacterial species (ESKAPEE group strains)
Specificity_Population_Set: Six bacterial species (ESKAPEE group strains)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Proof-of-concept laboratory study: system tested on spiked laboratory samples at the bench (under laboratory environment); no clinical deployment, external validation or prospective evaluation reported

Conflicts_of_Interest: none declared

Dataset_Size: 12 strains (six MDR, six antimicrobial-susceptible); ATR spectra of dried cell pellets at 109-1012 cfu/mL before and after antimicrobial incubation

Title: Rapid Identification of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Using MALDI-TOF MS and Machine Learning from over 20,000 Clinical Isolates
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort; Prospective cohort
Funder_Names: Taiwan Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST109-2113-M-039-001); China Medical University (CMU109-MF-04); China Medical University Hospital (DMR-109-148 and DMR-110-139)
Population_Description: Clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates (MSSA and MRSA) from patient specimens. Development set: 8,258 CMUH cases (4,309 MRSA, 3,949 MSSA) from the China Medical University Hospital clinical microbiology laboratory, January 2018 to June 2021. External set: an additional 12,101 mass spectra collected 2018-2020 from four hospitals (FYH, NTUH-YL, SHH, HTCH).
Top_Predictive_Features: MALDI-TOF MS spectral peaks (m/z) ranked by SHAP. Top-ranked feature: m/z 6,590 to 6,599; then m/z 5,520 to 5,529; m/z 3,030 to 3,039; m/z 3,760 to 3,769; and m/z 6,550 to 6,559.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: 10 ML algorithms (light gradient boosting machine [LightGBM], gradient boosting, logistic regression, extreme gradient boosting, extra trees, random forest, linear SVM, decision tree, K neighbors and naive Bayes) each run with 5 bin sizes (1-Da, 5-Da, 10-Da, 15-Da, 20-Da) with 5-fold cross-validation, ranked by F1 (Table S1). Selected combination: LightGBM with 10-Da binning. Reported AUC/sensitivity/specificity: CMUH 2018-2019 training 0.91/0.82/0.85; CMUH 2020-2021 prospective test 0.91/0.83/0.85; FYH 0.78/0.83/0.65; NTUH-YL 0.88/0.72/0.88; SHH 0.85/0.74/0.80; HTCH 0.86/0.83/0.73.
Best_Performing_Model: LightGBM with 10-Da binning - the combination selected by the F1 score from 10 ML algorithms x 5 bin sizes; on the primary CMUH data set it reached AUC 0.91, sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.85
Sensitivity_Population_Set: CMUH 2020-2021 prospective test set (1,311 MRSA and 1,145 MSSA isolates)
Specificity_Population_Set: CMUH 2020-2021 prospective test set (1,311 MRSA and 1,145 MSSA isolates)
AUROC_Population_Set: CMUH 2020-2021 prospective test set, approximately 2,500 isolates (the primary data set under study); the same AUC of 0.91 is reported for the CMUH 2018-2019 training set
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: A prospective test on approximately 2,500 CMUH isolates (January 2020 to June 2021, AUC 0.91) plus external validation on more than 12,000 isolates from four other hospitals (AUC 0.78-0.88); no CDS integration or routine clinical use is reported.
Reported_Limitations: The rapid screening assay cannot replace more sensitive and specific methods of MRSA detection; performance was somewhat lower in NTUH-YL, SHH and HTCH than CMUH, and significantly lower at FYH (AUC 0.78) owing to a specificity of 0.65 attributed to Vitek 2 misclassification of MRSA as MSSA.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: No formal harm assessment. The authors state the rapid screening assay cannot replace more sensitive and specific methods of MRSA detection, and report misclassification at FYH where strains predicted as MRSA were identified as MSSA in the FYH AST reports.
Sample_Size: 8,258 CMUH cases (4,309 MRSA and 3,949 MSSA) for the primary data set; 5,802 CMUH spectra used for model training and internal validation; 12,101 further mass spectra from four external hospitals (20,359 clinical isolates in total)
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared - "The authors declare no conflict of interest." and "We declare no competing interests."
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: De-identified MALDI-TOF MS data deposited in the Zenodo database (record 5502292); clinical data sets from five hospitals (CMUH, FYH, NTUH-YL, SHH, HTCH)
Dataset_Size: 20,359 clinical isolates in total (5,802 CMUH spectra for training/internal validation plus 12,101 external mass spectra)
Geographic_Representativeness: Four external hospitals chosen as representatives of North Taiwan (SHH), Middle Taiwan (FYH), South Taiwan (NTUH-YL) and East Taiwan (HTCH) plus CMUH in Middle Taiwan - all five sites are in Taiwan.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Clinical samples were collected from blood, cerebrospinal fluid, ascites, pleural fluid, body fluid, sputum, tissue, bile, stool, urine, and other clinical specimens.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus: binary discrimination of clinical isolates as MRSA or MSSA from MALDI-TOF mass spectra, without conventional AST.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus - methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA)
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (methicillin; penicillinase-resistant penicillins)
Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin (used in the protein-ligand docking simulation); oxacillin and cefoxitin are referred to only in a cited report of false-susceptible results
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: The MRSA/MSSA label is the routine clinical AST result: all MSSA and MRSA strains were confirmed by a Phoenix AST system (CMUH, NTUH-YL, SHH, HTCH) and a VITEK2 AST system (FYH); the ML model predicts this binary label from MALDI-TOF spectra.
AI_Purpose: Machine learning (LightGBM) applied to MALDI-TOF MS spectra to map peak features onto antibiotic resistance and rapidly discriminate MRSA from MSSA, with SHAP-based interpretation of the top features and docking simulation of the leading marker.
Num_Models_Compared: 10 ML algorithms, each run with five bin sizes (50 algorithm/bin-size combinations compared with 5-fold cross-validation; Table S1)
Feature_Engineering: MALDI-TOF MS raw data extraction, resampling to a fixed 1 Da sampling rate, TopHat baseline correction, square-root transformation, Savitzky-Golay smoothing, conversion to m/z ratios over 2,000-20,000 Da, min-max scaling to 0-1, and binning of peaks into bins with averaged intensities.
Feature_Selection_Method: Peak binning (peaks in the same m/z bin treated as one attribute, intensities averaged); bin size and ML algorithm selected by F1 score; SHAP used to rank feature importance.
Num_Features_Total: Not stated numerically - the binned m/z attributes span the m/z 2,000 to 20,000 Da range at the chosen bin size (10 Da in the final model)
Num_Features_Selected: Top 10 molecular features reported by SHAP (Fig. 2); the classifier itself retains all binned m/z attributes
Software_Libraries: LightGBM (light gradient boosting machine); SHAP; Phyre2 for homology modelling; PyRX version 0.8 with PyMol for docking simulation
Other_Metrics: F1 score (used only as the criterion for selecting bin size and algorithm; no numerical F1 value is reported)
Baseline_Method: Head-to-head comparison of five bin sizes across 10 ML algorithms under 5-fold cross-validation, ranked by F1 score (Table S1); no non-ML or clinical baseline is reported.
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation used to compare bin size and algorithm combinations, with the CMUH 2018-2019 spectra serving as the training and internal validation set.
Train_Test_Split: Training: CMUH cases from 2018 to 2019. Testing: the CMUH 2020-2021 prospective data set and the four external hospital data sets.
External_Validation_Description: An additional 12,101 mass spectra collected during 2018-2020 from Feng Yuan Hospital (FYH), National Taiwan University Hospital Yunlin Branch (NTUH-YL), Shuang Ho Hospital (SHH) and Hualien Tzu Chi Hospital (HTCH); AUC ranged from 0.78 to 0.88.
Overfitting_Method: Generalisability addressed by collecting data from five clinical sites with retrospective and prospective tests rather than by formal overfitting diagnostics.
Clinical_Insights: The top feature at m/z 6,590 to 6,599 was identified as UPF0337 protein SACOL1680, a mutated form of UPF0337 protein SA1452 of MSSA; docking suggests methicillin binds SA1452 but not SACOL1680, a possible mechanism of methicillin resistance.
Generalisability_Details: Isolates were collected from five clinical sites with retrospective and prospective tests specifically to ensure ML model generalization.
Maturity_Evidence: Prospective test on approximately 2,500 CMUH isolates (2020-2021) and validation on more than 12,000 isolates from four external clinical sites; no CDS integration or routine clinical use reported.
Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory workflow: after MALDI-TOF MS analysis of cultured clinical strains the spectra are classified as MRSA or MSSA by the ML model within about 10 s, instead of the 18 h to 48 h needed by conventional AST methods.
End_User_Described: Physicians - the model can be integrated into current clinical workflows and support physicians in prescribing proper antibiotic treatments
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Following culture, MALDI-TOF analysis of the clinical strain, then the ML model classifies the spectrum as MRSA or MSSA within about 10 s (Fig. 1b), replacing the 18 h to 48 h conventional AST step.
Barriers_List: The rapid screening assay cannot replace more sensitive and specific methods of MRSA detection; different data formats for identification and AST results across sites required custom data-processing pipelines; lower specificity at FYH (0.65).
Facilitators_List: The MALDI-TOF MS-based ML model can be highly integrated into current clinical workflows and save time for physicians seeking proper antibiotic treatment.
Future_Directions: Integration of the MALDI-TOF MS-based ML model into current clinical workflows to save time for physicians, as a rapid screening assay that complements rather than replaces more sensitive and specific MRSA detection methods.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 1 (MALDI-TOF MS spectral peaks); the AST phenotype is used only as the outcome label
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapely Additive exPlanations) values
Novel_Predictors_Details: First discovery and validation of MRSA markers at this scale; the top feature at m/z 6,590 to 6,599 was identified as a protein whose sequence had not been identified with a reliable bottom-up proteomics method.
Limitation_Categories: Assay cannot replace more sensitive and specific MRSA detection methods; lower model performance at some external sites, with FYH specificity of 0.65 attributed to Vitek 2 misclassification; performance somewhat lower at NTUH-YL, SHH and HTCH than CMUH.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Different clinical sites use different data formats for identification and AST results, requiring regular expressions and text mining to pair clinical information with MALDI-TOF MS data; data preparation and cleaning were needed to ensure MS data quality across the five sites.
Reporting_Clarity: Data sizes and performance by clinical site are reported in Table 1; the comparison of bin sizes and ML algorithms is relegated to supplementary Table S1, and no confidence intervals or F1 values are printed.

Title: Risk predict model using multi-drug resistant organism infection from Neuro-ICU patients: a retrospective cohort study
Funder_Names: Research Fund of Guizhou Provincial Health Commission; Science and Technology Joint Funds of Zunyi Science and Technology Bureau & The First People's Hospital of Zunyi
Population_Description: 297 consecutive Neuro-ICU patients discharged from a grade-A tertiary hospital in Guizhou province, China (Jan 2018-Apr 2020); 131 infected with MDRO (infection rate 44.11%).
Top_Predictive_Features: Multivariable (binary logistic regression) independent risk factors: antibiotics (OR 8.064 - the most important factor), artery blood pressure monitoring (OR 7.479), tracheal intubation (OR 6.140), pneumonia (OR 5.755), fever (OR 5.209), albumin (OR 0.920, protective/higher level lower risk). Importance method: adjusted odds ratios from multiple logistic regression (Table 2).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Binary logistic regression risk prediction model (five clinical predictors + albumin); reported AUC 0.887 (95% CI 0.849-0.925), sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 78.9%, Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.831, Youden index 0.652, cutoff 0.476. No comparator models were evaluated.
Best_Performing_Model: Binary logistic regression risk prediction model (the only model developed and evaluated; decision metric = AUC 0.887 on the 297-patient Neuro-ICU cohort)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Neuro-ICU patients, n = 297 (model construction cohort)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Neuro-ICU patients, n = 297 (model construction cohort)
Specificity_Population_Set: Neuro-ICU patients, n = 297 (model construction cohort)
AUROC_Population_Set: Neuro-ICU patients, n = 297 (model construction cohort)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Single-centre retrospective development of a logistic risk model evaluated only by apparent ROC performance on the same 297 patients; the authors state there was no further verification of the prediction model and no assessment of its impact on actual MDRO incidence.
Reported_Limitations: Single-centre retrospective design, data from one hospital in one province that cannot represent the region or country (possible bias); small sample (small Neuro-ICU population, only two years of data); no further validation of the prediction model and no investigation of its impact on actual MDRO infection incidence.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethics committee approval obtained (2017-215); patient information anonymised and deidentified before analysis so informed consent was waived; research performed per the Declaration of Helsinki. No AI-specific governance or risk discussion.
Sample_Size: 297 patients (131 MDRO-infected, 166 non-MDRO)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients aged >= 18 years; patients staying in the ICU for >= 48 h; patients who were transferred to the general ward after being transferred from the ICU.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients with incomplete data or an MDRO infection that has occurred.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 297 patients, 131 MDRO-infected (infection rate 44.11%)
Geographic_Representativeness: Authors state the single tertiary hospital in one province cannot represent the actual situation in the region or the whole country; patients lost to transfer or death meant the exact infection rate could not be calculated.
Specimen_Type_Detail: sputum, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and midstream urine
Primary_AMR_Outcome: MDRO (multi-drug-resistant organism) infection in Neuro-ICU patients
Pathogens: Acinetobacter baumannii; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Pseudomonas pyocyaneum; Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; Escherichia coli
Drug_Classes: sulfonamides, quinolones and β-lactam antibiotics
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDRO defined per the 2010 international standardized definition of MDROs jointly proposed by the United States and other countries; patients grouped by whether they were infected or colonized with MDRO, judged from aseptically collected sputum, blood, cerebrospinal fluid and midstream urine samples.
AI_Purpose: Develop and validate a risk prediction model for MDRO infection in Neuro-ICU patients from independent risk factors, to evaluate risk and provide reference for preventive treatment and nursing intervention.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single binary logistic regression model; no comparator models developed or benchmarked)
Feature_Engineering: Data collection items designed from literature/expert discussion: general demographic information (gender, age), treatment circumstances (invasive operation, level of consciousness), laboratory indicators and the patient's own physical conditions; no engineered transformations described.
Feature_Selection_Method: Univariate analysis followed by multivariate (binary logistic regression) screening of risk factors
Software_Libraries: SPSS 20.0
Other_Metrics: Youden index 0.652; optimal cutoff value 0.476
Clinical_Insights: Antibiotic use was the most important predictor (OR 8.064); invasive artery blood pressure monitoring and tracheal intubation destroy physiological integrity and local immune function; lower serum albumin associated with higher infection risk; fever and pneumonia also predictors; GCS severity score did not predict MDRO.
Data_Repository: Supplementary material of the online article (Springer Nature, DOI 10.1038/s41598-023-42522-2)
Generalisability_Details: Authors note data from one tertiary hospital in one province cannot represent the region or the whole country, that the cohort excludes patients transferred out or who died, and that the exact infection rate could not be calculated.
Maturity_Evidence: Development and apparent-performance evaluation on the same 297-patient cohort (ROC AUC 0.887); the authors state there was no further verification of the prediction model and no assessment of its impact on actual MDRO incidence - level 1.
Integration_Point: Screening of patients for multidrug-resistant bacteria on admission to the neurologic intensive care unit
End_User_Described: physicians, pharmacists, and nurses
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Authors propose multidisciplinary coordination - clinicians and pharmacists co-managing therapeutic medication, routine MDR screening after ICU admission, and nurses active in day-to-day MDRO prevention and management.
Future_Directions: Reinforce multidisciplinary coordination so physicians, pharmacists and nurses play a more active role; make MDR screening a routine part of post-admission care; pharmacists to guide standardised medication regimens; nurses to lead day-to-day MDRO prevention.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Adjusted odds ratios (OR, 95% CI) from the multiple logistic regression model; the paper ranks antibiotics as the most important factor
Novel_Predictors_Details: The authors contrast their findings with the past: their model identified artery blood pressure monitoring and tracheal intubation, whereas previous work reported urinary tubes and feeding tubes as the main indwelling instruments associated with MDRO infection.
Limitation_Categories: Single-centre retrospective design / non-representative setting; small sample size; no validation of the model and no assessment of its clinical impact.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Patients transferred to other hospitals or who died during ICU stay were excluded from the analysis, so the exact MDRO infection rate could not be calculated.
