Title: Extending outbreak investigation with machine learning and graph theory: Benefits of new tools with application to a nosocomial outbreak of a multidrug-resistant organism
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: Swiss National Science Foundation
Population_Description: Patients of a 900-bed tertiary-care university hospital in Bern, Switzerland, whose medical records were generated during the first 2 years of the VRE outbreak: 560 VRE-positive patients (cases) compared with 86,684 controls tested or untested (N = 87,244); all patients including children were labelled
Age_Mean_Median: VRE positive: median 73 years [IQR 63 –82]; VRE negative or not tested: median 58 years [IQR 33 –75]
Data_Source_Other: Hospital IT systems (time and resource management system and device-tracking systems) supplying employee-contact, room and medical-device records
Top_Predictive_Features: Decision-tree importance: No. of different antibiotics 0.214; Charlson score, mean 0.191; No. of rooms 0.145; Age 0.107; Charlson score (last) 0.104; No. of hospitalizations 0.067; No. of surgeries, all stays 0.066; Length of stay (per 5 days) 0.064; ICU stay (at any time) 0.020; Sex 0.011; Patient had surgery at any time 0.010
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Task_Type_Other: Network graph / eigenvector centrality analysis of transmission pathways
All_Models_Evaluated: 1) Multivariable logistic regression (risk factors: age aOR 1.4 per 10 years; ICU stay aOR 1.5; Charlson score aOR 1.1; no. of different antibiotics aOR 1.6; no. of rooms aOR 1.1, all P < .001; no discrimination metric reported). 2) Decision tree, maximum depth 6 (feature importance: antibiotics 0.214, Charlson mean 0.191, rooms 0.145; confirmed the logistic-regression findings). 3) Network graph / eigenvector centrality (screening efficiency 40.0% fewer screenings, 95% CI 17.3 – 54.6; screening benefit 102 additional VRE-positive patients detected, 95% CI 66 – 138, versus proximity-based screening).
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Validation was performed within the same hospital: the oncology ward screened all patients every week, giving a ground truth against which the model's weekly predicted VRE-positive cases were compared with the observed cases; no external (other-hospital) validation was performed.
Reported_Limitations: Monocentric study, not validated against data from another hospital; incomplete data -- physician interactions not documented so employee contacts limited to nursing staff, and only IT-tracked (larger, non-portable) medical devices included; no fully integrated hospital-wide data warehouse, which slowed implementation; interpretations require consideration of data-source maturity, scope of included sources and potential confounding.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Data-governance constraints rather than ethical harms: interactions documented by healthcare workers were limited to nursing employees because physician interactions are not recorded at that granularity, and only IT-tracked medical devices were included. The study was approved by the Cantonal Ethics Committee (Bern, Project ID no. 2020-00173).
Sample_Size: 560 VRE patients (cases) and 86,684 controls (patients), N = 87,244 patients
Conflicts_of_Interest: All authors report no conflicts of interest relevant to this article.
Sex_Distribution: VRE positive: male 346 (61.8%); VRE negative or not tested: male 44,019 (50.8%)
Inclusion_Criteria: All patients (including children) with VRE acquisition during the outbreak period January 1, 2018-December 31, 2019 were labelled VRE-positive (cases); all other patients, whether tested or not, were assumed VRE negative (controls). Data were electronic medical records from the first 2 years of the outbreak.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Project-specific data warehouse at Bern University Hospital (Inselspital), integrating electronic medical records from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2019
Dataset_Size: 87,244 patients: 560 VRE positive and 86,684 VRE negative or not tested
Geographic_Representativeness: Single tertiary-care university hospital in Bern, Switzerland (900-bed, 60,000 admissions and 380,000 patient days per year), covering the whole hospital; the authors note that validation against data from another hospital would have improved the study.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: VRE colonization (VRE-positive, that is colonized or infected with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium), modelled as a binary outcome (0 = no, 1 = yes)
Pathogens: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VRE), sequence type 796 (ST796) predominant; all subtypes analysed
Drug_Classes: Glycopeptide (vancomycin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary VRE positivity from electronic medical records: the dependent variable of the logistic regression was colonization (0 = no, 1 = yes); patients were labelled VRE-positive (cases) if they had VRE acquisition during the outbreak period and all other patients, whether tested or not, were assumed VRE negative (controls).
AI_Purpose: To improve existing nosocomial outbreak investigation by applying machine learning (decision tree) and graph-theoretical network analysis to identify risk factors for VRE colonization, determine which patients should be screened, and locate transmission hot spots (devices, rooms, employees), and to compare the resulting prioritised screening with traditional proximity-based contact screening.
Feature_Engineering: No bespoke feature construction: the classification tree was built with the same independent and dependent variables as the logistic regression (the variables in Table 1); a minority-class oversampling step produced equal numbers of positive and negative samples.
Feature_Selection_Method: Logistic regression: most parsimonious model by forward selection then backward deletion, P > .10 inclusion criterion; decision tree: covariate importance ranking used to reveal the most predictive variables
Class_Imbalance_Method: Minority class oversampling, resulting in equal numbers of positive and negative samples
Software_Libraries: Python 3.7: pyodbc, numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, networkx, pytorch, seaborn, bokeh, Holoviz, Holoviews; R version 3.5 or newer: data.table, ggplot2, tableone, survey
Other_Metrics: Decision-tree feature importance (Table 3); screening efficiency: 40.0% fewer screenings compared with the current gold standard (95% CI, 17.3 – 54.6); screening benefit: 102 (95% CI, 66 – 138) VRE-positive patients detected who were missed by proximity-based screening
Baseline_Method: Proximity-based contact screening, described as the current gold standard (patients screened if hospitalized in the same room and ward as a newly detected VRE-positive patient in the prior 7 days)
Internal_Validation: Model validation on the oncology ward, which screened all patients every week, so that for each week the predicted VRE-positive cases from the model could be compared with the observed cases (ground truth); performance summarised as screening efficiency and screening benefit relative to proximity-based screening.
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: The decision tree provided thresholds that split the data appropriately and allowed insights not apparent from the logistic regression: patients receiving antibiotics and those aged >55 years were at higher risk for colonization. The network analysis identified 3 pathways linking the 560 VRE cases (healthcare personnel, medical devices, patient rooms) and produced a daily hotspot list of rooms, devices and employees ordered by likelihood of being colonized.
Generalisability_Details: The method provides the basis for a smart contact-tracing system for the next outbreak, independent of pathogen, and potentially for data-driven outbreak monitoring; the authors add that data-science interpretations should consider data-source maturity, the scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: predictions compared with the oncology ward's weekly screening ground truth within the same hospital; the authors state the study was monocentric and could have been improved by validating against data from another hospital.
Integration_Point: Outbreak management: the daily hotspot list is sent to the organisational unit that disinfects rooms and medical devices, and the network-graph method produces a prioritised screening list for patients in place of proximity-based contact screening.
End_User_Described: The organisational unit involved in disinfecting rooms and medical devices, plus those deciding how to isolate patients and clean devices and rooms.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The new prioritised screening list derived from the network graph is compared with the current gold-standard proximity-based screening; the hotspot list orders devices, healthcare personnel and patient rooms by likelihood of being colonized so that isolation, disinfection and potential screening of personnel can be targeted.
Barriers_List: Lack of a fully integrated hospital-wide data warehouse, which slowed implementation; information on physicians and other key personnel absent from the time and resource management system, so employee contacts were limited to nursing staff; only IT-tracked (larger, non-portable) medical devices captured; data-source integration and operationalisation were the most time-consuming and resource-intensive steps; the popularity of machine-learning methods can lead to an analysis-driven approach ("85% of data science projects fail").
Facilitators_List: Availability of a hospital-wide, fully integrated data warehouse as a prerequisite for fast implementation and actionable results; a clear project mandate with metrics for success defined before the project started; data maturity, scope of included sources and consideration of confounding factors.
Future_Directions: A smart contact-tracing system for the next outbreak, independent of pathogen, and potentially data-driven outbreak monitoring; defining appropriate metrics at project initiation; validation against data from another hospital; consideration of data-source maturity, scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Decision-tree feature importance (the rank of the covariate in splitting the data set: the higher the importance, the earlier the covariate is used in the branching process)
Novel_Predictors_Details: The decision-tree analysis allowed insights not apparent from the logistic regression: patients receiving antibiotics and those aged >55 years were at higher risk for colonization; number of rooms stayed in and patient-device interactions highlighted environmental contamination as an important factor.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Decision tree with a maximum depth of 6 levels, motivated by the complex interactions and multiple collinearities seen in the fitted statistical models; collinear variables were not estimated in the multivariable logistic model (Table 2 note).
Limitation_Categories: Monocentric / single-institution design and lack of external validation; incomplete data on physician and other personnel contacts; only IT-tracked medical devices; no fully integrated hospital-wide data warehouse; data-source maturity, scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Interactions documented by healthcare workers were limited to nursing employees because physician interactions are not documented at that granularity for in-patient care; for medical devices only interactions tracked in the IT systems were included, limiting the study to larger, often non-portable devices.
Reporting_Clarity: The article reports models, variables, software and the validation ward clearly, but the computation of the screening-efficiency and screening-benefit metrics is deferred to the Supplementary Material, and no discrimination metric (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or AUC) is reported for any model.
Page_References: Article pp. 1–7 (journal pp. 246–252); methods pp. 2–3; Table 1 p. 2; Table 2 p. 4; results pp. 4–5; Table 3, Table 4, limitations and funding p. 6

F1_Population_Set: Held-out test set of the TB Portal dataset (20%; 1,009 CXR images)
AUROC_Population_Set: Held-out test set of the TB Portal dataset (20%; 1,009 CXR images)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Evidence stops at internal validation: the ensemble was trained on 80% of the TB Portal dataset and evaluated on a held-out 20% (1,009 CXR images) with no external dataset. The web application was tested on 760 further Portal images and by 33 physicians for usability, but no prospective clinical evaluation or CDS integration is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Fast image analysis gave relatively unstable results (a stated shortcoming); the Portal dataset does not contain all drug-resistance types documented in the clinical literature, so the model should be retrained with new data; the recommended regimen must be kept current with WHO/national guidelines or the software becomes a distraction.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: If the recommended treatment regimen is not kept up to date, the software ceases to be an aid and becomes a distraction for physicians.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not framed as an equity analysis, but the authors argue the low-cost mobile application suits practitioners in resource-constrained settings and may reduce unnecessary tests and procedures.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Developers are said to need to make such applications transparent, safe and compliant with privacy and ethical norms to earn trust; no formal governance or regulatory assessment is reported.
Reviewer_Notes: Judgement calls: (1) Study_Setting coded Tertiary / hospital - the AI development is in silico on a public image archive, but the application was implemented and evaluated with physicians at 14 large hospitals. (2) Study_Design also ticks Qualitative (acceptability / usability) because a 33-participant task-based SUS evaluation was run; that evaluation is quantitative in instrument but is the review vocabulary's only home for an acceptability/usability study. (3) Provider_Facing_Applications deliberately omits 'Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)' because the model predicts the drug-resistance class from CXR images, which is neither genotypic nor spectral; the same output is captured under Diagnosis / species identification. (4) Accuracy/F1/AUROC values are for the best model (experiment 16, multiclass: AUC 95.1, F-measure 94.8, accuracy 93.4 on the held-out 20% test set). The 96.1% figure quoted in the abstract/conclusion is the deployed web application's accuracy on 760 further Portal images, and the 96.7% in the abstract is the SUS score, not a model metric. (5) Sensitivity, specificity and PPV are coded No: the paper reports only AUC, F-measure and accuracy. (6) Software_Language is Not specified - only TensorFlow (library) and HTML/JavaScript (web front end) are named, never the modelling language. (7) Lifecycle_P5 is ticked because a working web application was built and used by 33 physicians, while Clinical_Maturity stays at level 2 for lack of external validation. (8) Subgroup/performance-disparity fields are coded No; the per-class accuracy breakdown (Figure 4, Table 6) is part of the classification result, not a demographic subgroup analysis.
Sample_Size: 5,039 CXR images in the primary dataset (4,030 training / 1,009 testing); 760 images in the web-application test; 33 physicians in the usability test
Conflicts_of_Interest: No competing interests declared: the authors state the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Frontal, AP or PA chest X-ray views held in the TB Portal dataset with a TB drug-resistance class assigned at data entry from the DST profile (five classes).
Exclusion_Criteria: Rifampicin-resistant (RR) and isoniazid-resistant (Hr) TB were not assigned to any TB Portals dataset and, lacking detailed DST profiles to reorganise them, were not part of the classifier implementation.
Data_Types_Used: Imaging
Data_Source_Name: TB Portal / Portal dataset (tbportals.niaid.nih.gov)
Dataset_Size: 5,039 CXR images (4,030 training; 1,009 testing)
Geographic_Representativeness: The training/testing data come from the TB Portal, an open global drug-resistant-TB image-sharing platform, so the images are not from one country; the usability evaluation was limited to 33 physicians in northeastern Thailand, and the authors note the Portal dataset does not contain all drug-resistance types seen in practice.
Specimen_Type_Detail: chest X-ray (CXR) images; frontal, AP or PA views
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multiclass classification of drug-resistance type from a single CXR image into five WHO categories: DS-TB, DR-TB, MDR-TB, pre-XDR-TB and XDR-TB.
Drug_Classes: Anti-tuberculosis drugs: first-line anti-TB drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin), fluoroquinolones, and group A anti-TB drugs (bedaquiline, linezolid).
Specific_Antibiotics: isoniazid, rifampicin, fluoroquinolone, bedaquiline, linezolid
AMR_Outcome_Definition: TB type assigned at data entry from the drug susceptibility test (DST) profile, per WHO 2021 criteria: DS-TB no resistance; MDR-TB resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin; pre-XDR-TB MDR-TB plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone; XDR-TB pre-XDR-TB plus resistance to one additional group A drug (bedaquiline or linezolid).
AI_Purpose: To build an embedded ensemble deep learning CAD system (TB-DRD-CXR) that classifies drug-resistant TB types from a single CXR image and returns a recommended treatment regimen so physicians have AI support for the drug-resistance diagnosis decision.
Num_Models_Compared: 8 (7 homogeneous CNN architectures plus the proposed heterogeneous ensemble in Table 2); 16 parameter-combination experiments in Table 4
Feature_Engineering: Lung segmentation (two-model ensemble: patch CNN plus custom U-Net with 64*64 patches and a 20% lung-patch threshold), downscaling/resizing/normalising and patch extraction, three augmentation groups (A1-Aug reflection and linear scaling, A2-Aug rotation (-10 to 10 degrees)/translation (0-5 pixels)/shear (0-30 degrees), A3-Aug PCA-based perturbation), and two learning-rate strategies (ADADELTA and cyclical learning rate).
Hyperparameter_Method: Manual setting of per-architecture batch sizes (EfficientNetV2B3 16, EfficientNetV2M 2, ConvNeXtSmall 8; 2, 3, 5, 12, 10 and 8 for the comparison CNNs), 200 epochs, and learning-rate strategy (ADADELTA vs cyclical learning rate).
Software_Libraries: TensorFlow (web application); custom U-Net architecture
Hardware_Details: Intel i7 2.1 GHz (8 core) CPU, 32 GB RAM, Tesla V100 GPU (16 GB GPU RAM)
Other_Metrics: Time-based efficiency (ET) 4.16 goals/minute and overall relative efficiency (ORE) 100% for the web application; System Usability Scale (SUS) score 96.7; model size (MB), training time (minutes) and testing time (seconds per dataset) in Table 2; correct / wrong classification counts in Tables 1 and 6.
Baseline_Method: Homogeneous single-CNN and ensemble baselines: DenseNet201, ResNet101, NASNetMobile, EfficientNetB7, EfficientNetV2B3, EfficientNetV2M and ConvNeXtSmal (Table 2), plus the 'defender' configuration with no segmentation, no augmentation, ADADELTA and UWA (Table 4).
Baseline_Performance: Proposed method vs the CNN baselines: +28.8% (DenseNet201), +93.4% (NASNetMobile), +2.99% (EfficientNetB7), +48.0% (EfficientNetV2B3), +4.4% (EfficientNetV2M) and +7.6% (ConvNeXtSmal) accuracy; on average 30.6% more accurate than the state-of-the-art methods; within Table 4 segmentation added 25.8%, augmentation 8.1%, CLR 4.2% and HyVaN-AMIS 2.3% accuracy over their defender settings.
Internal_Validation: Hold-out test set: 80% training / 20% testing, 200 epochs
Overfitting_Method: Data augmentation (A1-Aug, A2-Aug, A3-Aug) to enlarge the training set
Clinical_Insights: Grad-CAM heatmaps are read clinically: innermost lung area for DR-TB, upper regions of both lungs for MDR-TB, middle-to-lower innermost area for Pre-XDR-TB, and the lower innermost areas of both lungs for XDR-TB; the model uses all six lung areas for non-TB classification.
Generalisability_Details: The authors state the model should be retrained with new data because the Portal dataset does not contain all drug-resistance types seen in the real world, and that fast-image analysis results were unstable.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only (80/20 train-test split of the TB Portal dataset, 4,030/1,009 CXR images); the deployed web application was then tested on 760 further Portal images (96.1% correct) and by 33 physicians for usability (SUS 96.7). No external dataset, no prospective clinical evaluation and no CDS integration is reported.
Integration_Point: Standalone web/mobile browser application (TB-DRD-CXR, https://itbru.com/TDRC/index.html) to which physicians upload or live-capture a CXR image; the server returns the predicted drug-resistance class and a recommended regimen. Not EHR- or LIS-integrated.
End_User_Described: medical staff and physicians; a pharmacist maintains the regimen list
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Users submit a CXR image file (or capture one live through the camera); a server makes the diagnosis and returns the drug-resistance class with treatment recommendations; the pharmacist updates the treatment plan; physicians use the recommendation as a guideline but must also weigh the patient's own information and drug response.
Barriers_List: Keeping the recommended regimen up to date with changing WHO / national DR-TB guidelines (otherwise the software distracts rather than helps); the Portal dataset missing drug-resistance types seen in practice; unstable results in fast image analysis.
Facilitators_List: Speed and accuracy of results, real-time analysis of large data volumes, specific treatment recommendations for clinicians, low cost without costly equipment or extensive training, and suitability for resource-constrained settings.
Future_Directions: Retrain the model with new data covering the drug-resistance types missing from the Portal dataset; research how best to interpret rapid image analysis; test other CNN ensembles; add automatic detection of drug-resistant types from photo galleries; explore unsupervised learning / clustering (k-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN) on the labelled data.
Limitation_Categories: Model/system limitations: unstable results in fast (live camera) image analysis; dataset coverage - the Portal dataset lacks the drug-resistance types most common in the real world; dependence on keeping the treatment regimen current with WHO/national guidance.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Dataset coverage and image-variability concerns: the Portal dataset does not include all documented drug-resistance types, and CXRs come from various sources and technologies so image quality between lab and physician can vary.
Page_References: pp. 1 (title, DOI, abstract), 3-4 (TB Portal dataset, 5,039 CXR images, 80/20 split), 8 (Table 1 strategies, Table 2 KPIs), 10 (Table 4, 16 experiments), 12-13 (best model and baseline comparison, Table 5), 14 (Table 6 web-application test, ET/ORE, SUS), 15 (Grad-CAM), 17-18 (limitations, future work), 19 (funding, conflicts, data availability).

Title: PREDICTION OF MUL TIDRUG-RESISTANT BACTERIA IN URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS IN THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Population_Description: Adult patients seen in an emergency department with a diagnostic suspicion of UTI and significant isolation of bacteria in urine culture; 414 patients, mean age 77.6 (SD 16.8) years, of whom 125 (30.2%) had an infection caused by a multidrug-resistant microorganism.
Top_Predictive_Features: Items of the Gonzalez del Castillo scale with their point weights: previous colonization 15; institutionalization 8; indwelling urinary catheter 6; severe dependence 5; > 3 cycles of antibiotics in the previous year 4; antibiotic treatment in < 3 months 4; skin and soft tissue infection 4; congestive heart failure 3; end-organ damage diabetes mellitus 3; recurrent urinary tract infections 3; hospital admission in < 3 months 3; age >= 80 years 2; moderate dependence 2; mild dependence 0.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: One model only, no comparators: the Gonzalez del Castillo et al. risk scale (six risk-point groups), evaluated on 414 ED patients with UTI. AUC-ROC 0.79 (95% CI 0.76-0.83); at the optimal cut-off of 9 points sensitivity 76.8%, specificity 71.6% and PPV 60.2%.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: 414 emergency department patients with UTI diagnosis and positive urine culture; optimal score cut-off 9 points
Specificity_Population_Set: 414 emergency department patients with UTI diagnosis and positive urine culture; optimal score cut-off 9 points
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: 414 emergency department patients with UTI diagnosis and positive urine culture; optimal score cut-off 9 points
AUROC_Population_Set: 414 emergency department patients with UTI diagnosis and positive urine culture (Gonzalez del Castillo scale score as the independent variable)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The Gonzalez del Castillo score, developed in another emergency department population, was applied to 414 patients with UTI and positive urine culture at a single ED and its discrimination was measured (AUC-ROC 0.79, optimal cut-off 9 points). The authors state that this is the first application of the scale to positive urine cultures and call for validation in other EDs, so no prospective evaluation or clinical decision support integration is reported (level 3).
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective analysis with possible bias in data collection; antibiotic therapy at home and in long-term facilities was taken from community electronic information systems, so patients treated or admitted outside that setting are not captured; single ED with a high percentage of multidrug-resistant strains, an elderly population and a high proportion of patients from residential centres, so results should be validated in other EDs with lower resistance rates and different patient profiles.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: The study was approved by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of the Hospital Santa Pau (reference No: IIBSP-OAM-2022-86). No specific ethical or governance risks of applying the predictive score are discussed.
Reviewer_Notes: Single-centre retrospective study of a published clinical risk score (Gonzalez del Castillo scale), not a machine-learning model: no model training, no code or data sharing, no fairness analysis, no decision-support platform. The score's outputs are point-based risk categories for empirical antibiotic prescribing in the ED.
Sample_Size: 414 patients with a UTI diagnosis (125 MDR, 289 non-MDR)
Conflicts_of_Interest: None of the authors has any potential financial conflict of interest.
Sex_Distribution: Female 284 (68.5%) of the total sample (MDR group 75 [60.0%]; non-MDR group 209 [72.3%])
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients seen in an emergency department with diagnostic suspicion of UTI and significant isolation of bacteria in urine culture (adult patients with a diagnosis of UTI and positive urine culture).
Exclusion_Criteria: Repeat visit episodes for the same patient were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: Hospital Santa Creu i Sant Pau (Barcelona, Spain) shared clinical history and the primary-care electronic prescription system; no named public dataset.
Dataset_Size: 414 patients (MDR n = 125; no MDR n = 289)
Missing_Data_Method: Not described: only the proportion missing is reported (missing information for a complete score calculation < 5% in all variables considered, most importantly antibiotherapy in the 3 previous months 4.5% and > 1 UTI episode in the previous year 4.5%); no imputation or exclusion method is stated.
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: one emergency department of a 650-bed tertiary-level hospital in Barcelona, Spain, with approximately 140,000 ED visits per year. The authors state that the results should be validated in other EDs with lower resistance rates and different patient profiles.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine (urine culture)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Infection by a multidrug-resistant microorganism: a UTI was considered to be caused by a multidrug-resistant microorganism when caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp., extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (ESBL), carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus faecium or Acinetobacter baumannii.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (n = 241; 68 multidrug-resistant), Klebsiella pneumoniae (n = 53; 24 multidrug-resistant), and, in the MDR definition, MRSA, multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp., ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae (including Proteus mirabilis and other Enterobacteriaceae species), carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus faecium and Acinetobacter baumannii.
Num_Pathogens: Not reported as a single count; the MDR definition names 6 organism groups (MRSA; multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp.; ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae; carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae; Enterococcus faecium; Acinetobacter baumannii).
Drug_Classes: No drug classes analysed: multidrug resistance is defined by organism/mechanism (methicillin resistance, multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas, ESBL production, carbapenemase production).
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA; Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary outcome: UTI caused by a multidrug-resistant microorganism versus not, where a UTI due to a multidrug-resistant microorganism was considered to be caused by any of MRSA, multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas spp., ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis and other Enterobacteriaceae species), carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus faecium, and Acinetobacter baumannii. Infection by a resistant pathogen is the dependent variable.
AI_Purpose: To evaluate the applicability of a predictive model (the Gonzalez del Castillo clinical scale) of infection by multidrug-resistant microorganisms in UTIs treated in an emergency department, in order to identify patients at high risk of multidrug resistance and guide empirical antibiotic treatment.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single published risk scale; no comparator models)
Feature_Engineering: None by the authors: the items of the published Gonzalez del Castillo score (age >= 80 years, congestive heart failure, end-organ damage diabetes mellitus, indwelling urinary catheter, recurrent urinary tract infections, institutionalization, > 3 cycles of antibiotics in the previous year, previous colonization, antibiotic treatment in < 3 months, hospital admission in < 3 months, functional status, skin and soft tissue infection) were applied with the weights assigned in the original scale.
Feature_Selection_Method: None: all items of the published Gonzalez del Castillo scale were retained as printed.
Num_Features_Total: 12 items (functional status counted once, with 3 levels)
Software_Libraries: Stata V. 13.0 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX)
Other_Metrics: PPV 60.2% and NPV 86.7% at the optimal cut-off of 9 points (NPV quoted on p. 4); sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV for each of the six risk-score groups (Table 3); 139 patients (33.6%) classified as high risk (> 9 points); odds ratios for each risk factor (Table 2).
Baseline_Method: None: the score was applied alone, with no comparator model or naive baseline; performance is only compared qualitatively with the score's original development study.
External_Validation_Description: The Gonzalez del Castillo et al. score, developed in a different emergency department population, was applied without modification to 414 patients seen in one ED with UTI and positive urine culture; discrimination (AUC-ROC 0.79, 95% CI 0.76-0.83) and an optimal cut-off of 9 points were evaluated in this independent sample.
Clinical_Insights: Previous colonization with a multidrug-resistant pathogen carries the highest score (15 points) and only about 10% of patients had a known prior multidrug-resistant pathogen; previous antibiotic therapy did not differ significantly between patients with and without MDR UTI although it was frequent overall; the authors conclude that the classic single risk criteria are inadequate and that risk factors must be combined in a score.
Generalisability_Details: The results come from a single ED with a high prevalence of multidrug-resistant strains, an elderly population and many patients from residential centres, and the authors state they should be validated in other EDs with lower resistance rates and different patient profiles; they argue the data may be applicable to most EDs in their environment given the global spread of resistance and population ageing.
Maturity_Evidence: External application of a published score to an independent single-centre sample with discrimination measured (AUC-ROC 0.79, 95% CI 0.76-0.83) and a proposed cut-off of 9 points; no internal development, no prospective evaluation, no integration into clinical systems and no routine use reported.
Integration_Point: Clinical decision point when prescribing empirical antibiotic treatment: ED patients with suspected UTI and positive urine culture pending identification; the score is proposed as an aid to prescribing, not as a software integration.
End_User_Described: The attending physician: the scale should be considered an aid to prescribing, without replacing the attending physician's clinical judgement.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The score is applied in the ED to patients with suspected UTI and positive urine culture, particularly outside the local antibiotic therapy protocols in the sepsis code, to support the decision on empirical treatment; it is an aid to prescribing and does not replace the physician's clinical judgement.
Barriers_List: Retrospective design with possible bias in data collection; antibiotic exposure data limited to patients treated or admitted within the community electronic information systems; single ED with a high percentage of multidrug-resistant strains, an elderly population and many patients from residential centres, limiting generalisability; sensitivity and specificity did not reach the optimal cut-off points (> 80%).
Facilitators_List: The score helps predict many of the daily situations attended in the ED and is especially useful outside the local antibiotic therapy protocols in the sepsis code; it combines several risk factors into one tool and is proposed as an aid to prescribing.
Future_Directions: Future studies should demonstrate the usefulness of this scale for bacterial isolates in samples of different sources; the authors also call for validation in other EDs with lower resistance rates and different patient profiles.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (clinical; microbiological; pharmacological; healthcare utilisation; sociodemographic; geographic - place of origin)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: A-priori clinical point weights assigned by the Gonzalez del Castillo et al. score; no statistical importance measure was computed.
Limitation_Categories: Study design (retrospective, data-collection bias); data completeness (antibiotic exposure outside the community electronic systems not captured); setting/generalisability (single ED, high MDR prevalence, elderly, residential-centre patients); performance (sensitivity and specificity below the optimal > 80% cut-off).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing information for a complete score calculation was < 5% in all variables considered, the most important being antibiotherapy in the 3 previous months (4.5%) and > 1 UTI episode in the previous year (4.5%); antibiotic therapy at home and in long-term facilities was captured from community electronic information systems, so patients treated or admitted outside that setting are missed.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear for a clinical validation study: study period, single-centre setting, population, outcome definition, metric definitions and 95% CI are reported, with the metrics shown per risk group. No code or data availability statement and no reporting guideline is named.
Page_References: pp. 1-6 (full article text layer); key evidence: p. 1 (abstract, aim, DOI), p. 2 (methods, population, MDR outcome definition, AUC-ROC), p. 3 (scale weights, Table 2, optimal cut-off, missing data), p. 4 (Table 3 metrics, limitations of comparison with the development study), p. 5 (limitations, competing interest), p. 6 (article summary).

Title: Instant detection of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing bacteria from the urine of patients using infrared spectroscopy combined with machine learning
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Funder_Names: Israel Innovation Authority (grant no. 71733)
Population_Description: Urine samples from 2616 different patients, tested in the bacteriology laboratory at Soroka University Medical Center (Israel); only samples infected with Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae were used for the model (2249 samples: 1746 E. coli, 503 K. pneumoniae)
Data_Source_Other: Urine samples supplied by the bacteriology laboratory at Soroka University Medical Center (SUMC); FTIR spectra measured in-house for the study
Top_Predictive_Features: Individual wavenumbers (features) of the second-derivative FTIR spectra, ranked in descending order of mutual-information score; 100 features selected, scores of the ten best shown in Fig. 6a and distributions of the best three in Fig. 6b (individual wavenumbers are not printed in the text)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest (RF): accuracy 98% for taxonomic classification (combined E. coli + K. pneumoniae vs other UTI bacteria). RF for ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative: AUC 0.90, accuracy 80%, sensitivity 81%, specificity 80%, PPV 59%, NPV 92% (Table 2). RF for ESBL-positive vs other cephalosporin-resistance mechanisms: AUC 0.82, accuracy 77%, sensitivity 79%, specificity 70%, PPV 89%, NPV 52% (Table 3). Several sophisticated classifiers were screened but only RF is named; UMAP used for dimensionality reduction/visualisation and PCA did not show good cluster separability.
Best_Performing_Model: Random forest (RF) classifier
Accuracy_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative urine samples (combined E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae; 591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative (591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
Specificity_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative (591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative (591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
AUROC_Population_Set: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative (591 ESBL-positive, 1658 ESBL-negative)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Random forest classifier developed and evaluated on a single-centre urine-spectra dataset using 5-fold cross-validation, with 5-fold nested cross-validation on the training set for hyperparameter estimation (number of features and number of trees); no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical integration is reported
Reported_Limitations: The success rate of identifying ESBL bacteria was not especially high; enlarging the dataset is expected to enable more sophisticated classifiers and improve success rates; linking spectral changes to a specific biological element of the cell is difficult because of the limitation of infrared spectroscopy
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Study performed under the approval of the Ethical Helsinki Board from Soroka University Medical Center (SUMC); no safety hazards, serious risks or dangers reported; no other ethical or governance issues discussed
Sample_Size: 2249 urine samples infected with E. coli or K. pneumoniae (1746 E. coli, 503 K. pneumoniae) out of 2616 samples from 2616 different patients; the ESBL analysis used 591 ESBL-positive and 1658 ESBL-negative isolates
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Urine samples from patients infected with Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae; other UTI gram-negative bacteria were excluded because of their low incidence
Exclusion_Criteria: Bacteria other than E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae (367 samples infected with other UTI bacteria) were not included in the ESBL classification because of their low incidence
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Other
Data_Source_Name: Soroka University Medical Center (SUMC) bacteriology laboratory urine sample collection
Dataset_Size: 2616 urine samples from 2616 different patients (2249 infected with E. coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae, 367 with other UTI bacteria); the ESBL classification used 591 ESBL-positive and 1658 ESBL-negative isolates
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: urine samples supplied by the bacteriology laboratory at Soroka University Medical Center (SUMC), Beer-Sheva, Israel
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Classification of bacteria obtained directly from patient urine as ESBL-positive or ESBL-negative, regardless of species, plus differentiation of resistant isolates by mechanism of resistance (ESBL production vs other cephalosporin-resistance mechanisms)
Pathogens: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae; a mixed group of other UTI bacteria (367 samples) used only in the preliminary taxonomic classification
Num_Pathogens: 2 (Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae) plus a mixed 'other UTI bacteria' group
Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins (resistance to all cephalosporins defines ESBL-positive; another mechanism defines resistance to at least one cephalosporin)
Specific_Antibiotics: cephalexin, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime axetil, cefuroxime, ceftazidime
AMR_Outcome_Definition: ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative established by the classical methods (MALDI-TOF species identification and disk diffusion ESBL testing) as the gold standard; ESBL-positive samples were resistant to all cephalosporins, and the second sub-category was ESBL-negative but resistant to at least one cephalosporin antibiotic by another mechanism
AI_Purpose: To examine the potential of FTIR spectroscopy-based machine learning (random forest) to detect ESBL-producing bacteria directly from patient urine within about 40 minutes and to differentiate resistance mechanisms, without identifying the bacterial species first
Num_Models_Compared: Several classifiers were screened ('several sophisticated classifiers were applied'); only the random forest is named and reported. UMAP and PCA were used for dimensionality reduction/visualisation, not as predictive models.
Feature_Engineering: Atmospheric compensation; Savitzky-Golay smoothing with 13 points; spectra cut to the 1800-900 cm-1 fingerprint region; Concave Rubber Band baseline correction (64 equal-sized ranges, minima fitted with a polynomial and subtracted, repeated five times); vector normalisation and offset correction; second derivative of the spectra used in all analyses
Feature_Selection_Method: Mutual information (MI) score per wavenumber of the second-derivative spectra, wavenumbers arranged in descending MI order; nested K-fold multiple iterations adding five features at a time until the best-performing set was found
Num_Features_Total: Not stated; candidate features are the individual wavenumbers of the second-derivative spectra in the 1800-900 cm-1 fingerprint region
Num_Features_Selected: 100 (mutual-information selected features for the ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative stage; number not stated for the other stages)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Instance weighting: costs proportional to the inverse priors of the training set, raising the weight of the smaller class
Hyperparameter_Method: 5-fold nested cross-validation on the training set to estimate the number of features and the number of classifier trees
Hardware_Details: Nicolet-i10 infrared microscope FTIR spectrometer with a liquid nitrogen-cooled mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector, transmission mode; spectra measured 4000-650 cm-1 with 128 co-added scans at 4 cm-1 resolution
Other_Metrics: AUC 0.90 for ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative classification (Table 2); AUC 0.82 for ESBL-positive vs other cephalosporin-resistance mechanisms (Table 3); accuracy 98% for the taxonomic classification (Table 1)
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation (data divided into five equal subsets maintaining the class ratio; four train, one test, repeated five times); 5-fold nested cross-validation on the training set for hyperparameter estimation
Train_Test_Split: Cross-validation rather than a single split: four of five subsets used for training and the fifth for test, rotated five times
Clinical_Insights: The main spectral changes between ESBL-positive and ESBL-negative isolates are in amide I (1728-1627 cm-1), amide II (1627-1520 cm-1) and the carbohydrate region (1196-900 cm-1); absorption of ESBL-negative isolates is significantly lower in the carbohydrate region (1200-1000 cm-1) and at the 1081 cm-1 carbohydrate band; the differences may partly reflect plasmid-borne resistance genes rather than ESBL production alone
Generalisability_Details: The next step would include all gram-negative UTI bacteria once sufficient data are collected from low-incidence bacteria; enlarging the dataset is expected to allow more sophisticated classifiers and better success rates
Maturity_Evidence: Internal 5-fold cross-validation with nested 5-fold cross-validation for hyperparameters on a single-centre urine-spectra dataset; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment reported
Integration_Point: None described; the method is proposed for use in bacteriology laboratories
End_User_Described: bacteriology laboratories and prescribing physicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: A patient's urine sample is received, measured by FTIR spectroscopy and classified by the trained random forest as ESBL-positive or ESBL-negative within about 40 minutes, instead of at least 48 hours with classical phenotypic methods, so that physicians can prescribe targeted antibiotics instead of random broad-spectrum antibiotics
Future_Directions: Include all gram-negative UTI bacteria once enough data are collected from low-incidence bacteria; enlarge the dataset to enable more sophisticated classifiers and improve the success rates
Predictor_Categories_Count: 1 (laboratory / microbiological spectroscopic features: selected wavenumbers of the second-derivative FTIR spectra)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Mutual information (MI) scores calculated for each wavenumber of the second-derivative spectra, ranked in descending order

Title: Characterising global antimicrobial resistance research explains why One Health solutions are slow in development: An application of AI-based gap analysis

WHO_Region: AFR; AMR; EMR; EUR; SEAR; WPR
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Other
Study_Design_Other: Bibliometric / AI-based evidence-gap analysis of the published literature
Funder_Names: National Natural Science Foundation of China; Ningbo S&T project
Population_Description: Published AMR research literature: 254,738 AMR-related articles (title, keywords, abstract) indexed in Scopus, 2003-2023, of which 220,798 remained after filtration. No human participants, isolates or clinical records; the unit of analysis is the publication.
Data_Source_Other: Scopus bibliographic database (title, keywords, abstract, DOI); complete downloaded list provided in additional file
System_Level_Applications: AMR surveillance / trend prediction; Resistance gene annotation (ARG)
Target_End_User: Researcher; Surveillance analyst / public health; Programme manager / policymaker
All_Models_Evaluated: One AI/NLP pipeline only (tokenization, POS tagging with a pre-trained transformer model, lemmatization, noun phrase extraction, NER for country names, inverted-index retrieval; hierarchical clustering for research stages). No competing models: the pipeline correctly categorized 97.4 % of papers for AMR and 98.5 % by One Health sector.
Best_Performing_Model: NLP-based (AI) model - the only model evaluated; correctly categorized 97.4 % of the papers for AMR and 98.5 % according to One Health sector
Accuracy_Value: 97.4 % (categorisation for AMR); 98.5 % (categorisation by One Health sector)
Accuracy_Population_Set: 3,000 papers randomly sub-selected from the 254,738-publication database and manually verified
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The NLP/AI model was validated only by comparing predicted scores with manual scores for 3,000 papers randomly sub-selected from the same Scopus database; no external, multi-source or prospective validation and no clinical deployment is reported. Reported_Limitations: No full-text interrogation possible for all assessed articles; a single bibliographic database (Scopus) used, which may decrease documents identified through NER; English-language search restriction (language bias); imprecise sampling terms in abstracts; One Health definitions not specific and needing refinement.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Risk that literature-derived signals are misread as true burden: where research capacity is limited, few publications may reflect lack of research resources rather than low disease burden ('observing limited disease burden may be due to a lack of resources for research and nothing is reported').
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Capacity imbalances between LICs and HICs; scarce integrated AMR research in African LICs; no LIC publications covering all five One Health sectors; only one of the 100 most cited papers related to LICs; LICs have few publications across all pathogen types.
Reviewer_Notes: Bibliometric / NLP evidence-gap analysis of the published AMR literature (254,738 articles, 2003-2023), not a clinical prediction study: no patients, isolates, laboratory results or clinical outcomes. The AI component is a text-mining pipeline (topic/term categorisation, NER, retrieval, clustering), so performance coding rests on the paper's own manual-validation figures (97.4 % / 98.5 %).
Sample_Size: 254,738 publications in the database; 3,000 manually screened; 220,798 publications after filtration
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
Inclusion_Criteria: Documents whose titles, keywords or abstracts contained 'antimicrobial resistance' and related alliance names or abbreviations; searches restricted to 2003-2023 and to English-language peer-reviewed sources. Books, letters, notes, conference papers, editorials and errata excluded as sources with unknown levels of peer review.
Exclusion_Criteria: Books (whole books or chapters), letters, notes, conference papers, editorials and errata were not included (sources with unknown levels of peer review); non-English manuscripts; publications outside 2003-2023.
Data_Types_Used: Free text / clinical notes; Other
Data_Source_Name: Scopus
Dataset_Size: 254,738 publications (220,798 after filtration) from 178 sampling countries
Geographic_Representativeness: Global: 254,738 publications from 178 recognised sampling countries across all income levels (HIC, UMIC, LMIC, LIC) and all world regions; research countries identified by NER in abstracts.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: No clinical outcome. The outcome analysed is AMR research activity: publication counts by country, region and income level, One Health sector, pathogen, pathogen-drug combination (e.g. MRSA), ARG (e.g. mecA) and AMR surveillance method (AST, PCR, WGS, metagenomics).
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Staphylococcus aureus; Salmonella spp.; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Acinetobacter spp.; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Enterobacter spp.; Acinetobacter baumannii; Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Streptococcus pneumoniae; Proteus spp.; Campylobacter spp.; Shigella spp.; Enterococcus faecium; Enterococcus faecalis; Haemophilus influenzae; Neisseria gonorrhoeae; Staphylococcus epidermidis; Proteus mirabilis; Enterobacter cloacae; Helicobacter pylori; Serratia spp.; Salmonella typhi; Streptococcus pyogenes; Streptococcus agalactiae; Serratia marcescens; Klebsiella oxytoca; Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; Vibrio cholerae; Providencia spp.; Morganella spp.; Enterobacter aerogenes; Clostridioides difficile; Salmonella paratyphi
Num_Pathogens: 34 pathogen species/groups listed in Table 1 (plus A. baumannii and A. spp. counted separately)

Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin, carbapenems, vancomycin, penicillin, ampicillin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, clarithromycin, colistin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: XDR; ESBL; AmpC; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA; VRE; Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: AMR is a term-presence label: an article is counted as AMR research when the title, keywords or abstract contains 'antimicrobial resistance' and related terms, and its One Health sector(s) are assigned from the presence of AMR words in the abstract (Tables S1-S3). ARB, ARG and pathogen-drug topics are coded by mention frequency.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To apply AI/NLP methods to the whole AMR literature: harvest and sort 254,738 articles into a database and inverted-index information retrieval system, extract research country, ARB and ARG information, categorise articles into One Health sectors, and map global AMR research activity to expose knowledge gaps and guide One Health solutions.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (single AI/NLP categorisation pipeline, benchmarked against manual screening of 3,000 papers; no model-to-model comparison)
Feature_Engineering: NLP text pre-processing: tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, lemmatization, and noun phrase / alias / abbreviation extraction; inverted indexes built for each noun phrase for Boolean (conjunction, disjunction, negation) complex searches.
Software_Libraries: lxml / ElementTree in Python; spaCy via R package Spacyr (version 1.2.1); a pre-trained transformer-based AI model for POS tagging
Other_Metrics: Search speed (~0.6 microseconds per query); percentage of papers correctly categorised (97.4 % AMR, 98.5 % One Health sector); quantification methods and bias level of the AI classification results in Tables S1-S3.
Baseline_Method: Manual screening by two reviewers (Cai Chen and Shu-Le Li) of titles, abstracts and full texts, with disagreements resolved by a senior researcher; each paper received a manual identification score (0 = false, 1 = true) for AMR relevance and category membership.
Internal_Validation: Manual verification of 3,000 randomly sub-selected papers from the same database; manual scores compared with the predicted scores of the AI-based identification.
Generalisability_Details: The authors argue the database and AI method can be updated and reinterrogated over time as a general method for quantifying AMR trends across sectors and countries, but caution that literature-based AI cannot capture burden where research capacity is limited.
Maturity_Evidence: Highest evidence is internal validation: the NLP/AI model was benchmarked against manual screening of 3,000 papers randomly sub-selected from the same Scopus database, and the categories were assigned from AMR word presence in abstracts. No external dataset, prospective use, EHR/LIS integration or clinical deployment is reported. An open-access database and retrieval system are offered for future use.

End_User_Described: Users of the AMR database and information retrieval system, for whom a user manual is provided ('the detailed guidance for users is provided in the user manual').
Barriers_List: Limited laboratory infrastructure, incomplete National Action Plans, inadequate financial support in low-income settings, limited local research capacity, poor harmonisation of methods between sectors, and single-database (Scopus) plus English-language literature coverage.
Facilitators_List: Capacity building (new laboratories, instruments, guidance and training, integrated monitoring), increasing co-developed research outputs, harmonising culture-based and molecular methods across sectors, and the open-access database with NLP methods for equitable data sharing.
Future_Directions: Reduce capacity imbalances between LICs and HICs, harmonise methods across sectors (culture-based with genomic/metagenomic), refine One Health term definitions, and update/reinterrogate the database over time.

Data_Quality_Concerns: Titles, keywords and abstracts may not reflect a manuscript's true content; imprecise sampling terms in abstracts reduce NER recall; One Health definitions are not specific, so sector terms need refinement.
Reporting_Clarity: Methods and results are described in narrative form with heavy deferral to supplemental tables (S1-S31) not in the main text, so feature lists, bias quantification and per-country tables are not verifiable from the PDF alone; the text layer carries typos ('perfomed', 'limitaitons').
