Title: Empirical Mode Decomposition and k-Nearest Embedding Vectors for Timely Analyses of Antibiotic Resistance Trends
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: European Union Seventh Framework Programme (DebugIT project, grant agreement ICT-2007.5.2-217139)
Population_Description: Weekly aggregated antibiogram resistance time series from the University Hospitals of Geneva microbiology laboratory spanning a decade (2002–2011), for four pathogens (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumonia, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus) tested against a set of antibiotics — 26 organism–antibiotic time series.
Data_Source_Other: ARTEMIS transnational antimicrobial resistance monitoring system (DebugIT)
Top_Predictive_Features: Low-frequency EMD components (the residue / mean trend and components C6+) add the most forecasting value; high-frequency components C1 and C2 degrade accuracy (by 4.6% and 1.0%); components C3–C5 have no significant impact (gains −0.4% to +0.1%).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Clinician / prescriber; Infection prevention and control team; Surveillance analyst / public health
All_Models_Evaluated: RW (random walk baseline); KNN (k-NN on the raw signal, m=6); DECA; DECF; DECS — all evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) at 1-, 3- and 12-week-ahead horizons. DECF and DECS significantly outperformed the other models (P≤.004); DECS marginally better than DECF but not significantly (P≈.05). DECF 135 wins / 17 losses; DECS 118 wins / 25 losses.
Best_Performing_Model: DECS
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The forecaster was trained and tested by leave-one-out cross-validation on a decade of weekly resistance time series (internal validation only); no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Data aggregated from several wards (ward-specific analyses may differ); limited to time series of pathogens that present some level of resistance; bursting patterns not tested (model unlikely to forecast bursts); irregular time series containing null values not investigated.
Reviewer_Notes: Forecasting / method-development study combining empirical mode decomposition (trend extraction) with a k-nearest-neighbor forecaster on retrospective, weekly aggregated antibiogram data from a single institution (HUG, Geneva, Switzerland); unit of analysis is 26 organism–antibiotic resistance time series. Best-performing model DECS (not significantly better than DECF).
Sample_Size: 26 organism–antibiotic resistance time series, each comprising 520 weekly data points (January 2002–December 2011); minimum 350 weeks training, 170 test points.
Conflicts_of_Interest: CL serves currently as a PLOS ONE editor.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: ARTEMIS (DebugIT transnational antimicrobial resistance monitoring system)
Dataset_Size: 26 time series × 520 weekly data points
Specimen_Type_Detail: antibiograms (susceptibility-test results)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Weekly resistance rate — the percentage of resistant antibiogram results out of the total (including intermediate results) for each organism–antibiotic time series; the model forecasts short- and medium-term resistance trends.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumonia, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus
Drug_Classes: aminoglycoside; aminopenicillin; amoxicillin-clavulanic acid; cefepime; 3rd generation cephalosporin; fluoroquinolone; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; piperacillin-tazobactam; carbapenem; ceftazidime; ciprofloxacin; benzylpenicillin; clindamycin; macrolide
Specific_Antibiotics: AMI (aminoglycoside); AMP (aminopenicillin/ampicillin); AMC (amoxicillin-clavulanic acid); FEP (cefepime); CF3 (3rd-generation cephalosporin); FLU (fluoroquinolone); SXT (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole); TZP (piperacillin-tazobactam); CAR (carbapenem); CAZ (ceftazidime); CIP (ciprofloxacin); PEN (benzylpenicillin); CLI (clindamycin); MAC (macrolide)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Weekly resistance rate = percentage of resistant antibiogram results out of the total antibiograms (including intermediate results), computed per organism–antibiotic time series.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To build a novel, fully data-driven method combining trend extraction (empirical mode decomposition) with a k-nearest-neighbor machine learning forecaster to provide timely short- and medium-term forecasting of antibiotic resistance trends for enhanced biosurveillance systems.
Feature_Engineering: Resistance time series decomposed by EMD into IMF components plus a residue; non-contributing high-frequency components filtered out; remaining components delay-embedded into vectors of dimension m.
Feature_Selection_Method: Relevant EMD component selection via DECF (frequency threshold — components with cycle < 10 weeks excluded) or DECS (Wu & Huang statistical significance test against the first IMF); optimal embedding dimension m by fractal dimension.
Hyperparameter_Method: Leave-one-out cross-validation to determine the number of nearest neighbours k; optimal embedding dimension m determined by the fractal-dimension method (also tested against naive m={3,6,10}).
Baseline_Method: Random walk (RW)
Baseline_Performance: RW 1-week-ahead MAE across the KP/SA series 1.40–10.97 (largest errors of all models; e.g., KP7 10.97, SA6 1.40)
Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation adapted to time-series forecasting
Train_Test_Split: Minimum 350 weeks training; test set of 170 data points.
CV_Folds: Leave-one-out (one future point held out at a time)
Overfitting_Method: Four time series (EC 4, KP 2, PA 5, SA 5) used to determine the optimal embedding dimension were excluded from the final training and test sets to avoid overfitting bias.
Generalisability_Details: The trend extraction and forecasting methodologies make no assumption about the underlying data model, so the authors state the method could be generalized to other time-varying clinical events and readily applied to ward-specific data.
Maturity_Evidence: Leave-one-out cross-validation on a decade of weekly resistance time series (internal validation only) — no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment reported.
Integration_Point: Proposed as input to clinical decision support systems for antibiotic prescribing and to outbreak-detection biosurveillance (not deployed).
End_User_Described: Care providers / clinicians (empirical therapy) and infection control groups
Future_Directions: Investigating correlation of other time-dependent clinical factors (e.g., antibiotic consumption) with decomposed resistance trends; combining the forecasting methodology with burst detection models to improve prediction accuracy.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Relative gain in mean absolute error (MAE) from incrementally including higher-frequency EMD components
Limitation_Categories: Ward-level aggregation; limited to resistant pathogens; bursting patterns not testable; irregular (null-containing) time series not investigated
Data_Quality_Concerns: Data aggregated across wards; time series limited to pathogens with some level of resistance; null-containing (irregular) series not investigated.

Title: Development and validation of a novel prediction model for Carbapenem-resistant organism infection in a large-scale hospitalized patients
Funder_Names: Health and family planning Program of Pudong New Area Health Commission (PW2021B-05); Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Hospital Sailing project (PRYQH202305)
Population_Description: Hospitalized patients (inpatients) of Pudong New Area People’s Hospital, Shanghai, China, with at least one microbial culture during hospitalization; 131390 eligible inpatients, randomly split 7:3 into training (n = 91973) and validation (n = 39417) cohorts.
Age_Range: >18 years (categorised as <40, 40-62, 63-75, >75 years); patients aged ≤ 18 years excluded
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Univariable logistic regression (odds ratios with 95% CI, Table 3) and multivariable logistic regression nomogram (AUC 0.935 training cohort; AUC 0.937 validation cohort)
Best_Performing_Model: Multivariable logistic regression nomogram (highest AUC: 0.937 in the validation cohort vs 0.935 in the training cohort)
AUROC_Population_Set: Validation cohort (n = 39417) of hospitalized patients
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Random 7:3 split of a single-centre cohort into training (n = 91973) and validation (n = 39417) cohorts, with bootstrap resampling (1000 resamples); no external or prospective evaluation.
Reported_Limitations: Exclusion of patients with incomplete variables may cause selection bias; single-centre design; external effectiveness and generalizability require multicentre studies.
Reviewer_Notes: Retrospective single-centre development and internal validation of a logistic-regression nomogram for CRO infection. Performance is reported only as AUC (training 0.935, validation 0.937) with calibration and decision curves; no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV/F1 figures are given. Class imbalance (CRO 0.49%) is not addressed.
Sample_Size: 131390 hospitalized patients (inpatients): training cohort n = 91973, validation cohort n = 39417
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors report no conflicts of interest relevant to this article.
Inclusion_Criteria: Hospitalized patients who received at least one microbial culture during hospitalization.
Exclusion_Criteria: (1) Patients with polymicrobial bacteria including MRSA, VRE infections, or invasive fungal disease; (2) patients with any unknown epidemiology and clinical information; (3) age ≤ 18 years.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 131390 inpatients (training n = 91973; validation n = 39417)
Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case analysis only: patients with unknown epidemiology and clinical information were excluded, and exclusion of patients with incomplete variables is acknowledged as a source of selection bias; no imputation reported.
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre (Pudong New Area People’s Hospital, Shanghai, China); no multicentre or non-Chinese data; generalisability to other regions untested.
Specimen_Type_Detail: sputum, urine, blood, feces and other secretions
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Carbapenem-resistant organism (CRO) infection in hospitalized patients — binary outcome (Non-CRO vs CRO).
Pathogens: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP); carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB); carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA); carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE)
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems
AMR_Outcome_Definition: CRO infection diagnosed according to CDC criteria: positive culture of CRO plus high clinical suspicion from the patient’s clinical symptoms, signs and examination results (e.g. fever patterns, inflammatory markers).
AI_Purpose: To build and validate a risk nomogram that predicts CRO infection in hospitalized patients, to support personalised treatment decisions and infection control.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (univariable logistic regression and multivariable logistic regression nomogram)
Feature_Engineering: Age categorised by percentile into <40, 40-62, 63-75 and >75 years; other variables recorded as binary indicators (e.g. temperature above 38 degrees for two days) or as two-level categories (duration of antibiotic therapy <5 vs ≥5 days; length of hospital stay <10 vs ≥10 days).
Feature_Selection_Method: Univariate logistic regression screening, then multivariable logistic regression; non-significant variables were not included in the nomogram
Num_Features_Total: 18 candidate predictor variables (the listed variables excluding the CRO infection outcome)
Other_Metrics: AUC (training cohort 0.935; validation cohort 0.937); calibration curve; decision curve analysis (DCA); odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals
Internal_Validation: Random 7:3 split into training (n = 91973) and validation (n = 39417) cohorts; bootstrap with 1000 resamples
Clinical_Insights: The nomogram is built from the 9 independent risk factors; duration of antibiotic therapy (days) was the variable with highest predictive ability for CRO infection, and the tool is intended to flag patients at risk early.
Generalisability_Details: Single-centre Chinese cohort; the authors state that clinical feasibility should be evaluated by assessing external effectiveness and generalizability in multicentre studies.
Maturity_Evidence: Random 7:3 internal split with a held-out validation cohort (AUC 0.937 validation vs 0.935 training) and 1000-resample bootstrap; single centre, no external validation and no prospective evaluation.
Integration_Point: Clinician decision-making (no EHR/LIS integration or workflow described)
End_User_Described: clinical doctors
Facilitators_List: All model variables are easily obtained from routine clinical data, which supports clinical applicability
Future_Directions: External effectiveness and generalizability should be assessed in multicentre studies
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Nomogram point scale from the multivariable logistic regression model (individual point values shown only in Fig. 1)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Temperature above 38 degrees for two days had not previously been reported as a risk factor for CRO infection but was included in the nomogram (and was significant in both univariate and multivariate analysis).
Limitation_Categories: selection bias from excluding patients with incomplete variables; single-centre design; need for external/multicentre validation
Data_Quality_Concerns: incomplete variables and unknown epidemiology/clinical information (patients excluded rather than imputed); repeat isolates from the same site excluded and only initial isolates considered
Reporting_Clarity: Clear for methods, model performance (AUC, calibration, DCA), ethics and limitations; the nomogram point values appear only in Fig. 1 and no accuracy/sensitivity/specificity figures are reported; no reporting guideline named.
Page_References: Key content: title/abstract p. 1; methods pp. 2-3; Tables 1-3 pp. 3-5; nomogram and validation figures pp. 3 and 6; discussion/limitations p. 7; end matter p. 7

Title: A machine-learning-based model for automated recommendation of individualized treatment of rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Research Foundation Flanders (FWO); National Institute on Allergy and Infectious Diseases / National Institutes of Health (NIAID/NIH)
Population_Description: Patients with rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) for whom individualized treatment is recommended; and physicians/clinicians who use the CDSS
Data_Source_Other: Whole genome sequencing (WGS)-derived drug resistance profiles
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest classifier (100 trees, max depth 10, scikit-learn defaults): recommendation accepted by experts in 89%, 95%, and 95% of cases across 3 rounds; patient-level leave-one-out cross-validation
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Externally validated on 64 unique WGS-derived drug resistance profiles not present in the training dataset; assessed in a clinical trial and routine care setting
Reported_Limitations: No 'truth'/gold standard for the optimal regimen; patient- or pathogen-related considerations not fully captured; knowledge base based on 2019 data and expert opinion; drug price variability across regions; lack of transparency of the machine learning model; developed 2019-2021 before BPaL(M); limited to the South African setting
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: CDSS is a decision support tool, not a substitute for clinical judgement; risk of resistance amplification due to suboptimal adherence
Sample_Size: 3895 treatment regimen-expert feedback pairs (from 268 unique WGS-derived resistance profiles)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype
Dataset_Size: 3895 treatment regimen-expert feedback pairs (268 unique WGS-derived resistance profiles)
Missing_Data_Method: Median score of the other physicians used for one missing questionnaire item
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Prediction/recommendation of the optimal individualized treatment regimen for rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB)
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones; rifamycins; diarylquinolines (bedaquiline); phenazines (clofazimine); oxazolidinones (linezolid); aminoglycosides; thioamides; carbapenems; nitroimidazo-oxazoles; ethambutol; pyrazinamide; cycloserine/terizidone; para-aminosalicylic acid
Specific_Antibiotics: levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, rifabutin, bedaquiline, clofazimine, linezolid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, isoniazid, ethionamide, prothionamide, imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin, streptomycin, cycloserine, terizidone, para-aminosalicylic acid, delamanid, pretomanid, high-dose rifampicin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Resistance determined by WGS-derived genotypic drug resistance profile (variants interpreted per the 2021 WHO catalogue of mutations); outcome is rifampicin resistance
AI_Purpose: To automate the translation of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data into an individualized RR-TB treatment regimen recommendation for clinicians
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (random forest classifier)
Feature_Engineering: Binary regimen features used directly as input; continuous features normalized 0-1 and also transformed into quartile classes (very high/high/low/very low); negative features inverted so higher values equal patient benefit
Feature_Selection_Method: Expert/stakeholder-defined drug and regimen features (no computational selection)
Num_Features_Total: 9 drug features + 14 regimen features = 23
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn; React; Django; REDCap
Other_Metrics: Model recommendation acceptance by experts (89%, 95%, 95% across 3 rounds); treatment recommender recommendation probability; technology acceptance model domain scores (e.g., perceived usefulness 79%, ease of use 84%)
Internal_Validation: Patient-level leave-one-out cross-validation
CV_Folds: Leave-one-out (patient level, no fixed fold count)
External_Validation_Description: 64 unique WGS-derived drug resistance profiles not present in the training dataset (accessed on 2020.01.13)
Generalisability_Details: Study limited to South Africa; prospective studies needed to demonstrate effectiveness in other high burden settings
Maturity_Evidence: External validation on 64 unique WGS-derived resistance profiles not in the training dataset; use in a pragmatic clinical trial (SMARTT) and routine care
Integration_Point: Point of care — individualized RR-TB treatment recommendation via interactive webapp during clinical consultation
End_User_Described: Clinician / physician treating RR-TB patients
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinician logs in, reviews patient list and WGS resistance profile, enters contra-indications/toxicity/stockouts, and receives an updated real-time regimen recommendation; iterative until physician accepts, then a pdf report is generated for the medical file
Barriers_List: Required digital infrastructure and training; physicians hesitant to deviate from national treatment guidelines; rural settings lack reliable internet/email access; some physicians use personal devices without infrastructure support
Facilitators_List: High perceived ease of use and usefulness; webapp allows real-time re-run of the model during consultation and generates a pdf for paper records
Future_Directions: Prospective studies to demonstrate effectiveness in other high burden settings; a second version of the CDSS for the BPaLM era; re-training the model with treatment outcomes from large-scale use; training physicians on new guidelines and knowledge
Feature_Interactions_Method: Machine learning model (random forest) reported to capture complex interactions between drug and regimen features
Limitation_Categories: No gold standard for optimal regimen; incomplete capture of patient/pathogen considerations; reliance on 2019 data and expert opinion; drug price variability; lack of model transparency; developed pre-BPaL(M) era; limited to South African setting
Data_Quality_Concerns: Knowledge base built from published and unpublished data available in 2019, complemented by expert opinion when data scarce
Reporting_Clarity: Good — detailed reporting of model development, drug and regimen features, and acceptance results; multi-column tables are garbled in the text layer

Title: Accurate prediction of antimicrobial resistance and genetic marker of Staphylococcus aureus clinical isolates using MALDI-TOF MS and machine learning - a cross DRIAMS and Taiwan database
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Chung Shan Medical University (grant number: CSMUH No: CS1-23228)
Population_Description: Clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates: 4874 S. aureus (788 ORSA, 4086 OSSA) from DRIAMS and 416 invasive S. aureus isolates (189 ORSA, 227 OSSA) from the CS database (Chung Shan Medical University Hospital), of which 183 (44.0%) were mecA-positive MRSA and 233 (56.0%) mecA-negative MSSA
Data_Source_Other: Public MALDI-TOF MS / antimicrobial susceptibility database (DRIAMS) plus an institutional clinical microbiology database (CS)
Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP (Shapley value) top features: 2423-2426 m/z, 4496-4499 m/z and 3764-3767 m/z (top five overlapping features for oxacillin resistance by agar dilution and mecA presence); 2423-2426 m/z among the top three for ERY, CLI, TET and TMP/SMX; 3020-3023 m/z and 4523-4526 m/z (top five for ERY and CLI resistance among ORSA); 7169-7172 m/z (OSSA, ERY and CLI resistance)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: LightGBM; MLP (Multilayer Perceptron); Random Forest; KNN (K Neighbors Classifier); Ada Boost; Logistic Regression; plus a Deep Neural Network (DNN) with transfer learning for crossing databases. Metrics reported: accuracy, AUROC, AUPR. Examples: DRIAMS ORSA - MLP clindamycin AUROC/AUPR 0.81/0.90 and tetracycline 0.87/0.94; LightGBM erythromycin 0.81/0.87 (Supplementary Table 1). CS database ORSA - KNN best except tetracycline (LightGBM better) (Supplementary Table 2). CS database S. aureus with LightGBM - mecA existence 0.878/0.955/0.963; oxacillin resistance (agar dilution) 0.876/0.961/0.969; oxacillin resistance (Vitek 2) 0.845/0.931/0.926 (Table 1). DNN with transfer learning from DRIAMS - oxacillin 0.893/0.891/0.834; clindamycin 0.842/0.781/0.851; erythromycin 0.921/0.818/0.936; tetracycline 0.632/0.639/0.620; TMP/SMX 0.947/0.917/0.886 (Table 2)
Best_Performing_Model: LightGBM - highest AUROC/AUPR on the primary (CS) database: oxacillin resistance by agar dilution accuracy/AUROC/AUPR 0.88/0.96/0.97 and mecA existence AUROC/AUPR 0.955/0.963 (Table 1). The paper also names MLP as superior for most tier 1 antibiotics among ORSA in DRIAMS and KNN for ORSA in the CS database (except tetracycline), so no single model is best across databases
Accuracy_Population_Set: S. aureus isolates from the CS database (n = 416); oxacillin resistance determined by agar dilution
AUROC_Population_Set: S. aureus isolates from the CS database (n = 416); oxacillin resistance determined by agar dilution (0.961 in Table 1)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model development with ten-fold cross-validation on the two source databases (each fold used once as the testing set); Table 2 refits the DNN with 60% CS training, 20% validation and 20% prediction. No prospective or routine-clinical evaluation is reported
Reported_Limitations: Two databases with distinct phylogenic strains, sample sizes, susceptibility profiles and MALDI-TOF instruments; retrospective datasets used for model development; no standard protocol for MALDI-TOF MS with ML (pre-processing, training, validation, testing); efficacy and speed limited by mass spectra quality and resolution and by noise/variability in small datasets
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethical approval reported from two committees; ML-based resistance prediction is presented as a research tool, with the authors cautioning about comparing performance across models, study designs and datasets
Sample_Size: 4874 S. aureus isolates (788 ORSA, 4086 OSSA) from DRIAMS; 416 invasive S. aureus isolates (189 ORSA, 227 OSSA) from the CS database
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest in relation to this study.
Inclusion_Criteria: Non-duplicate, clinically invasive S. aureus strains (isolated from sterile sites) collected from September 2018 to August 2021 in the CS database; S. aureus clinical isolates with MALDI-TOF MS profiles from DRIAMS
Exclusion_Criteria: Duplicate isolates excluded (only non-duplicate strains were collected)
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results; Gene presence / AMR genotype
Data_Source_Name: DRIAMS (Database of Resistance Information on Antimicrobials and MALDI-TOF Mass Spectra); CS database (Chung Shan Medical University Hospital, Taiwan)
Dataset_Size: DRIAMS: over 300 000 fungal and bacterial MALDI-TOF MS isolates from four laboratories, of which 4874 S. aureus were analysed; CS database: 416 invasive S. aureus isolates
Geographic_Representativeness: DRIAMS isolates come from four clinical microbiology laboratories in Switzerland; the CS database is a single medical centre in central Taiwan. The two-database comparison is transnational but neither sample is population-representative of a defined catchment
Specimen_Type_Detail: clinically invasive S. aureus strains (isolated from sterile sites)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antimicrobial resistance of Staphylococcus aureus against tier 1 antibiotics (oxacillin, erythromycin, clindamycin, tetracycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) and presence of the mecA gene
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (oxacillin); macrolides (erythromycin); lincosamides (clindamycin); tetracyclines (tetracycline); folate pathway inhibitors (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin (OX); erythromycin (ERY); clindamycin (CLI); tetracycline (TET); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary susceptible vs intermediate/resistant classification for each tier 1 antibiotic; oxacillin MIC <=2 mg/L classified as OSSA, otherwise ORSA (CLSI); presence/absence of mecA by PCR classified as MRSA and MSSA
AI_Purpose: To compare the efficacy and accuracy of various ML classifiers on MALDI-TOF MS profiles for predicting antimicrobial resistance to tier 1 antibiotics and the mecA genetic marker in clinical S. aureus, and to test transfer learning from a large national database (DRIAMS) to an institutional database (CS)
Num_Models_Compared: 5 ML classifiers compared on the same spectra (Adaboost, MLP, KNN, LightGBM, LR), plus Random Forest and LR described in the methods and a DNN with transfer learning for cross-database prediction
Feature_Engineering: Mass spectra binned into 3 m/z bins from 2000 m/z to 20000 m/z giving a 6000-dimensional vector per sample; variance stabilisation of m/z, smoothing, baseline removal, intensity calibration and trimming; inter-peak distance ratio (IDR) used to refine peak identification
Feature_Selection_Method: No explicit feature selection reported; all binned m/z features (6000-dimensional vector) were used by the models, with SHAP used only to quantify the contribution of individual m/z features
Num_Features_Total: 6000 (3 m/z bins from 2000 to 20000 m/z per sample)
Num_Features_Selected: 6000 (all binned features used); the top 20 impactful features are reported for interpretation via SHAP
Class_Imbalance_Method: AUPRC (area under the precision-recall curve) reported alongside AUROC because of the imbalanced nature of the classes; Ada Boost described as adjusting weights of incorrectly classified instances in imbalanced data
Hyperparameter_Method: Extensive tuning of model hyperparameters using cross-validation within the training data
Other_Metrics: AUPR (area under precision-recall) reported alongside accuracy and AUROC for every model; no sensitivity, specificity, NPV, F1, kappa, MCC, RMSE or MAE
Baseline_Method: Comparison with previously published DRIAMS performance for oxacillin resistance (AUROC/AUPR 0.80/0.49) and head-to-head comparison of the ML classifiers within each database
Baseline_Performance: Published DRIAMS oxacillin resistance AUROC/AUPR 0.80/0.49, versus 0.93/0.93 with the Vitek 2-based model in the current study
Internal_Validation: Ten-fold cross-validation: the dataset was split into ten equal parts and each portion served in turn as the testing set; Table 2 used 60% CS training with 20% validation and 20% prediction, and DRIAMS-based fine-tuning
Train_Test_Split: Ten-fold cross-validation (nine portions training, one testing per fold); transfer learning experiment: 60% CS training, 20% CS validation, 20% CS prediction
Overfitting_Method: Increase in sample size for conservative training and layer transfer via transfer learning to avoid overfitting; ten-fold cross-validation and within-training hyperparameter tuning to keep performance consistent with the limited dataset sizes
Clinical_Insights: Overlapping m/z features (2423-2426, 4496-4499 and 3764-3767 m/z) predict both mecA presence and oxacillin resistance, and 2423-2426 m/z also contributes to resistance prediction for ERY, CLI, TET and TMP/SMX; grouped features outperform single peaks such as 2415 +/- 2.00 m/z, which only predicts PSM-mec
Generalisability_Details: Performance depends on database characteristics and the ML algorithm; differences in phylogenic strains, sample size, susceptibility profiles, MALDI-TOF instruments and technical variability explain the divergent predictive contributions; transfer learning from DRIAMS improved ERY, CLI and TET prediction in the CS database but not OX or TMP/SMX
Maturity_Evidence: Ten-fold cross-validation on the source databases is the only validation performed; the transfer-learning model is evaluated on held-out CS data (20%). No prospective use or clinical deployment is reported

AUROC_Population_Set: Test set of the aggregate dataset, N-12 model (Table 1)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation only: the 5,606-image training set was assessed by five-fold cross-validation and a separate 1,408-image test set was held back for final evaluation. The model was embedded in the TB-DRC-DSS web application, which was tested on 428 images drawn at random from the test dataset and rated by 31 medical staff, but no external validation or prospective clinical evaluation is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Multiclass drug-resistance classification and TB detection accuracy is not yet 100%, leaving room for better segmentation, augmentation, normalisation and denoising; the web application still needs therapy follow-up and further decision support; treatment regimens change with emerging resistance, so the pharmacist must follow WHO regimens and use data mining of patient drug-reaction data. (The related-work section also notes the small number of instances typical of deep learning for medical imaging.)
Reviewer_Notes: Presented as the first model able to determine TB and the type of drug resistance from a single CXR image and to display an appropriate treatment regimen; delivered as the TB-DRC-DSS web application (https://itbru.com/TDRC01/) with source code at https://github.com/aiosmartlab/AMIS-Ensemble-DL.
Sample_Size: 5,606 training and 1,408 test CXR images (7,008 in the aggregate dataset)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Data_Types_Used: Imaging; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: Portal dataset (TB Portals, NIAID); Montgomery County CXR dataset; Shenzhen CXR dataset; Dataset B (compiled by institutes under the Ministry of Health, Republic of Belarus); Kaggle public chest X-ray (COVID-19 and pneumonia) dataset
Dataset_Size: 7,008 CXR images in the aggregate dataset (5,606 train / 1,408 test); portal dataset 5,019 TB CXR images; Dataset A 800 images; Dataset B 306 images; Dataset C 6,432 images
Geographic_Representativeness: Data are pooled from several countries and sources - Montgomery County (USA) and Shenzhen (China) in Dataset A, institutes under the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Belarus in Dataset B, the multi-country TB Portals and the Kaggle repository - but geographic representativeness is not analysed or discussed.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Classification of chest X-ray images into five classes - TB-negative (non-TB), drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB), drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) - with a recommended treatment regimen returned by the TB-DRC-DSS.
Drug_Classes: Anti-tuberculosis (anti-TB) drugs; no specific agent or drug class is named - the paper refers to the recommended TB treatment regimen that the pharmacist updates.
AMR_Outcome_Definition: The label of each CXR image is the patient's drug-susceptibility category obtained from drug susceptibility testing (not read off the image): binary DS-TB vs DR-TB pairs and the MDR-TB and XDR-TB resistance categories.
AI_Purpose: Detect TB and classify the drug-resistance category from a chest X-ray image, and provide treatment recommendations, through the TB-DRC-DSS decision support system.
Num_Models_Compared: 12 proposed models (N-1 to N-12) compared with one another, plus performance compared against 13 published methods from the literature
Feature_Engineering: Lung-field image segmentation with a modified U-Net (EfficientNetB7 encoder), image augmentation, cropping, normalisation and enhancement of the CXR images before the three heterogeneous CNNs, followed by UWA / AMIS-WCE / AMIS-WLCE decision fusion of the CNN outputs.
Hyperparameter_Method: AMIS metaheuristic used to find the optimal decision-fusion weights (Wi and Sij); fixed training settings of batch sizes 16 (MobileNetV2), 2 (EfficientNetB7) and 8 (DenseNet121), 200 epochs and the Adam algorithm
Software_Libraries: TensorFlow; HTML and JavaScript for the web application; CNN architectures MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB7, DenseNet121 and a modified U-Net with EfficientNetB7 encoder
Other_Metrics: Confusion matrices (Figure 1); per-class accuracy (non-TB 98.99%, DS-TB 92.2%, DR-TB 97.1%, MDR-TB 88.7%, XDR-TB 91.1%); average percentage difference versus prior methods (Table 4); TB-DRC-DSS per-class % correct classification (Table 8); six-item user agreement questionnaire scored out of 10 (Table 9).
Baseline_Method: Published single-architecture and feature-based comparators (VGG16, ResNet50, EfficientNet, MobileNetv2, FuseNet, MAG-SD, CoroNet, TBXNet) and prior drug-resistance models (Karki et al. ResNet18, Tulo et al. mediastinal shape, Jaeger et al. texture/shape/edge, Kovalev et al., Ureta and Shrestha CNN)
Baseline_Performance: Portal dataset, DS vs DR: best prior AUC 93.6 (Tulo et al.) and 79.0 (Karki et al.) vs proposed 97.2 AUC / 95.2 accuracy. Dataset A: best comparator TBXNet 98.9 vs proposed 99.4; Dataset B: TBXNet 99.2 vs proposed 99.3; Dataset C: TBXNet 95.1 vs proposed 97.4.
Internal_Validation: Five-fold cross-validation on the 5,606-image training set, with a separate 1,408-image (20%) held-out test set for final evaluation
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% test (5,606 training images, 1,408 test images)
Overfitting_Method: Dropout layers in the modified U-Net decoder to improve generalisation and prevent over-fitting; residual blocks to avoid vanishing gradients; data augmentation
Clinical_Insights: The Grad-CAM heatmaps show which lung sectors drive each class: non-TB uses all six lung areas, DS-TB the lung interior from top to bottom, DR-TB the upper left and right sectors, and MDR-TB and XDR-TB the lower and upper left/right sectors, with MDR-TB using the inner and XDR-TB the outer portion of the lung.
Generalisability_Details: Performance is compared across datasets from different sources and countries (Dataset A: Montgomery County and Shenzhen; Dataset B: Belarus; Dataset C: Kaggle), but there is no discussion of applicability to other patient populations or settings.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: five-fold cross-validation of the 5,606-image training set and a held-out 1,408-image test set; the model was then embedded in the TB-DRC-DSS web application, tested on 428 images drawn at random from the test dataset and rated by 31 medical staff. No external validation or prospective clinical evaluation is reported.
Integration_Point: TB-DRC-DSS web application: the user uploads a CXR image, the deep learning model predicts the disease type, and the system returns medication recommendations for that disease
End_User_Described: Physicians who are TB specialists (pulmonologists and internal medicine); the pharmacist administers the TB-DRC-DSS and updates the treatment regimen prescribed to the physician
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Medical staff upload CXR image files from their personal computers; the image is forwarded to a server that diagnoses the disease and suggests appropriate drugs and medications; the pharmacist updates the treatment regimen; the recommendation is sent back to the user.
Future_Directions: Three research gaps: (1) develop a more accurate model for multiclass drug-resistant classification and TB detection (better image segmentation, augmentation and normalisation, and denoising); (2) extend the web application to support therapy follow-up and further decisions based on the recommended protocol; (3) let the pharmacist follow WHO treatment regimens, record the patient's drug reaction and use data mining to adapt the regimen as resistance emerges.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Grad-CAM (GradCAM heatmap visualisations on the X-ray images)
Limitation_Categories: Accuracy ceiling (classification is not 100% accurate) and scope for better image preprocessing (segmentation, augmentation, normalisation, denoising); web application lacks therapy follow-up and downstream decision support; regimens must be updated as treatment resistance emerges, requiring WHO-conformant pharmacist input and data mining of patient drug reactions.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Drug-susceptibility labels associated with each image are not produced from the image itself but obtained through drug susceptibility testing, and the analysis pools heterogeneous public datasets from different countries and institutions.
Reporting_Clarity: Generally clear, with minor internal inconsistencies: Table 9 is headed '30 doctors' while the text and abstract report 31 medical staff, and the 'Total' row of Table 8 sums the percentage columns to 463.8% and 36.2%.

Title: Development of Predictive Models to Inform a Novel Risk Categorization Framework for Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli–Caused Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection
Journal_Source: Clinical Infectious Diseases (CID), Infectious Diseases Society of America; volume 79, issue 2, pp. 295–304
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: GSK
Population_Description: Female patients aged ≥12 years with a UTI diagnosis (no evidence of complicated UTI) and a positive urine culture for E. coli within ±7 days of diagnosis; enrollees also needed documented pyuria and a confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test result for at least 1 agent in the 4 antibiotic classes of interest.
Age_Mean_Median: Mean age ranged from 49.7 to 50.4 years across the training and test cohorts for each antibiotic class
Top_Predictive_Features: Top predictors by absolute standardized log odds ratio: race; number of previous UTI episodes (recurrence); US Census Bureau region (particularly residence in the South); prior nonsusceptibility to β-lactams; prior treatment with fluoroquinolones.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: LASSO models (per antibiotic class; the paper's optimal algorithm, test-cohort AUROC 0.66–0.72); random forest algorithms (compared against LASSO via (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation, not selected as optimal); 4 final logistic regression models built on the union of the top 10 LASSO predictors — mean (SE) test-cohort AUROC 0.67 (0.010) for NTF, 0.66 (0.004) for SXT, 0.66 (0.005) for β-lactams, 0.72 (0.005) for fluoroquinolones.
Best_Performing_Model: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) predictive models — named the optimal predictive algorithm across all 4 antibiotic classes on mean AUROC and clinical interpretability; test-cohort AUROC 0.66–0.72
AUROC_Population_Set: Test cohorts (temporal validation); LASSO predictive models for nonsusceptibility to each of the 4 antibiotic classes
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were internally bootstrapped and temporally validated in the test cohorts of the same EHR dataset (training 1 October 2016–31 December 2018; test 1 January 2019–29 February 2020). No external validation was performed; the authors call for validation in different clinical settings and ex-US populations, so the highest level supported is internal validation.
Reported_Limitations: 1) Models and framework are not a decision algorithm recommending optimal antibiotic treatment; 2) population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates could not be included because the data were unavailable (Census Bureau region used as a proxy); 3) models were developed among patients who were mostly White and from the Midwest, limiting generalisability to diverse US populations; 4) models were anchored on the date of the susceptibility test result rather than the uUTI diagnosis date.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Race was identified as a predictor of nonsusceptibility and the authors note it should not be given a causal interpretation or used alone to inform treatment decisions, because it correlates with socioeconomic indicators that were not available in the data.
Sample_Size: 87 487 patients with confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test results (NTF n = 82 225; SXT n = 82 921; β-lactams n = 83 935; fluoroquinolones n = 81 223)
Conflicts_of_Interest: R. K. S. is a paid consultant to GSK. W. Y. C., K. K.-S., D. I., F. K., C. G., M. M., L. P., and J. R. are employees of Analysis Group, Inc., a consultancy that received funding from GSK to conduct this study. A. V. J., F. S. M.-G., P. S., D. F., M. T. P., and J. H. are employees of and shareholders in GSK. R. C. has served as a paid consultant to GSK.
Sex_Distribution: All female (study population restricted to female patients ≥12 years)
Inclusion_Criteria: Female patients ≥12 years of age with a diagnosis of UTI, without evidence of complicated UTI, and a positive urine culture for E. coli within ±7 days of the UTI diagnosis; documentation of pyuria within ±7 days of diagnosis; and a confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test result of the urinary E. coli isolate for at least 1 agent within the 4 antibiotic classes of interest within ±7 days of the UTI diagnosis.
Exclusion_Criteria: Evidence of complicated UTI
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: Optum's de-identified Electronic Health Record (EHR) dataset
Dataset_Size: 87 487 patients (NTF n = 82 225; SXT n = 82 921; β-lactams n = 83 935; fluoroquinolones n = 81 223)
Missing_Data_Method: Multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), assuming data were missing at random; results were largely consistent using MICE versus a complete case analysis.
Ethnicity_Details: Race distribution reported as 85.1%–85.5% White across training and test cohorts (model predictor categories: White [ref.], Black, Asian, Other/unknown); ethnicity (e.g. Hispanic/Latino) is not separately reported.
Geographic_Representativeness: Patients were mostly from the Midwest (63.8%–66.3%) and mostly White, across US Census Bureau regions; US-only data, so generalisability to other populations is limited.
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine culture; urinary E. coli isolate
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Nonsusceptibility (intermediate or resistant) of the patient's urinary E. coli isolate to each of 4 antibiotic classes: NTF, SXT, β-lactams, and fluoroquinolones (4 separate endpoints/models).
Drug_Classes: Nitrofurantoin (nitrofuran); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (folate-pathway inhibitor); β-lactams; fluoroquinolones
Specific_Antibiotics: Nitrofurantoin (NTF); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SXT); β-lactams; fluoroquinolones; fosfomycin is mentioned only as another first-line guideline option.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; ESBL
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Nonsusceptibility at the class level was defined by a urinary E. coli isolate categorized as “intermediate” or “resistant” to at least 1 of the respective antibiotic agent(s) within each class based on susceptibility test results.
AI_Purpose: To develop and validate predictive models estimating the probability that a female patient's urinary E. coli isolate is nonsusceptible to each of 4 antibiotic classes for uUTI, to identify key predictors of nonsusceptibility, and to build a novel risk categorization framework (low/moderate/high risk) to inform empiric prescribing.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 algorithm types compared (LASSO and random forest) via (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation; 8 fitted models in total (4 LASSO models and 4 final logistic regression models, one per antibiotic class)
Feature_Engineering: Candidate features (demographics, clinical characteristics, microbiology-related characteristics) were evaluated over a 12-month lookback period prior to the susceptibility test result date; Table 3 footnotes show window-based derivations (e.g. previous UTI episodes excluding the uUTI diagnosis date; antibiotic treatment from 6 months prior to 3 days preceding diagnosis; counts of oral antibiotic prescriptions and ED visits).
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO, with the top 10 predictors per class ranked by absolute standardized log odds ratio; the union of the top 10 predictors across the 4 LASSO models (22 features) was used in the final logistic regression models.
Num_Features_Selected: 22 features for each final logistic regression model (union of the top 10 predictors from the 4 LASSO models)
Hyperparameter_Method: (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation used to select the optimal algorithm (LASSO vs random forest); LASSO models fitted in the training cohort with internal bootstrap validation.
Software_Libraries: SAS (version 9.4, SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina) and Python (version 3.9); no specific libraries named
Other_Metrics: AUROC with standard error; predicted probability distributions (mean/SD, median/IQR, min–max) versus observed nonsusceptibility rates; calibration (mean calibration and calibration plots); odds ratios with 95% CIs and P values; proportions of patients in each risk category.
Baseline_Method: Previously published predictive models for antibiotic nonsusceptibility in uUTI (reference 17); US prevalence of nonsusceptibility to each antibiotic class is used as the comparator for the risk categories.
Internal_Validation: Internal bootstrap validation of the LASSO models in the training cohort (mean AUROC and SE); temporal validation in the test cohorts with the SE of the AUROC derived using 200 bootstrapping samples; model selection by (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation.
Train_Test_Split: Temporal split: susceptibility test result date 1 October 2016–31 December 2018 = training cohort; 1 January 2019–29 February 2020 = test cohort.
Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Feature importance / permutation importance
Clinical_Insights: The risk categorization framework separates risk better than US prevalence alone: a patient's probability of a truly nonsusceptible SXT isolate rises to 53.9% if their isolate is categorized high risk and falls to 15.3% if low risk, versus a 25.4% baseline prevalence; the proportion of patients with high-risk isolates was 3- to 12-fold higher among those with truly nonsusceptible isolates.
Generalisability_Details: Models were developed among patients who were mostly White and from the Midwest, with E. coli–caused uUTI, which may limit applicability to diverse US populations and to uUTI caused by other uropathogens; race and Census Bureau region were retained as predictors to improve external validity; future validation in different clinical settings and ex-US populations is proposed.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal bootstrap validation in the training cohort and temporal validation in the test cohorts (same Optum EHR dataset, different time periods); no external or prospective validation is reported.
Integration_Point: Not integrated; proposed future integration into clinical workflows via a data visualization tool that would present patients' predicted probabilities and risk profiles to clinicians.
End_User_Described: Clinicians treating uUTI (to inform empiric prescribing)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians would derive an isolate's predicted probabilities of nonsusceptibility to the 4 antibiotic classes, generate risk profiles, and integrate the framework into clinical workflows via a data visualization tool to assist empiric treatment decisions; the models are not a decision algorithm.
Barriers_List: Models are not a decision algorithm; population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates were unavailable; models developed among mostly White patients from the Midwest (limited generalisability); predictions anchored on the susceptibility test result date rather than the uUTI diagnosis date; race cannot be interpreted causally or used alone for treatment decisions.
Facilitators_List: First evaluation of nonsusceptibility to 4 commonly prescribed antibiotic classes for uUTI in the US using a large rich EHR database; features identified from a comprehensive literature search plus clinical expert input; two complementary approaches (predictive models with temporal validity and a risk categorization framework).
Future_Directions: Validate the models in different clinical settings and in ex-US populations, and recalibrate them to include population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates; use the models and framework to develop a data visualization tool integrated into clinical workflows.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Absolute standardized log odds ratio from the LASSO models (top 10 predictors per model, combined across models).
Limitation_Categories: Framing/scope (not a decision algorithm); missing data on population-level features (local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates); population representativeness / generalisability (mostly White, Midwest, E. coli only); timing of the prediction anchor (susceptibility test result date vs uUTI diagnosis date); race cannot be interpreted causally and socioeconomic indicators were unavailable.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing information on candidate features was limited and results were largely consistent using MICE versus complete case analysis; population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates were not available in the data source.
Page_References: Article pp. 295–304 (CID 2024;79(2)); abstract p. 295; methods pp. 296–297 (data source, population, endpoints, model development); results pp. 297–301 (final model performance Table 2 p. 299; predictor log ORs Table 3 pp. 300–301); limitations pp. 302–303; conclusions pp. 303–304. Page 11 is a pharmaceutical advertisement, not part of the article.

Title: Development a risk prediction nomogram for multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection in gastrointestinal fistula patients during the perioperative period
Journal_Source: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
Funder_Names: Anhui Provincial Department of Education institutions key scientific research project (2023AH053380, 2022AH052319); Health Commission of Anhui Province Key Scientific Research projects (AHWJ2022a026); Jiangsu Provincial Department of Science and Technology key research and development projects (BE2021727)
Population_Description: 266 hospitalised patients with gastrointestinal fistulas who underwent surgical treatment at Anhui No. 2 Provincial People's Hospital (Jan 2022-Jul 2024); 157 (59.02%) tested positive for multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection and 109 (40.98%) tested negative; the 266 cases were randomly split 2:1 into a training cohort (n=177) and a validation cohort (n=89).
Age_Mean_Median: 56.23 ± 16.02 years (training cohort, n=177); 55.22 ± 15.77 years (validation cohort, n=89)
Top_Predictive_Features: Nomogram points assigned to the six independent predictors: preoperative neutrophil level 100 points (highest), preoperative WBC level 92.1 points, postoperative WBC count 34.2 points, secondary surgery 30.3 points, length of hospital stay 20.3 points, postoperative CRP level 13.8 points.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: One model was developed and evaluated: a nomogram built from multivariable logistic regression with six independent predictors (secondary surgery, length of hospital stay, preoperative WBC, preoperative neutrophil count, postoperative WBC, postoperative CRP). Reported performance - AUC 0.905 (95% CI 0.864-0.947) in the training cohort and 0.793 (0.690-0.896) in the validation cohort; accuracy 0.825/0.693; sensitivity 0.889/0.692; specificity 0.781/0.694; PPV 0.736/0.545; NPV 0.911/0.810; Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.970 (training) and 0.674 (validation). No comparator models were evaluated.
Best_Performing_Model: Nomogram based on multivariable logistic regression (the only model developed and evaluated; decision metric = AUC 0.905 in the training cohort and 0.793 in the validation cohort)
Accuracy_Value: 0.825 (training cohort); 0.693 (validation cohort)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
Specificity_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
AUROC_Population_Set: Training cohort (n=177) and validation cohort (n=89) from the 266-patient single-centre study cohort
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The model was developed on a training cohort and evaluated on a validation cohort created by randomly splitting the same 266 single-centre patients 2:1, with discrimination (AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow) and DCA reported for both. No external cohort and no prospective evaluation: the authors state further prospective studies are necessary before widespread clinical application, so the highest level the evidence supports is internal validation.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective single-centre design subject to some degree of selection bias; limited number of case observations from a small sample size and a single centre; further prospective studies needed to validate the nomogram's accuracy before widespread clinical application; antibiotic use was not included as a factor because of the complexity of antibiotic-therapy information (many patients had already received antibiotics before transfer).
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethics approval by the medical ethics committee of Anhui No. 2 Provincial People's Hospital; study conducted per the Declaration of Helsinki with written informed consent from all participants; the paper declares no generative-AI use. No AI-specific governance, deployment or monitoring risk discussion.
Sample_Size: 266 patients with gastrointestinal fistulas (157 multidrug-resistant-positive, 109 negative); 329 pathogenic strains isolated
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Sex_Distribution: Training cohort (n=177): female 79, male 98. Validation cohort (n=89): female 41, male 48.
Inclusion_Criteria: (1) Diagnosis of gastrointestinal fistula: any discharge from the gastrointestinal tract, which may include abdominal abscesses or spontaneous drainage through a stoma; (2) undergoing surgical treatment during hospitalisation; (3) perioperative cultures of sputum, blood, pus, bile, etc. indicating infections with multidrug-resistant bacteria and fungi; (4) diagnosis of multidrug-resistant bacteria defined as bacteria resistant to three or more commonly used antimicrobial agents that are typically sensitive.
Exclusion_Criteria: (1) Patients with gastrointestinal fistulas who did not receive surgical treatment; (2) patients who died within 24 hours post-surgery or were discharged.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Hospital information system of Anhui No. 2 Provincial People's Hospital (Hefei, China)
Dataset_Size: 266 patients with gastrointestinal fistulas; 329 pathogenic strains isolated (84 Gram-positive, 215 Gram-negative, 30 fungal)
Missing_Data_Method: Indicators with more than 20% missing values were discarded before the multivariable analysis (this is why preoperative PCT and CRP were excluded from the multivariate model).
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-centre study: all 266 patients were enrolled at Anhui No. 2 Provincial People's Hospital, Hefei, China; the authors acknowledge a small sample size from a single centre, and there is no external or geographically distinct validation cohort.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Perioperative cultures of sputum, blood, pus, bile; resistant strains came from blood (26%), drainage (17%), sputum (15%), pus (14%) and conductor housings (12%)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection in patients with gastrointestinal fistulas during the perioperative period (positive perioperative cultures; 157/266 patients, 59.02%)
Pathogens: Gram-positive: Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus haemolyticus, Staphylococcus aureus, Human staphylococcus subspecies, Enterococcus raffinosus, Staphylococcus sciuri, Staphylococcus warneri, Enterococcus gallinarum, Staphylococcus capitis, Enterococcus vulgare, Streptococcus anginosus. Gram-negative: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter aerogenes, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Enterobacter cloacae, Serratia marcescens, Klebsiella oxytoca, Citrobacter freundii, Corynebacterium striatum, pseudomonas fluorescens. Fungal: Candida albicans, Candida parapsilosis, Candida glabrata, Candida tropicalis, Candida guilliermondii, filamentous fungi.
Drug_Classes: Penicillins and beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor combinations (penicillin, amoxicillin, ampicillin, piperacillin, piperacillin/tazobactam, ampicillin/sulbactam, cefoperazone/sulbactam, ceftazidime/avibactam), cephalosporins (cefazolin, cefuroxime, cefoxitin, ceftazidime, cefepime, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime), carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem), monobactam (aztreonam), aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin), fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin), tetracyclines (tigecycline, doxycycline), polymyxins (polymyxin B), glycopeptides (vancomycin), oxazolidinones (linezolid), lipopeptides (daptomycin), macrolides (erythromycin), rifamycins (rifampicin) and folate-pathway inhibitors (trimethoprim).
Specific_Antibiotics: gentamicin, levofloxacin, tigecycline, ciprofloxacin, daptomycin, erythromycin, linezolid, penicillin, rifampicin, tetracycline, vancomycin, amoxicillin, piperacillin/tazobactam, piperacillin, ampicillin/sulbactam, ampicillin, cefazolin, cefuroxime, cefoxitin, cefoperazone and sulbactam, ceftazidime, cefepime, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, aztreonam, imipenem, meropenem, amikacin, doxycycline, trimethoprim, polymyxin B, ceftazidime and avibactam
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Multidrug resistance is defined as bacteria that exhibit resistance to three or more commonly used antimicrobial agents that are typically sensitive; the study outcome is a positive perioperative culture (sputum, blood, pus, bile, etc.) for multidrug-resistant bacteria or fungi, with resistance mechanisms (CRE, ESBL, CR-PA, CR-AB) and per-antibiotic resistance rates reported separately.
AI_Purpose: Develop and validate a risk-prediction nomogram for multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection in patients with gastrointestinal fistulas during the perioperative period, so that clinicians can assess infection risk before surgery and target infection prevention and antibiotic selection.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single nomogram based on multivariable logistic regression; no comparator models were developed or benchmarked)
Feature_Engineering: No engineered transformations reported: 37 candidate indicators were taken directly from the hospital information system (surgical characteristics, comorbidity, clinical outcome, ICU and hospital stay, and preoperative/postoperative laboratory values) and screened by univariate then multivariable logistic regression; 'postoperative' was defined as the most recent test at the specimen that indicated multidrug-resistant bacteria or fungal infection, or results 5-10 days post-surgery if there was no such infection.
Feature_Selection_Method: Univariate logistic regression screening followed by variable selection in a multivariable logistic regression model
Num_Features_Total: 37 clinical indicators (training cohort)
Software_Libraries: R packages: regplot (nomogram), pROC (ROC curve/AUC), rmda (decision curve analysis)
Other_Metrics: Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit P = 0.970 (training cohort) and 0.674 (validation cohort); variance inflation factors 1.203-2.079 for the seven covariates; optimal cut-off 0.624; NPV 0.911 (training) and 0.810 (validation).
Internal_Validation: The 266 included cases were randomly divided 2:1 into a training cohort (n=177) for model development and a validation cohort (n=89) for assessing predictive performance; discrimination (AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test) and decision curve analysis were reported for both cohorts.
Train_Test_Split: Random 2:1 split; training cohort n=177, validation cohort n=89
Clinical_Insights: The authors read the nomogram weights clinically: secondary surgery (reoperation) is a considerable setback that heralds adverse clinical outcomes and is itself an independent risk factor; prolonged hospital and ICU stays create a favourable environment for multidrug-resistant organisms; preoperative WBC/neutrophil and postoperative WBC levels reflect systemic inflammatory status; and postoperative CRP is an independent risk factor, so the model informs targeted infection prevention and rational antibiotic use.
Generalisability_Details: The authors state that although the study was divided into training and validation cohorts, further prospective studies are necessary to validate the nomogram's accuracy before widespread clinical application; the small single-centre sample also limits generalisability.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence for the level: 2:1 random split of the 266 single-centre patients into training (n=177) and validation (n=89) cohorts, with AUC 0.905 (training) and 0.793 (validation), Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.970 and 0.674, and DCA in both cohorts. No external validation, no prospective evaluation, no CDS integration - internal validation only.
Integration_Point: Perioperative risk assessment of patients with gastrointestinal fistulas requiring surgery, to identify those at high risk of multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection and target infection prevention and antibiotic selection.
End_User_Described: healthcare providers / clinicians
