Title: Predictive phage therapy for Escherichia coli urinary tract infections: Cocktail selection for therapy based on machine learning models
Journal_Source: PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences), 2024, Vol. 121, No. 12, e2313574121
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Canine Welfare Grant from The Dog's Trust; National Council of Science and Technology of Mexico (CONACYT); University of Edinburgh; University of Glasgow; Roslin Institute PhD studentship supported by the BBSRC
Population_Description: 314 uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) strains from urinary tract infections in canine (n = 203) and human (n = 111) patients in the Edinburgh area (human urine n = 81 and human blood n = 30 isolates), whole genome sequenced; a further 10 newly isolated clinical strains were held back for validation
Data_Source_Other: Study-generated interaction dataset: 314 sequenced E. coli isolates challenged with 31 phage in artificial urine growth assays (plus Illumina whole genome sequences)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: 31 Random Forest regression models (one per phage, MUVR package, recursive feature reduction); average RMSE 8-23 across models (interaction score range 0-100); classifier metrics at a threshold of 60 with F1 highest for the generalist phage CHAP1 (0.83)
Best_Performing_Model: Random Forest ML model for the generalist phage CHAP1 (highest F1 = 0.83; F1 chosen as the performance metric)
F1_Population_Set: 301 of the 314 isolates, used for model training and testing; one 75-25 split with 10-fold cross-validation
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest evidence level is external validation: models trained on 301 of the 314 isolates were applied to 10 newly isolated clinical UPEC strains not in the training set, and predicted bespoke cocktails were compared with observed bespoke cocktails and a general cocktail in artificial urine and canine urine
Reported_Limitations: Proof-of-principle study with a single species (E. coli) and 31 phage; artificial urine cannot reproduce the variability of real urine (pH, osmolarity, host factors); most genomic features are grouped genes with no clear annotation, so receptor and resistance mechanisms cannot be dissected; a high rate of False Negatives can leave too few phage predicted active for cocktail design; feature extraction from long-read data of complex samples untested; wider adoption requires changes in licensing and management of expectations
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: False Negatives are preferred to False Positives from a cocktail perspective, but a high False Negative rate can leave a paucity of phage predicted as active; antagonism was seen where a general cocktail scored higher (worse) than its best constituent phage, and bacterial resistance evolved against the general cocktail for some strains
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: ML models replicate biases in their training datasets (illustrated by phage A01, whose imbalanced dataset produced a model prone to False Negatives), and accuracy falls when models are applied to strains from a different population structure
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Safety and registration issues for predictive phage therapy, and licensing plus management of expectations of clinicians and the public
Reviewer_Notes: Extra review notes: (a) the study's unit of analysis is one Random Forest model per phage, so the best model is taken as CHAP1 (F1 = 0.83, the highest and the one the paper highlights); (b) the paper reports no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, AUROC, NPV, AUPRC, kappa, MCC, MAE or calibration figures in the article text - recall and precision values live in SI Appendix Fig. S2, which is not in the PDF; (c) no antimicrobial susceptibility testing, no patient-level clinical data and no environmental/SES variables are used; (d) no compute hardware is described
Unresolved_Items: Numeric recall and precision for the CHAP1 model are in SI Appendix Fig. S2 and per-model RMSE in SI Appendix Table S2 - not available in the article PDF, so Sensitivity_Reported/Precision_PPV_Reported are answered No per the spec note; the number of protein-variant features in the initial model is never stated; whether the Supplementary-Materials field means 'the study has SI' or 'the extractor used SI' is ambiguous
Sample_Size: 314 E. coli isolates (203 canine, 81 human urine and 30 human blood); 301 of the 314 used for ML model training and testing after filtering fragmented assemblies
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: E. coli isolates from canine and human urinary tract infections (plus human bacteraemia blood isolates) that were whole genome sequenced; for the ML analysis, isolates whose assemblies were not fragmented (<600 contigs), giving 301 of the 314 isolates
Exclusion_Criteria: Isolates with fragmented assemblies (>=600 contigs) were excluded from ML model training and testing, leaving 301 of the 314 isolates
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; Other
Data_Source_Name: Enterobase (workspace:97040, ecoli_train); Illumina sequencing by MicrobesNG
Dataset_Size: 31 phage x 314 isolates (>9,000 interactions, each in triplicate against a no-phage control); >27,000 growth curves in total
Geographic_Representativeness: Strains were collected from canine and human patients presenting at local clinics in the Edinburgh area only; the authors describe the collection as representative subpopulations rather than a geographically comprehensive sample of UPEC
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine (E. coli isolated from canine and human urinary tract infections) and blood (human bacteraemia isolates)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Phage activity (phage susceptibility) of each E. coli isolate, quantified as an interaction score: the ratio of the area under the growth curve with phage to that of the no-phage control x 100
Drug_Classes: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins (named as first-line UTI antibiotics in humans and pets; background, not modelled)
Specific_Antibiotics: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; fluoroquinolones; cephalosporins (background only; no antimicrobial susceptibility testing performed)
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary Infection/No Infection label from the measured and predicted interaction scores at a threshold of 60: score <60 = infection (active interaction), score >60 = no infection
AI_Purpose: To train ML models on bacterial whole genome sequence features to predict phage activity against individual E. coli isolates, so that effective phage cocktails can be selected without manual screening
Num_Models_Compared: 31 (one Random Forest model per phage)
Feature_Engineering: Pangenome analysis (panaroo v1.2.9) of the 301 bacterial sequences to define predicted genes as protein variants (PVs), encoded as binary presence/absence vectors for each isolate
Feature_Selection_Method: Recursive feature reduction using the MUVR package: an initial model with all PVs, then top-ranking features retained to build a smaller model, repeating while RMSE stayed similar
Class_Imbalance_Method: F1 chosen as the performance metric to account for class imbalance; imbalanced interaction datasets (up to 85:15) were investigated for model bias via confusion matrices; a predefined F1 cutoff of 0.6 used for practical selection
Software_Libraries: MUVR (random forest regression and feature reduction); panaroo (v1.2.9); prokka (v1.14.5); gplots (v3.1.3); Enterobase Tool Kit (EToKi); SkanIt Software (Thermo); PRISM (GraphPad)
Other_Metrics: RMSE (score prediction); F1, recall and precision (classification at threshold 60); False Positive and False Negative counts for the CHAP1 model (7% FN, 10.8% FP); paired t tests with P values for cocktail comparisons
Internal_Validation: One 75-25 training/testing split with 10-fold cross-validation (MUVR)
External_Validation_Description: 10 newly isolated clinical UPEC strains (3 canine and 7 human) not used in model training were genome sequenced and run through the models; predicted and observed bespoke cocktails were then tested in artificial urine and canine urine
Generalisability_Details: Models should hold within a similar population structure to the training set but accuracy falls on strains from different population structures; the strain collection covers local canine and human UPEC isolates only, and more generalist phage are needed to make cocktail selection broadly applicable
Maturity_Evidence: External validation on 10 independent sequenced clinical isolates: predicted bespoke cocktails were more effective than a generic cocktail and comparable to bespoke cocktails built from measured activity
Integration_Point: Clinical laboratory diagnostic sequencing: isolate genome sequence is fed to the models to select phage cocktails for the patient
End_User_Described: Clinicians (human and veterinary) and the general public as recipients of phage therapy; expectations of both must be managed
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Direct sequencing of nucleic acids from clinical samples (e.g. urine) gives the bacterial genome, which is run through the phage ML models to predict active phage and build a bespoke cocktail, with the interaction dataset continually reinforced by new observations
Barriers_List: Artificial urine cannot capture the complexity of real urine (pH, osmolarity, host response); most genomic features are unannotated grouped genes; class imbalance limits model reliability for narrow-host-range phage; feature extraction from long-read/mixed samples untested; licensing and expectation management needed for clinical adoption
Facilitators_List: High-throughput interaction platforms (e.g. 50 x 96-well plates) can generate the required training datasets quickly; direct sequencing of clinical samples already works for E. coli in canine urine; generalist phage with higher activity increase model reliability and cocktail options
Future_Directions: Include more generalist phage in interaction datasets and prefer phage targeting at least 30% of the population (class imbalance below 85:15); combine associative and function-based features in future phage selection pipelines; test feature extraction from long-read data of complex samples; continually reinforce the learning dataset with clinical sequencing; move into clinical practice with licensing and expectation management
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Recursive feature reduction / top-ranking feature selection with the MUVR package; no named features or importance values are reported
Limitation_Categories: Methodological: unannotated genomic features, no functional dissection, class imbalance, proof-of-principle scope, untested long-read/mixed-sample feature extraction. Applicability: artificial urine does not represent real urine; local strain population only. Translation: licensing, registration, safety, expectation management
Data_Quality_Concerns: High-quality training sets with phenotypic interaction data are critical; interaction datasets for some phage were highly imbalanced (up to 85:15); most features are grouped genes with no clear annotation, so functional meaning is uncertain
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: the interaction-score definition, the threshold of 60, and the formulas for precision, recall and F1 are all given in Materials and Methods, with per-model RMSE and F1 reported
Page_References: pp. 1-9 (main article); model results pp. 3-6; Materials and Methods pp. 7-8

Title: Risk factors and predictive model for nosocomial infections by extensively drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
Journal_Source: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
Funder_Names: Science Technology Department of Zhejiang province, China (LGC22H200018); Jinhua Science and Technology Bureau, Zhejiang province, China (2021-3-026)
Population_Description: Hospitalized patients at Jinhua Central Hospital infected with Acinetobacter baumannii: 212 XDRAB-infected and 347 non-XDRAB (NXDRAB) AB-infected, 559 in total; randomly split 7:3 into a training set (391) and a test set (168).
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: Paper ranks 10 LASSO-selected features (lambda.1se) and 8 independent risk factors from multivariable logistic regression and the nomogram (importance = LASSO coefficients / logistic ORs): ICU stay 1-7 days (OR=3.970), ICU stay >7 days (OR=12.316), hypoproteinemia (OR=3.249/3.261), glucocorticoid use (OR=2.371), urinary catheterization (OR=2.148), mechanical ventilation (OR=2.737), diabetes mellitus (OR=2.435), carbapenem use (OR=6.649), b-lactamase inhibitor use (OR=4.146); smoking history and CRP were in the LASSO 10 but not retained.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: One model only - a multivariable logistic regression nomogram (no model comparison): training-set C-index 0.932, AUC 0.9322; test-set AUC 0.9291 (0.929); Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.47.
AUROC_Population_Set: Training set, n=391 (internal validation); test set, n=168 (validation set)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation with 1000 bootstrap samples from the training set (C-index 0.932) and a held-out test set that the authors label 'external' but which is a 7:3 random split of the same single-centre cohort; the authors themselves state that external validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries is still necessary.
Reported_Limitations: Single-centre study (coefficients may vary; geographic bias; limited generalizability; external validation with other institutions, regions and countries necessary); retrospective data from electronic medical records and laboratory systems may be incomplete and some intended factors could not be included; selection bias unavoidable; future prospective studies needed.
Reviewer_Notes: Single-model nomogram study (LASSO + multivariable logistic regression); no models are compared, so model-level metric fields were answered for the one nomogram on its primary dataset (training set n=391) and the fields for metrics the paper never computes are 'No'.
Unresolved_Items: Whether the 7:3 random-split test set that the authors call 'external validation' should be coded as external validation (level 3) or internal validation (level 2) for Clinical_Maturity_Level.
Sample_Size: 559 patients (212 XDRAB-infected, 347 non-XDRAB AB-infected); training set 391 cases, test set 168 cases
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: 1. Patients hospitalized at Jinhua Central Hospital from January 2021 to December 2023. 2. Patients meeting the CDC criteria for A. baumannii infection. 3. Clinically infected AB specimens include sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, urine, pleural fluid, ascites, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, wound secretions and puncture fluid. 4. Only the first AB infection in each patient. 5. XDRAB defined as a strain susceptible to only one or two drugs with potential antifusobacterial activity (mainly polymyxins and tigecycline).
Exclusion_Criteria: 2. Patients infected with pathogens other than AB or colonized with AB without clinical infection. 3. Patients with AB infection detected within 48 hours of admission, transferred out within 48 hours of admission, who died, or who abandoned treatment. 4. Patients with significant missing clinical data. (Also: contaminated samples or duplicate strains from the same patient.)
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: Jinhua Central Hospital (single-centre electronic medical records and laboratory systems)
Dataset_Size: 559 patients; 35 candidate variables screened by LASSO
Missing_Data_Method: VIM package used to visualize missing-value distribution; factors with more than 10% missing values excluded; MICE package multiple imputation for factors with less than 10% missing values.
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre in Jinhua, Zhejiang, China (Jinhua Central Hospital), January 2021 - December 2023; the authors acknowledge geographic bias and limited generalizability.
Specimen_Type_Detail: sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, urine, pleural fluid, ascites, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, wound secretions, and puncture fluid
Primary_AMR_Outcome: XDRAB infection (nosocomial) among hospitalized A. baumannii-infected patients, modelled against non-XDRAB AB (NXDRAB) infection.
Pathogens: Acinetobacter baumannii (extensively drug-resistant, XDRAB; and non-XDRAB AB)
Drug_Classes: aminoglycosides; carbapenems; quinolones; beta-lactamase inhibitors; broad-spectrum cephalosporins
Specific_Antibiotics: tobramycin; amikacin; gentamicin; imipenem; meropenem; levofloxacin; ciprofloxacin; piperacillin-tazobactam; cefoperazone-sulbactam; ceftazidime; ceftriaxone; cefepime
AMR_Outcome_Definition: XDRAB is defined as a strain of A. baumannii susceptible to only one or two drugs with potential antifusobacterial activity (mainly polymyxins and tigecycline); the outcome is XDRAB infection versus non-XDRAB AB infection.
AI_Purpose: To establish a practical infection prediction model (LASSO regression variable selection plus multivariable logistic regression, visualized as a nomogram) that lets clinicians assess the risk of XDRAB infection and guide early isolation and treatment.
Feature_Engineering: ICU admission time recoded into three intervals (no ICU admission / 1-7 days / >7 days) calculated from admission to first AB detection; hypoproteinemia defined as serum albumin below 30 g/L; NLR and other blood parameters collected.
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO regression with 10-fold cross-validation (lambda.1se = 0.03450), keeping 10 non-zero-coefficient features for the multivariable logistic regression.
Num_Features_Selected: 10 (non-zero coefficients at lambda.1se); 8 retained as independent risk factors in the nomogram
Hyperparameter_Method: 10-fold cross-validation to determine the lambda value; lambda.min = 0.0065 (24 variables) versus lambda.1se = 0.03450 (10 variables), lambda.1se selected.
Software_Libraries: glmnet; rms; VIM; MICE (R packages)
Other_Metrics: C-index 0.932 (training) / 0.929 (testing); AUC 0.9322 (training) and 0.9291 (test); Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.47; OR with 95% CI for each risk factor; decision curve analysis and clinical impact curve.
Baseline_Method: Univariate comparison of XDRAB versus NXDRAB groups (independent samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U-test for continuous variables, chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables).
Internal_Validation: 1000 bootstrap samples from the training set; C-index 0.932; Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.47; calibration curve close to the 45-degree line.
Train_Test_Split: 7:3 randomization by R software - training set 391 cases, test set 168 cases
External_Validation_Description: Test set of 168 cases from the same 7:3 random split of the single-centre cohort (AUC 0.9291); not an independent external cohort - the authors state external validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries is necessary.
Overfitting_Method: LASSO penalisation to reduce dimensionality and multicollinearity-induced overfitting; internal validation by 1000 bootstrap samples.
Clinical_Insights: Clinicians can quickly assess the risk of XDRAB infection from existing clinical data and implement timely isolation and treatment; early transfer from ICU to general wards for eligible patients could reduce risk; rational use of carbapenems and b-lactamase inhibitors remains crucial.
Generalisability_Details: Single-centre, single-country cohort; coefficients may vary under different circumstances; external validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries is necessary.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation with 1000 bootstrap samples (C-index 0.932) and a held-out test set (AUC 0.9291) drawn from the same single-centre cohort; the authors state external validation with other institutions, regions and countries is still necessary - no prospective or deployed use.
Integration_Point: Early risk assessment of hospitalized patients (nomogram scoring from existing clinical data) to trigger timely isolation and treatment.
End_User_Described: Clinicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians score the nomogram from existing clinical data to assess XDRAB risk and implement timely isolation and treatment; the paper notes early transfer out of the ICU for eligible patients.
Future_Directions: External validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries; prospective studies to validate the findings further; more prospective studies on glycaemic control and XDRAB infection.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (sociodemographic, behavioural, clinical, laboratory, pharmacological, healthcare utilisation)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: LASSO regression coefficients at lambda.1se and multivariable logistic regression odds ratios; nomogram points scaled from the regression coefficients.
Limitation_Categories: Single-centre design / geographic bias / limited generalizability; retrospective data from electronic medical records and laboratory systems (incomplete data, intended factors not included); selection bias; need for external validation and prospective studies.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Retrospective data from electronic medical records and laboratory systems may be incomplete and some intended factors could not be analysed; individual missing values in continuous variables handled by exclusion (>10% missing) or MICE multiple imputation.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear, TRIPOD-guided reporting of variable selection, model development, internal and external validation, calibration and clinical utility.

Sample_Size: 11,996 KP specimens identified from 165,299 bacterial specimens; 11,127 specimens analysed for LEV resistance and 11,623 for CIP resistance
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared
Inclusion_Criteria: Klebsiella pneumoniae specimens identified by MALDI-TOF MS that underwent AST for levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin with the VITEK 2 system
Exclusion_Criteria: Specimens with intermediate AST results: 869 excluded from the LEV analysis (leaving 11,127) and 373 from the CIP analysis (leaving 11,623)

Data_Source_Name: No public dataset named - local Tri-Service General Hospital and 4 district hospital MALDI-TOF MS/AST data (January 2021-December 2023)
Dataset_Size: 165,299 bacterial specimens; 11,996 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates (11,127 LEV analysis, 11,623 CIP analysis)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single country (Taiwan); specimens from Tri-Service General Hospital and 4 district hospitals, no wider geographic sampling reported
Specimen_Type_Detail: bacterial specimens / Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) specimens (routine clinical samples; specimen site not stated)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance of Klebsiella pneumoniae to levofloxacin (LEV) and ciprofloxacin (CIP), classified from MALDI-TOF MS spectra using machine learning
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones (quinolones)
Specific_Antibiotics: Levofloxacin (LEV); ciprofloxacin (CIP)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible phenotype from VITEK 2 AST interpreted with CLSI clinical breakpoints; specimens with intermediate results excluded

Feature_Engineering: m/z ranges segmented into 1-unit intervals with a +/- 2-unit tolerance for grouping; peak intensity values for resistant and susceptible strains extracted and logarithmically transformed; segments with feature importance below 0.01 filtered out as background noise
Feature_Selection_Method: Feature importance thresholding (segments with a feature importance value below 0.01 removed as background noise)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Resampling with sklearn.utils: downsampling of over-represented classes and upsampling of underrepresented classes

Baseline_Performance: Ciprofloxacin: logistic regression testing AUC 0.84, accuracy 0.78; LDA testing AUC 0.80, accuracy 0.77 (versus random forest AUC 0.95, accuracy 0.87)
Internal_Validation: Temporal hold-out: October-December specimens used as the validation set, validated against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
Train_Test_Split: Temporal split - January to September specimens for training, October to December specimens for validation
Clinical_Insights: The same top 15 m/z spectral features are associated with resistance to both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, suggesting a universal resistance mechanism despite the different modes of action; these spectral markers could support rapid resistance detection

End_User_Described: health care professionals (clinicians)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Sample collection, MALDI-TOF MS analysis and AI-CDSS resistance prediction integrated into the antibiotic resistance-testing workflow; predicted resistance determination in approximately 3 days versus the conventional 4-day timeline for standard AST
Stewardship_Details: Antimicrobial stewardship benefit is claimed (faster resistance determination is said to enhance stewardship and ensure appropriate and effective treatment) but no stewardship outcome was measured
Barriers_List: Resistance mechanisms not mediated at the protein-peptide level or outside m/z 2000-20,000 are not captured; intermediate AST results excluded and remain unpredictable; dataset balancing and feature selection are intricate; limited data and antibiotic access challenges in low- and middle-income countries
Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is already indispensable for rapid and accurate microorganism identification in routine laboratories; ML plus MALDI-TOF is a faster route than NGS/PCR; a web-based AI-CDSS is easily distributed to health care professionals

Title: Leveraging large-scale Mycobacterium tuberculosis whole genome sequence data to characterise drug-resistant mutations using machine learning and statistical approaches
Country_Countries: 66 countries across all WHO regions (Europe 37.4%, Africa 24.5%, South East Asia 15.4%, Western Pacific 11.1%, Americas 8.9%, Other 2.8%); study institutions in the United Kingdom
Funder_Names: UKRI (BBSRC BB/X018156/1; MRC MR/X005895/1; EPSRC EP/Y018842/1)
Population_Description: 35,777 M. tuberculosis isolates with WGS (> 20-fold coverage) and corresponding phenotypic drug-susceptibility test (pDST) data, sourced from 66 countries across all WHO regions
Data_Source_Other: Public repositories/archives of Illumina whole genome sequences with linked phenotypic drug-susceptibility test data for M. tuberculosis isolates
Top_Predictive_Features: Aggregated counts of rare variants per gene (highest total information gain for aggregated pncA mutations, PZA); loss-of-function variants (ethA 15/32 prioritised, pncA Glu173fs OR 182.28, Rv0678, Rv2752c); RIF- and INH-resistance mutations rank highly (permutation feature importance/information gain)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest (RF) and gradient boosted trees (GBT) on feature sets F1, F2, F3 and F1 + ; best AUC per drug (Table 2): INH RF + F2 96.50; RIF RF + F2 96.60; EMB GBT + F1 91.70; PZA GBT + F2 88.30; STM RF + F2 89.60; AMK RF + F1 90.70; CAP RF + F2 84.10; KAN GBT + F2 91.00; CIP GBT + F2 95.40; OFL GBT + F2 88.10; MOX GBT + F2 89.10; ETH GBT + F2 86.30; LEV GBT + F1 93.50; RFB GBT + F2 94.90. External comparisons: DE19 (GBT-CRM, AUC 95.5-97.9), KO19 (AUC 84.4-97.8), GR22 (CNN, AUC 82.3-98.1), TB-Profiler (sensitivity 87-97% first-line, 79.2-92.2% second-line)
Best_Performing_Model: Random forest with the F2 feature set (RF + F2) - highest AUC in the study (RIF, AUC 96.6)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
Specificity_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
AUROC_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation only: stratified five-fold cross-validation with randomised grid search on the training set and a 20% hold-out test set; no external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment reported
Reported_Limitations: Limited predictive performance for some drugs (e.g. CAP) that could benefit from larger sample size or broader genomic coverage; confounding from population structure; feature representation (one-hot encoding leading to sparse matrices and reference bias); difficulty comparing models across datasets due to varying software requirements, input formats and reproducibility issues in prior publications; variant interactions not yet explored
Reviewer_Notes: Unit of analysis: the paper's Table 2 names a different best model per drug and no single overall best model. Coded RF + F2 (random forest, F2 feature set) as "best performing" because it attains the highest AUC in the study (RIF 96.6); the Accuracy/Sensitivity/Specificity/PPV/NPV/AUROC values are that model's RIF row. Other models' figures are in All_Models_Evaluated.
Sample_Size: 35,777 M. tuberculosis isolates (primary dataset); 33,087 isolates in the RIF hold-out test set (RF + F2)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: M. tuberculosis isolates with publicly available Illumina WGS (> 20-fold coverage) plus corresponding pDST data; 35,777 isolates retained of 50,723 sourced from public repositories/archives
Exclusion_Criteria: Monomorphic SNPs, variants in non-unique regions of the genome (e.g. pe/ppe genes) and variants with > 10% missing calls were excluded; only loci with a non-major allele frequency > 0.1% (F1/F2) or > 0.5% (F3) were retained
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: "35k" dataset: publicly available M. tuberculosis WGS and pDST data (sample accession numbers in the GitHub repository SSID08/TB-ML)
Dataset_Size: 35,777 isolates (from 50,723 sourced); F1 56-143 variants, F2 895-1428 variants, F3 5603-10,487 variants
Missing_Data_Method: Variants with > 10% missing calls were excluded
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates sourced from 66 countries covering all WHO regions: Europe 13,381 (37.4%), Africa 8756 (24.5%), South East Asia 5518 (15.4%), Western Pacific 3964 (11.1%), Americas 3176 (8.9%), Other 982 (2.8%)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary phenotypic drug resistance (pDST) to each of 14 anti-TB drugs, plus MIC phenotypes categorised into four incremental levels (Susceptible, Low resistance, High resistance, Resistant/Extreme) based on ECOFF thresholds
Drug_Classes: First-line anti-TB drugs (INH, RIF, EMB, PZA); second-line injectables (STM, AMK, CAP, KAN); fluoroquinolones (CIP, OFL, MOX, LEV); rifabutin (RFB); ethionamide (ETH); bedaquiline (BDQ) and clofazimine (CLF) in the loss-of-function and MIC analyses
Specific_Antibiotics: INH, RIF, EMB, PZA, streptomycin (STM), OFL, MOX, levofloxacin (LEV), amikacin (AMI), capreomycin (CAP), kanamycin (KAN), CIP, ethionamide (ETH) and RFB; BDQ and CLF also analysed
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; XDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistance/susceptibility from pDST for each drug; MIC phenotypes categorised into four incremental levels (Susceptible, 'Low' resistance, 'High' resistance, and Resistant ['Extreme']) based on recommended ECOFF thresholds; genotypic MDR/pre-XDR/XDR categories from TB-Profiler
AI_Purpose: To apply and evaluate ensemble tree-based machine learning (RF, GBT) on a large-scale WGS and pDST dataset to predict binary drug resistance for 14 drugs and MIC phenotypes, and to characterise drug-resistance mutations
Num_Models_Compared: 2 algorithms (RF, GBT) across feature sets F1, F2, F3 and F1 + ; 4 external comparators (DE19, KO19, GR22, TB-Profiler)
Feature_Engineering: Presence/absence (one-hot) encoding of SNPs and indels as 1/0 in a numpy matrix; F1 supplemented with aggregated counts of rare variants (MAF < 0.1%) predicted by SnpEff to have moderate-to-high functional impact (F1 + ); lineage predicted by TB-Profiler appended to the feature matrices
Feature_Selection_Method: bedtools intersect to retain drug-resistance-associated genes from the TB-Profiler list; MAF filtering (> 0.1% for F1/F2, > 0.5% for F3); permutation feature importance to rank variants
Num_Features_Selected: F1 56-143 variants; F2 895-1428 mutations; F3 5603-10,487 variants
Hyperparameter_Method: Randomised Grid Search with stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set (specified parameters and ranges, Table S7)
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn (v1.4.1), XGBoost Python API (1.7.6), numpy; TB-Profiler; SnpEff (v5.1); BWA-mem (v0.7.17); Trimmomatic (v0.39); samtools; GATK GenotypeGVCFs (v4.1.3.0); bedtools (v2.31); MASS and nnet packages in R
Other_Metrics: Conditional odds ratios for LOF variant associations; relative-risk ratios from multinomial ordinal regression across MIC categories; information gain from permutation feature importance
Baseline_Method: Deelder et al. 2019 (DE19, GBT-CRM); Kouchaki et al. 2019 (KO19, best ensemble tree model with dimensionality reduction); Green et al. 2022 (GR22, CNN); TB-Profiler (in-silico rule-in classification)
Baseline_Performance: DE19 (n = 16,507) GBT models AUC 95.5-97.9, sensitivity 69.7-91.1%, specificity 94.2-98.9%; KO19 (n = 13,167) AUC 84.4-97.8; GR22 (n = 22,615) AUC 82.3-98.1 with higher sensitivity across all drugs; TB-Profiler sensitivity 87-97% first-line and 79.2-92.2% second-line
Internal_Validation: 20% hold-out test dataset plus stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set with randomised grid search for hyperparameter and classification-threshold optimisation
Overfitting_Method: MAF filtering to control the number of input features; 80/20 train-test split with hold-out evaluation; stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set
Clinical_Insights: Loss-of-function mutations in pro-drug activation genes (pncA for PZA, ethA for ETH, mshA) as resistance mechanisms; Rv0678 LOF mutations linked to BDQ/CLF cross-resistance via MmpS5-MmpL5 efflux; putative novel markers Rv3861 Ile27fs (STM) and Rv1907c Asp48fs (INH) absent from the WHO catalogue; inhA promoter variants associated with extreme INH resistance
Data_Repository: GitHub repository: https://github.com/SSID08/TB-ML (contains sample accession numbers, feature importance values and analysis code)
Generalisability_Details: Authors note that comparing models across datasets is challenging because of varying software requirements, input formats and reproducibility issues in prior publications, suggest standardised Docker-container environments (ML-TB), and call for direct same-dataset comparisons to separate sample-size from architecture effects

Barriers_List: Difficulty comparing models across datasets (varying software requirements, input formats, reproducibility issues in prior work); limited predictive performance for some drugs such as CAP requiring more samples/genomic coverage; confounding from population structure; sparse matrices and reference bias from one-hot encoding
Facilitators_List: Standardised containerised environments (Docker containers within ML-TB) for model comparison and reproducibility; interpretable targeted feature sets (drug-specific regions); aggregation of rare variants to capture under-sampled resistance mutations
Future_Directions: Optimising models for practical deployment; direct comparisons on the same dataset to separate sample-size from architecture effects; exploring variant interactions on MIC phenotypes; quantitative MIC resistance prediction with ML; functional validation of novel variants for genetic DST libraries
Predictor_Categories_Count: 1 - genomic/microbiological features (presence/absence of WGS variants and lineage) only
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Permutation feature importance (information gain)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Two potential novel frameshift mutations observed across independent lineages and absent from the WHO mutation catalogue: Rv3861 Ile27fs (STM, OR = 7.0) and Rv1907c Asp48fs (INH, OR = 4.0)
Limitation_Categories: Model performance limited for some drugs (CAP) - needs larger sample size or broader genomic coverage; confounding by population structure; filtering of lineage-specific and synonymous mutations debated; feature representation (one-hot encoding) causing sparse matrices and reference bias; type of ML representation affects interpretability and deployment; variant interactions not examined; challenges comparing models across datasets
Data_Quality_Concerns: Potential pDST errors/phenotype misclassification; variants with > 10% missing calls excluded; monomorphic variants and non-unique genomic regions (pe/ppe) excluded; reference bias and sparse matrices from one-hot encoding on multi-lineage data
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: Table 2 reports, per drug, the best model with N, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and accuracy, with feature-set and model definitions in the caption; hyperparameter ranges and supplementary results in Tables S1-S11
Page_References: pp. 1-10 (Table 2 p. 3; Table 1 p. 3; Table 3 p. 6; Table 4 p. 7; Methods pp. 8-9; key results pp. 2-7)

Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection of MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) from nasal and inguinal/perineal screening ESwabs on chromogenic media: agreement of PhenoMATRIX/PhenoMATRIX PLUS image classification with the manual reading (sensitivity, specificity).
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA). Other organisms named only as mixed-growth false positives: Enterobacterales, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Bacillus sp.
Drug_Classes: Not modelled: the endpoint is detection of methicillin resistance (cefoxitin/mecA), not an antimicrobial class outcome.
Specific_Antibiotics: cefoxitin (disk diffusion AST confirming methicillin resistance)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA; Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MRSA positive/negative on CHROMID MRSA chromogenic plates (presumptively positive = green colonies on manual reading); positives confirmed by qPCR targeting femA and mecA and by disk diffusion AST on all femA-positive isolates.
AI_Purpose: Automated reading of chromogenic culture plate images: sorting plates as MRSA positive/negative, automatic release of negative results to the LIS and automatic discharge of negative plates from the incubators.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (PhenoMATRIX and PhenoMATRIX PLUS; assessed on different specimen sets)
Feature_Engineering: No hand-crafted features: several high-resolution digital images per plate taken under different light and exposure conditions at two incubation time points (0 h and 18 h) fed to the CNN.

Baseline_Method: Manual reading of the digital culture images by technologists (reference standard); qPCR targeting femA and mecA plus disk diffusion AST for confirmation of presumptive positives.
Baseline_Performance: Manual reading was the reference standard: PhenoMATRIX PLUS showed 100% sensitivity (no false negative among 1,409 specimens) and 95.2% specificity; for PhenoMATRIX, 99.9% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity against manual work-up.
Internal_Validation: Temporal validation: settings trained on 6,771 specimens and validated on 17,223 non-duplicate specimens prospectively analysed between 09 February 2022 and 08 May 2023; discrepancies reviewed by clinical microbiologists.
Train_Test_Split: Training: 6,771 non-duplicate specimens (machine learning phase); validation: 17,223 non-duplicate specimens; separate evaluation: 1,409 specimens for PhenoMATRIX PLUS.
Generalisability_Details: Authors state the software could be implemented, after thorough validation, on a broad panel of culture-based analyses such as urines, GBS screening and other infection-control screening specimens.
Maturity_Evidence: Performance of both versions established against manual reading on consecutive routine specimens, with PhenoMATRIX PLUS prospectively releasing negative results to the LIS and discarding negative plates in the routine workflow; no external or randomised evaluation.
Integration_Point: Bacteriology laboratory WASPLab line (imaging after 18 h of incubation) with automatic notification of negative MRSA results to the Laboratory Information System, further validated by the Valab expert system before updating the electronic patient record.
End_User_Described: Laboratory technologists (who read culture images and release results) and the infection control team.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Negative MRSA results are automatically sent to the LIS by PhenoMATRIX PLUS, validated by the Valab expert system and used to update the electronic patient record without delay; presumptively positive plates are sent to the reading folder for technologist review and confirmatory tests.
Barriers_List: Time-consuming manual reading of negative plates and extended time to results; laboratory operating hours limiting the day shift; laboratory workload bottlenecks requiring priority criteria by specimen type; shortage of qualified personnel; availability of the WASPLab for plate discharge.
Facilitators_List: Total laboratory automation (WASPLab) giving 24/7 image availability; automatic release of negative results to the LIS set as a high priority so results are sent around the clock; automatic discharge of negative plates when the WASPLab is available (low priority).
Future_Directions: Broader application of the software to other culture-based analyses (urines, GBS screening, other infection-control screening) after thorough validation; studies of the precise impact on personnel load and productivity, patient outcomes, antimicrobial prescriptions and cost-savings.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 2 (chromogenic culture-plate images / microbiological colony features; incubation time point)
Limitation_Categories: Unmeasured workflow/personnel impact; unexplored downstream clinical effects; absence of patient-outcome, prescribing and cost analyses; single-centre routine setting.
Data_Quality_Concerns: False positives driven by mixed growth of Enterobacterales, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Bacillus sp. (about 85% of false positives) and by non-specific colours on chromogenic plates; two false negatives from small, pale colonies with poorly specific features.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear methods and full 2x2 tables (Tables 1-2) with 95% CIs; minor internal inconsistencies (abstract sensitivity 99.8% vs 99.9% in the results text; abstract positivity 866/17,223 vs 868/17,223 in the results text).

Title: Proof of concept study on early forecasting of antimicrobial resistance in hospitalized patients using machine learning and simple bacterial ecology data
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: Hôpital Européen Marseille; SESSTIM (Aix Marseille Univ, Inserm, IRD); PhD grant from ISSPAM, Aix Marseille Université
Population_Description: Hospitalised patients: 30,975 antibiograms isolated from 13,166 patients in 6 ward types (emergency room 25%, critical care 24%, surgery 20%, medicine 19%) at the Hôpital Européen Marseille, 2014-2020; specimens mainly urine 41%, lower respiratory tract 23%, blood 14%, abscesses 12%
Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP ranking for the NN models, by stage: (1) history of MDR bacterial carriage in the last 3 months, a strong predictor at all stages with high absolute SHAP values (prior positive carriage lowers, prior negative carriage raises predicted susceptibility); (2) aspect on direct examination, significant at stage 2; (3) cultural feature, largest contribution at stage 3 'culture'; (4) at stage 4 'species', species then cultural features are the strongest contributors; specimen origin, ward type and date had a less significant effect at all stages
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Frequentist (FRQ), Bayesian (BAY), logistic regression (LR), AdaBoost (ADA), Gradient Boosting (GBS), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), Bagging (BAG), Random Forest (RF) and neural networks (NN), compared on mean AUROC at each stage of the bacteriological process on the 2020 validation dataset. Overall mean AUROC of all models rose from 0.594 (stage 1 'sampling') to 0.708 (stage 2 'direct'), 0.773 (stage 3 'culture') and 0.847 (stage 4 'species'). BAY, NN, FRQ and XGB performed much better than GBS, ADA, BAG, RF and LR. NN had the highest mean AUROC (0.823) and the highest AUROC at each stage except stage 4, where BAY reached 0.918. For the least frequent situations BAY held mean AUROCs of 0.824 (stage 3) and 0.917 (stage 4); NN dropped from 0.693 to 0.512 at stage 1 and from 0.811 to 0.658 at stage 2; FRQ fell from 0.893 to 0.662 at stage 4; LR was worst at all stages (mean AUROC 0.554)
Best_Performing_Model: BAY (Bayesian inference) models and NN (neural network) models — named best on mean AUROC
AUROC_Value: 0.918 (BAY model, stage 4 'species', all isolates); highest NN mean AUROC 0.823 across stages
AUROC_Population_Set: 2020 validation dataset (all isolates); stage 4 'species' for the BAY model
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Monocentric retrospective proof-concept study: models developed on the 2014-2019 dataset (80% training / 20% testing) and evaluated on the separate 2020 validation dataset (4,354 antibiograms) from the same hospital; the authors describe the work as a proof of concept and no external or prospective validation has been performed
Reported_Limitations: Low performance at the early stage 1 'sampling' (mean AUROC 0.693) because only a few features were included; no demographics, comorbidities or history of antibiotic treatment; AUROCs vary widely between antibiotics; concept drift complicates use of the date; predictions and performance are specific to the Hôpital Européen Marseille ecology; rare situations are poorly predicted; intervention studies and implementation science are still needed
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Data-protection governance only: use of anonymised bacterial ecology data under the GDPR; the wider project received authorisation DR-2020-047 from the French national commission for data protection (CNIL); the authors note that patient-related sensitive data are strictly controlled in Europe
Reviewer_Notes: Unit of analysis: the BAY and NN models named as best; AUROC taken from the 2020 validation dataset (all isolates) which the authors state is the dataset used for the reported results. Judgments: Breakpoint_Guideline = Other (French CA-SFM and European EUCAST guidelines); Infection_Type = Other (models cover a wide range of infected body sites, not one syndrome); Regulatory_Approval_Mentioned = No (the only regulatory mention is a CNIL data-protection authorisation, not a device/software clearance); Lifecycle_P5 left blank (deployment is aspirational, only a prototype is being tested at HEM); Study_Design ticked as development + retrospective cohort (the authors do not label the 2020 evaluation an external validation study)
Sample_Size: 30,975 antibiograms from 13,166 patients (cleaned dataset)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: All antibiograms performed by the bacteriology laboratory of the Hôpital Européen Marseille between January 2014 and December 2020, extracted from the laboratory information system
Exclusion_Criteria: Likely contaminants of bacterial culture, duplicates, and screening specimens (rectal and nasal swabs) sampled for MDR carriage; isolates with intermediate susceptibility were considered resistant
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables
Data_Source_Name: Hôpital Européen Marseille bacteriology laboratory information system (bacterial ecology data: positive cultures and antibiograms)
Dataset_Size: 44,026 antibiograms performed 2014-2020; cleaned dataset 30,975 antibiograms from 13,166 patients; 26,621 antibiograms (80% training + 20% testing, 2014-2019) and 4,354 validation antibiograms (2020)
Missing_Data_Method: Recommended expert rules on intrinsic and cross-resistance were used when susceptibility to a specific antibiotic was not available; when no similar situation existed in the training dataset a susceptibility probability of 0.5 was attributed so isolates were not excluded from AUROC estimation
Geographic_Representativeness: Single French general hospital (Hôpital Européen Marseille), in the popular central districts of a city of nearly 900,000 people in south-eastern France; the authors state the predictions reflect the specific bacterial ecology of that hospital; multi-centre evaluation planned in six French hospitals
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine (41%), lower respiratory tract (23%), blood (14%), abscesses (12%)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Probability of antimicrobial susceptibility (binary susceptible / resistant) to 22 single antibiotics and 25 antibiotic combinations, predicted for each bacterial isolate at each of the four pre-antibiogram stages
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (29%), Staphylococcus aureus (12%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (10%), Enterococcus faecalis (9%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (8%); also Enterobacteriaceae-like and non-fermentative Gram-negative rods, Staphylococcus-like and Enterococcus-like Gram-positive cocci; the species variable had 384 possible values
Num_Pathogens: 384 (number of possible values of the species variable)
Drug_Classes: Penicillins/aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate), cephalosporins (cefazolin/oxacillin, cefotaxime/ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefepime), monobactam (aztreonam), carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem), aminoglycosides (amikacin, gentamicin), fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin), folate pathway inhibitors (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), glycopeptide (vancomycin), rifamycin (rifampicin), lincosamide (clindamycin), macrolides, oxazolidinone (linezolid), nitroimidazole (metronidazole)
Specific_Antibiotics: 22 single antibiotics: Amoxicillin; Amox-Clav; Oxacillin/cefazolin; Pip-Tazo; Cefotaxime/ceftriaxone; Ceftazidime; Cefepime; Aztreonam; Imipenem; Meropenem; Ertapenem; Amikacin; Gentamicin; Ciprofloxacin; Levofloxacin; TMP-SMX; Vancomycin; Rifampicin; Clindamycin; Macrolides; Linezolid; Metronidazole — plus 25 antibiotic combinations
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Susceptibility (susceptible or resistant) of each bacterial isolate to 22 single antibiotics and 25 antibiotic combinations; isolates with 'intermediate' susceptibility were considered resistant; missing susceptibility was filled using expert rules on intrinsic and cross-resistance
AI_Purpose: Predict the probability of antimicrobial susceptibility (and explain the contribution of cofactors) in hospitalised patients at four stages before the antibiogram is available, using only historical bacterial ecology data, to assist clinicians choosing empirical antimicrobial therapy; a prototype ML-CDSS was developed
Num_Models_Compared: 9 model families compared (FRQ, BAY, LR, ADA, GBS, XGB, BAG, RF, NN); SVM models were excluded after exploratory analysis; one dense multilayer NN classifier per antibiotic per stage
Feature_Engineering: Features built from antibiogram metadata: type of ward, body-site origin of the specimen, previous MDR bacterial carriage in the last 3 months, aspect at direct Gram stain, cultural feature, bacterial species, plus clinical-relevance (contaminant) and duplicate flags; the sampling date was normalised between 0 and 1, and categorical variables were label-encoded after comparing one-hot and label encoding
Num_Features_Total: 3-4 per stage
Hyperparameter_Method: Exhaustive grid search with 10-fold cross-validation over the training dataset
Software_Libraries: Scikit-Learn (ensemble-based machine learning models); Keras and KerasClassifier (neural networks); SHAP Python package (interpretability); Gradio (prototype web application)
Other_Metrics: Mean AUROC per model, stage and antibiotic, with AUROC distributions and between-antibiotic standard deviations (0.03-0.17); prediction omission rate for FRQ (0.7% stage 1 to 10.2% stage 4); root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of susceptibility between isolate categories; Spearman's rank correlation between NN SHAP values and BAY likelihood ratios (0.57; p = 0.0033)
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression (LR), used as the baseline model
Baseline_Performance: LR was the worst model at all stages, mean AUROC 0.554
Internal_Validation: 80% training / 20% testing split of the 2014-2019 dataset with 10-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning, then evaluation on all 2020 antibiograms held out from training
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% testing of the 2014-2019 data (26,621 antibiograms, of which 4,915 in 2019 alone); validation on all 2020 data (4,354 antibiograms)
External_Validation_Description: None performed; external evaluation is planned in an ongoing multi-centre study in six French hospitals including HEM
Overfitting_Method: Dropout layers after each hidden dense layer and batch normalisation in the neural networks; XGB's higher regularisation mitigates overfitting; hyperparameters chosen by exhaustive grid search with 10-fold cross-validation
Explainability_Methods: SHAP; Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model; Other
Clinical_Insights: History of MDR carriage in the last 3 months is a strong predictor at all stages (prior positive carriage lowers, prior negative carriage raises predicted susceptibility); the cultural feature dominates at the culture stage and species then culture type at the species stage; in a worked scenario predicted susceptibility to CTX/CRO was 0.87 at the culture stage (good probability) and 0.40 at the species stage (bad probability, for Citrobacter koseri in critical care); NN SHAP values and BAY likelihood ratios were moderately consistent (Spearman 0.57, p = 0.0033)
Data_Repository: No repository; anonymised data available from author S. Rebaudet upon reasonable request with a material transfer agreement
Generalisability_Details: The authors hypothesise that the overall architecture of the algorithms is generalisable and that similar models could be adapted to other hospitals trained with local bacteriological data; to be evaluated in an ongoing multi-centre study in six French hospitals and through an interoperable health data warehouse in eight hospitals, comparing federated learning with centralised and local approaches
Maturity_Evidence: Retrospective monocentric design; hyperparameters tuned by exhaustive grid search with 10-fold cross-validation on the training data; performance reported on the 2020 validation dataset (4,354 antibiograms) held out from the 2014-2019 training+testing data; no external, prospective or clinical-impact evaluation
Integration_Point: Prototype web application (Gradio, private HuggingFace space) being tested at HEM; planned embedding in the laboratory information management system (LIMS) to provide preliminary probabilistic antibiograms, in EMR systems or health data warehouses, or as a stewardship dashboard
End_User_Described: Hospital doctors/prescribers selecting empirical antimicrobial therapy; on-call infectiologists giving antimicrobial stewardship advice; antimicrobial stewardship teams (dashboard flagging prescriptions of low susceptibility probability)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Predictions at four stages matched to laboratory turnaround: stage 1 'sampling' (Day 0, specimen origin), stage 2 'direct' (Day 0-1, direct Gram stain aspect), stage 3 'culture' (Day 1-2, cultural feature) and stage 4 'species' (Day 2-3, species identification), used to refine empirical therapy until the antibiogram is available
Stewardship_Details: Studies underway in six hospitals will retrospectively describe the susceptibility probability and spectrum width of prescribed empirical therapies to assess potential efficacy gains and safe de-escalations; a stewardship dashboard flagging prescriptions with low susceptibility probability is proposed
Barriers_List: GDPR restrictions on patient-related sensitive data; EMR data stored in heterogeneous formats and not readily accessible in all hospital facilities; no demographics, comorbidities or antibiotic history, limiting stage 1 performance; concept drift makes the date difficult to model; BAY models are burdensome to program; rare situations are unmet in the training data; the system must not replace practice guidelines or prescriber decisions
Facilitators_List: Only simple bacterial ecology data are needed, easily extracted from any laboratory information system without GDPR restrictions after on-site anonymisation; NN models can be implemented and tuned with open-source packages and scale to new input variables; FRQ/BAY models are intrinsically interpretable and SHAP explains the NN; the probability output is designed to enrich the prescriber's reasoning rather than replace it
Future_Directions: Include demographic features (age, sex, residence), comorbidities and history of antibiotic consumption; impute subsequent-stage data; model month and year separately with temporal sliding windows, concept-drift detectors and continuous learning; assess model uncertainty; multi-centre and federated evaluations; intervention studies followed by implementation science
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values for the NN models at population and individual level; feature-specific likelihood ratios for the BAY models
Limitation_Categories: Model performance: low AUROC at stage 1 with a limited feature set; metric variability between antibiotics. Data: absence of demographics, comorbidities and antibiotic history (GDPR); concept drift. Setting: single-centre data specific to one hospital's ecology; rare situations unmet in training. Methods: label encoding choice; BAY models burdensome to program. Evidence base: no prospective or clinical-impact evaluation yet
Data_Quality_Concerns: Removal of likely contaminants, duplicates and screening specimens before training; intermediate susceptibility recoded as resistant; missing susceptibility values filled by expert rules on intrinsic and cross-resistance; rare feature combinations absent from the training data cause prediction omissions; concept drift over time
Page_References: pp. 1-16 (full PDF text layer); title, abstract and DOI p. 1; dataset description and model comparison pp. 2-3; AUROC results pp. 3-5; best models p. 6; SHAP interpretability pp. 6-7; discussion, limitations and barriers pp. 8-10; methods pp. 10-14; data availability p. 14; acknowledgements p. 15; competing interests, ethics and supplementary note p. 16

Title: Amikacin Concentrations Predictive of Ototoxicity in Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis Patients
Journal_Source: Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 59:6337-6343)
Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health (grants R01AI097045 and R56AI111985-01)
Population_Description: 28 multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis (MDR-TB) patients in Botswana, aged 15 years or older, started on MDR-TB treatment and with serum amikacin concentration measurements
Age_Range: 15 years of age or older (eligibility criterion); age ranges by group 28-70 years (Table 3)
Top_Predictive_Features: CART variable ranking on the drug-dose/PK model: primary node cumulative days of therapy; cumulative AUC ranked second (improved on the primary node by another 87%); AUC0-24 score 34%; initial weight score 29%. Cumulative AUC thresholds from the concentration-only tree: 54,519 and 91,914 days*mg*h/liter.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance; Dose optimisation
All_Models_Evaluated: CART (classification and regression tree) models built in three steps with the Salford Predictive Miner System: (1) all potential predictors (AUROC 0.97 on the test sets); (2) pharmacokinetic/treatment factors only, primary node cumulative days of therapy, cumulative AUC second, AUC0-24 34%, initial weight 29% (AUROC 0.97); (3) drug concentrations only, identifying cumulative AUC thresholds of 54,519 and 91,914 days*mg*h/liter; plus a CART model forced to pick peak and trough, AUROC 0.46 on the test set. Also a 2-compartment population PK model (ADAPT 5), probit models (TC50 87,323 days*mg*h/liter, TC80 120,238) and frequentist group comparisons in STATA 13.
Best_Performing_Model: CART tree using cumulative days of therapy as the primary node with cumulative AUC second, test-set AUROC 0.97 - superior to the model forced to pick peak and trough (AUROC 0.46)
AUROC_Population_Set: Test set (internal cross-validation; random repeated training/test splits) for the CART model using drug-dose and pharmacokinetic factors
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model built and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation of each tree and random repeated training/test splits only; no external validation, no prospective evaluation of the model and no deployment, so the highest evidence-supported level is internal validation.
Reported_Limitations: Amikacin has a long half-life in cochlear tissue so hearing loss may occur long after therapy stops; only amikacin concentrations were measured although MDR-TB patients receive other ototoxic drugs; insufficient data on prior streptomycin exposure to examine that relationship; defining ototoxicity remains imprecise because conventional audiometers test only up to 8 kHz while amikacin affects hearing up to 20 kHz.
Sample_Size: 28 MDR-TB patients (patients, not isolates) with amikacin concentration measurements and audiometry assessments
Conflicts_of_Interest: T.G. has worked as a consultant for Astellas Pharma US, Inc., and LuminaCare Solutions and founded Jacaranda Biomed, Inc. All other authors have no conflicts to declare.
Inclusion_Criteria: All MDR-TB patients 15 years of age or older started on MDR-TB treatment between 1 January 2011 and 30 December 2012 with serum amikacin concentration measurements reported; at least one creatinine measurement within 1 month prior to or after the start of amikacin and one follow-up creatinine measurement (within the last 6 months prior to censoring).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Botswana national MDR-TB treatment programme (no named dataset)
Dataset_Size: 28 patients; 2 amikacin concentration samples per patient (1 h and 23.5 h after dose)
Geographic_Representativeness: All 28 patients were treated within one national MDR-TB programme in Botswana (one country, one programme), so the sample does not represent other settings.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Serum (plasma) amikacin concentrations; audiometry-confirmed hearing loss
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Ototoxicity (audiometry-confirmed hearing loss) attributable to amikacin treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis - not a drug-resistance outcome
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycoside (amikacin); fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin); thioamide (ethionamide); cycloserine; pyrazinamide
Specific_Antibiotics: Amikacin; levofloxacin; ethionamide; cycloserine; pyrazinamide (prior streptomycin exposure in 10 patients)
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Audiometry-determined neurosensory hearing loss defined as a shift or loss of 15 to 25 dB relative to baseline averaged at two or more contiguous frequencies in at least one ear, or loss of response at 3 consecutive frequencies where responses had previously been obtained; audiometry-confirmed hearing loss is synonymous with ototoxicity.
AI_Purpose: To identify clinical factors, including amikacin concentration thresholds, that predict ototoxicity in MDR-TB patients using an agnostic machine learning method (classification and regression tree analysis), and to derive threshold decision-making values for clinicians.
Num_Models_Compared: 3 CART models (all predictors; pharmacokinetic and treatment factors only, Figure 3; peak and trough forced) plus probit models for comparison
Feature_Engineering: Pharmacokinetic features derived from the population model (AUC0-24, cumulative AUC), cumulative dose and cumulative dose divided by weight, amikacin dose in mg/kg as daily and cumulative dose, time on amikacin therapy, peak and trough concentrations, plus clinical variables (age, gender, initial weight, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy). CART is used to break the collinearity of these highly correlated measures.
Feature_Selection_Method: CART classification and ranking subroutines (Gini splitting; predictors ranked in order of importance, with surrogate variables), tree pruning by AUROC and parsimony
Num_Features_Total: 14 candidate predictors listed (age, gender, initial weight, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy, amikacin dose, cumulative dose, time on amikacin therapy, daily dose mg/kg, cumulative dose mg/kg, AUC0-24, cumulative AUC, peak, trough)
Num_Features_Selected: not reported as a count; the final tree used cumulative days of therapy as the primary node and cumulative AUC second
Class_Imbalance_Method: Priors set to equal (equal probability assignment for all categories), with no penalty sets for misclassification
Software_Libraries: Salford Predictive Miner System; ADAPT 5 (including its SAMPLE subroutine); STATA version 13; COBAS INTEGRA assays
Other_Metrics: AUROC (0.97 test set for the best model; 0.46 for the peak/trough-forced model); CART relative improvement scores (87% for cumulative AUC, 34% AUC0-24, 29% initial weight); probit r2 for cumulative AUC 0.97, weight 0.95 and duration 0.98; cumulative AUC TC50 87,323 (CI 81,248-93,216) and TC80 120,238 days*mg*h/liter; correlations r2 between exposure measures
Baseline_Method: CART model forced to pick peak and trough concentrations as predictors - the parameters currently used for clinical dosing decisions
Baseline_Performance: AUROC 0.46 on the test set, inferior to the 0.97 of the duration-of-therapy and cumulative AUC model
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation of each tree, plus repeated random splitting of the data set into training and test data sets (predictive power assessed on the test set)
Train_Test_Split: Random repeated splits of the data set into training and test data sets; reported performance is that of the training-set-derived tree on the test set (test-set AUROC 0.97)
Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Feature importance / permutation importance
Clinical_Insights: Threshold cumulative AUC of ~87,232 days*mg*h/liter for a 10% probability of ototoxicity and ~120,000 for 20%; ototoxicity risk rises after ~6 months of therapy and approaches certainty at 9 months; peak and trough concentrations are not useful monitoring parameters; optimal blood-draw times for therapeutic drug monitoring were 0, 15 min, 2.5 h and 18.7 h.
Generalisability_Details: The authors argue the concentration-ototoxicity relationship is likely to hold as sample size increases because it was also identified by parametric probit models and is concordant with guinea pig animal experiments that give a biological basis for the findings.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: CART trees built with Gini splitting and 5-fold cross-validation, with repeated random training/test splits; no external validation data set, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment.
Integration_Point: Therapeutic drug monitoring and amikacin dosing decisions for MDR-TB treatment, using cumulative AUC and duration of therapy thresholds in place of peak and trough concentrations.
End_User_Described: Clinicians treating pulmonary tuberculosis / MDR-TB programmes
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Blood draws for amikacin therapeutic drug monitoring should be taken just before the dose and at 15 min, 2.5 h and 18.7 h after the dose rather than at peak and trough; cumulative AUC and duration thresholds are then used to judge the risk of ototoxicity during treatment.
Future_Directions: Measuring amikacin concentrations lets the optimal (safe) duration of therapy be calculated in the first week of therapy, and the identified sampling times (0, 15 min, 2.5 h, 18.7 h) should be used for therapeutic drug monitoring in tuberculosis programmes.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: CART importance ranking (relative improvement scores on the primary node)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Cumulative amikacin AUC and duration of therapy - and not the peak and trough concentrations currently used for dosing - are the predictors of ototoxicity; the AUC relationship was sigmoidal and gave explicit decision thresholds.
Feature_Interactions_Method: CART recursive partitioning, a nonparametric method examining linear and nonlinear interactions simultaneously, including interactions among the predictors of ototoxicity
Limitation_Categories: Toxicodynamic/outcome-measurement (long cochlear half-life, imprecise definition of ototoxicity, high-frequency hearing loss above audiometer range); unmeasured drug exposures (other ototoxic MDR-TB drugs, prior streptomycin); sample size
Data_Quality_Concerns: Audiometry is imprecise for amikacin ototoxicity: conventional audiometers test up to 8 kHz while amikacin affects hearing up to 20 kHz, so high-tone deafness may be missed; data on prior streptomycin exposure were insufficient; one of four patients with subjective hearing loss may not have met the definition.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear methods (CART, model software, cross-validation) but performance reporting is limited to AUROC and CART improvement scores/thresholds; no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or calibration is reported; small sample (28 patients).
Page_References: p. 1 title/abstract/citation; p. 2 study population, ototoxicity definitions and methods; p. 3 results and Tables 1-3; pp. 4-5 discussion and Figure 4; p. 6 funding, conflicts and references

Title: Machine learning-based prediction of antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis clinical isolates from Uganda
Funder_Names: Fogarty International Center of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Award Number U2RTW012116 (MakDARTA, Makerere University); National Science Foundation awards 2030508 and 1836650 (Open Science Grid); Wellcome Trust (CAMO-Net) Award No. 226692/Z/22/Z
Population_Description: 182 MTB clinical isolates per drug (from a Uganda dataset of 226 isolates) with clinical data variables (age, sex, HIV status), SNP mutations across the entire genome as predictors, and phenotypic drug-susceptibility data for four anti-TB drugs as the outcome; an independent South Africa dataset of 236 isolates was used for generalisability assessment
Data_Source_Other: Publicly available whole-genome sequence (WGS) data from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) with corresponding clinical data and drug-resistance phenotypes from previously published studies
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)

Sensitivity_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset, five-fold cross-validation on the training set
Specificity_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset, five-fold cross-validation on the training set

F1_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset, five-fold cross-validation on the training set
AUROC_Population_Set: Up-sampled Uganda (UG) dataset (Table 8), five-fold cross-validation on the training set

Data_Source_Name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) - BioProjects PRJEB10533, PRJNA481638, PRJEB10577, PRJEB2424, PRJNA559528 and PRJNA74965
Dataset_Size: 4994 variants across the entire MTB genome plus clinical variables; 182 MTB isolates per drug (145 training / 37 testing); 226 UG isolates in total; 236 SA isolates

Specific_Antibiotics: rifampicin (RIF), isoniazid (INH), ethambutol (EMB), streptomycin (STM)

Feature_Selection_Method: No separate feature-selection step; the top ten features per drug were ranked using the feature importance attribute of the tree-based models (XGBoost, GBC) or the absolute values of the logistic regression coefficients
Num_Features_Total: 4994 variants across the entire MTB genome plus clinical data variables
Num_Features_Selected: 10 per drug (top ten most important features identified for each drug)
Class_Imbalance_Method: SMOTE up-sampling applied to the training dataset; all models trained on both originally imbalanced and balanced datasets; severe class imbalance noted in the South Africa dataset
Hyperparameter_Method: gridsearchCV with cross-validation on the training set; optimal parameters: LR C=10, max_iter=300 (RIF) and C=5, max_iter=500 (STM); XGBoost learning rate 0.3, max_depth 3, n_estimators 100, subsample 1.0 (EMB); GBC learning rate 0.5, max_depth 9, n_estimators 100, subsample 0.7 (INH); other models used default parameters
Software_Libraries: Scikit-learn version 1.3.2
Hardware_Details: Open Science Grid (OSG) High Throughput Computing infrastructure supported by National Science Foundation awards 2030508 and 1836650; no CPU/GPU/memory specification reported
Other_Metrics: Recall (sensitivity), specificity, ROC_AUC and MCC reported for the best three models per drug (Tables 6-8) and for the best model per drug (Tables 9-10), each with 95% CI; precision and F1 score reported for the best models on the up-sampled UG dataset
Baseline_Method: TB profiler (WHO catalogue-based tool)
Baseline_Performance: On the UG dataset the best ML models had a higher ROC-AUC than TB profiler except LR for STM; LR mean sensitivity for RIF 0.75 vs TB profiler 0.5; XGBoost for EMB mean sensitivity 0.77 (same as TB profiler) with higher mean specificity 0.92 vs 0.88; TB profiler mean sensitivity for INH 0.82 vs GBC 0.76 with lower mean specificity 0.70 vs 0.75; on the SA dataset TB profiler outperformed all best models
Internal_Validation: Five-fold cross-validation on the training set with 95% CIs computed by bootstrap; performance also evaluated on a held-out Uganda test set of 37 isolates
Train_Test_Split: 80% training (145 MTB isolates) / 20% testing (37 MTB isolates) per drug
External_Validation_Description: South Africa (SA) dataset: WGS data from patients in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa; 236 of 399 MTB isolates included with complete phenotypic information for the four drugs; WGS available under NCBI SRA BioProject PRJNA559528

Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Known resistance genes confirmed (rpoB for RIF, katG for INH, rpsL for STM); novel SNPs detected in PE/PE-PGRS/PE-PPE genes (PE_PGRS18 with INH; PE_PGRS7, PPE34, PPE54 and PPE19 with RIF; PPE55 with STM); mutations in pykA (Rv1617), ureC (Rv1850) and cyp136 (Rv3059) associated with EMB resistance; conserved hypothetical proteins (Rv2059, Rv2082, Rv2828A, Rv2828c) and intergenic regions (oxyR-ahpC for INH; embC-embA for EMB) associated with resistance; HIV status a top feature for RIF and STM with a negative coefficient
Generalisability_Details: Best models trained on the Uganda dataset were applied to the South Africa dataset; LR for RIF and STM did not generalise while the boosting classifiers (GBC for INH, XGBoost for EMB) generalised better; TB profiler outperformed all best models on the SA dataset; the authors attribute the differences to varying proportions of resistant/susceptible isolates and lineage-specific genomic variation
Maturity_Evidence: Models trained and tuned on the Uganda dataset were evaluated on the independent South Africa dataset, which is external validation; no prospective evaluation, CDS integration or routine clinical use is reported
Integration_Point: Not reported - no clinical system or workflow integration described; deployment across diverse populations is framed only as future work
End_User_Described: Not reported - the paper names no specific end user for the models
