Future_Directions: Establish whether the novel resistance markers are causally involved in mediating resistance; investigate lineage-specific genomic variations and their impact on model performance; integrate multiple omics layers (transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics) with comprehensive clinical information; expand datasets to additional drugs and clinical factors; balance dataset size, class distribution and model complexity; apply the approach to other areas such as drug repurposing and cancer resistance prediction
Predictor_Categories_Count: 3 (microbiological/genomic - SNP mutations; sociodemographic - age and sex; clinical - HIV status)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance attribute for the tree-based models (XGBoost, GBC); absolute values of the logistic regression coefficients for LR
Novel_Predictors_Details: Novel SNPs within PE, PE-PGRS and PE/PPE genes: PE_PGRS18 (INH), PE_PGRS7 / PPE34 / PPE54 / PPE19 (RIF), PPE55 (STM); pykA (Rv1617), ureC (Rv1850) and cyp136 (Rv3059) (EMB); conserved hypothetical proteins Rv2059, Rv2082, Rv2828A, Rv2828c; mutations in intergenic regions (oxyR-ahpC for INH, embC-embA for EMB); HIV status among the top ten features for RIF and STM
Limitation_Categories: Model generalisability / cross-population performance; single reference genome; limited clinical data; multicollinearity not assessed; novel markers not yet causally established
Data_Quality_Concerns: Read contamination screening (23 reads excluded with less than 95% proportion of MTB); low-quality variant filtering; 21 isolates excluded (19 without phenotype data, 2 with empty VCFs); missing clinical values imputed; severe class imbalance in the SA dataset
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: model metrics and the best model per drug are reported in dedicated tables (Tables 6-10) with 95% confidence intervals

Title: Infection Inspection: using the power of citizen science for image-based prediction of antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli treated with ciprofloxacin
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Funder_Names: Oxford Martin School (Programme on Antimicrobial Resistance Testing); Wellcome Trust grant 110164/Z/15/Z; Clarendon Fund Scholarships; UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council grants BB/N018656/1 and BB/S008896/1; National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Health Protection Research Unit in Healthcare Associated Infections and Antimicrobial Resistance (NIHR200915) with UKHSA; NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre
Population_Description: 49,074 single-cell fluorescence microscopy images of ciprofloxacin-treated E. coli cells from five clinical bloodstream-infection strains (EC1, EC2, EC3, EC5, EC6); unit of analysis is the bacterial cell image, not patients.
Data_Source_Other: Research single-cell fluorescence microscopy image dataset generated for a previous study (Zagajewski et al. 2023)
Top_Predictive_Features: DNA Mean Standard Deviation of Intensity (median SHAP 0.109); Number of DNA Regions (0.085); Nucleoid Area Fraction (0.081); Membrane Form Factor (0.037); Membrane Major Axis Length (0.035); DNA Mean Integrated Intensity (0.028); DNA Standard Deviation of Integrated Intensity (0.013); Random Noise control (0.008).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Deep-learning model (ref 21): aggregated accuracy 75.3 ± 0.4%; sensitive cells 88.2 ± 0.4%, resistant cells 62.5  ± 0.9%; per-strain model accuracy EC1 84.9 ± 0.6%, EC2 81.6 ± 1.2%, EC3 71.0 ± 0.6%, EC5 86.2 ± 1.3%, EC6 76.3 ± 1.2%. Random Forest classifier (100 trees, min 3 samples/leaf): Mean Absolute Error 0.15 ± 0.01 on a holdout dataset. Citizen-scientist volunteers (comparator): 66.8 ± 0.1% overall, 66.4 ± 0.2% sensitive, 67.3 ± 0.2% resistant.
Best_Performing_Model: Deep learning model (highest accuracy: 75.3 ± 0.4% overall vs 66.8 ± 0.1% for volunteers)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Aggregated across all three dataset uploads (all images; Zooniverse users or the model)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The deep-learning classifier and the Random Forest were evaluated only on internal data (75–25 train-test split, cross-validation, holdout test set); no external validation or prospective clinical evaluation is reported and the platform is described as in early stages of development.
Reported_Limitations: Reliance on voluntary citizen-science contributions (variable data quality and quantity); no information on participating users; no quantitative feedback on the educational impact of tutorials; single antibiotic and small number of strains limiting generalisability; titration data only for EC1 and EC3.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Citizen scientists who contributed classifications were deemed contributors, not research participants, so no participant consent or ethics review applied to them; cells were analysed anonymously under a separate ethics approval.
Sample_Size: 49,074 single-cell images; 1,045,199 classifications by 5,273 volunteers (1,003,588 classifications by 4,927 users after removing training images)
Conflicts_of_Interest: A.K. is a co-founder and shareholder of Oxford Nanoimaging, whose wide-field microscope generated the original image data; the other authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Classifications performed from go-live (7 Feb 2023 17:40 UTC) to full dataset completion (10 May 2023 21:40 UTC).
Exclusion_Criteria: Classifications of images in the training/feedback dataset and classifications of "Image processing error" were removed; EC4 was excluded because its MIC equals the treatment concentration.
Data_Types_Used: Microscopy images; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 49,074 images total (initial dataset 11,074 images from 5 strains; second dataset 38,000 images of EC1 and EC3 at 9 ciprofloxacin concentrations)
Specimen_Type_Detail: micrographs of single E. coli cells (clinical isolates from bloodstream infections)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AI_Purpose: Train volunteers to classify single-cell images and use their classifications and misclassifications to identify which image features drive accurate ciprofloxacin-sensitive/resistant classification, making the machine-learning classifier more robust to atypical phenotypes.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (deep-learning image classifier vs citizen-scientist volunteers); a Random Forest classifier (100 trees) was also trained for feature-importance analysis
Feature_Engineering: Seven CellProfiler features measured per cell (number of DNA regions, mean and SD of integrated DNA intensity, mean SD of DNA intensity, nucleoid area fraction, membrane form factor, membrane major axis length); all measurements normalised with StandardScaler; a normally distributed random-noise feature added as a control.
Feature_Selection_Method: Seven features chosen a priori for potential biological relevance to the ciprofloxacin response (Fig. S2)
Num_Features_Total: 8 (7 image features + 1 random-noise control feature)
Software_Libraries: CellProfiler 4.2.6; Scikit-learn; NumPy; Kernel SHAP; Mask-RCNN (Matterport); SQLite / DB Browser for SQLite; R packages vegan 2.6-4, ggplot2 3.4.4, ggpubr 0.6.0, rstatix 0.7.2
Other_Metrics: Mean Absolute Error 0.15 ± 0.01 (Random Forest, holdout); per-strain Zooniverse and model accuracies (Table 1); accuracies by treatment concentration (Fig. 2b); Gini coefficient of volunteer participation 0.81; median SHAP values per feature.
Baseline_Method: Citizen-scientist (human) classification performance; normally distributed random-noise feature as a null baseline in the SHAP feature-importance analysis
Baseline_Performance: Volunteers 66.8 ± 0.1% overall accuracy (sensitive 66.4 ± 0.2%; resistant 67.3 ± 0.2%)
Internal_Validation: 75–25 train-test split with cross-validation (Mean Absolute Error) and a holdout test dataset
Clinical_Insights: DNA compaction and heterogeneity, and the space the nucleoid occupies within the cell, are the key features determining whether an E. coli cell is responding to ciprofloxacin treatment.
Generalisability_Details: Findings are limited to one antibiotic (ciprofloxacin) and a small number of E. coli strains, which limits generalisability to other antibiotics and pathogens.
Integration_Point: Single-cell imaging-based antimicrobial susceptibility test on a microfluidic device, usable as a point-of-care test
End_User_Described: Laboratory and clinical users of a rapid antibiotic susceptibility test (point-of-care healthcare settings)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Microfluidic device captures bacteria directly from the clinical sample; microscopy-based single-cell imaging gives an antibiotic-resistance result in under an hour, eliminating lengthy culturing steps; deployable as a point-of-care test.
Barriers_List: Antibiotic response phenotypes of common pathogens and antibiotics must be characterised first; method requires a fluorescence microscope and microfluidic chips; platform still in early stages of development.
Facilitators_List: Large, fast public participation through the Zooniverse citizen-science platform; a single-step, fast workflow and rich image features captured.
Future_Directions: Explore other bacterial species and antibiotics; improve training materials and guidelines; raise public awareness; assess impact of tools on user education; capture more data on volunteer decision-making.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Kernel SHAP values computed on a Random Forest classifier (mean absolute SHAP contribution per feature over all images)
Limitation_Categories: Data quality/quantity from voluntary contributions; lack of participant information; no evaluation of educational impact; limited strain and antibiotic scope; incomplete titration data
Data_Quality_Concerns: It relied on voluntary contributions from citizen scientists, which introduced variability in data quality and quantity.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: accuracy, 95% confidence intervals (Wald method with continuity correction), MAE, SHAP values and thresholds are reported explicitly.
Page_References: p. 1 abstract; Table 1 p. 3; Methods pp. 2–5; Results pp. 5–8; Fig. 2 pp. 6–7; Fig. 6 caption p. 11; Data availability p. 12

Title: Automated detection of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with the MRSA CHROM imaging application on BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation System
Funder_Names: Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD Life Sciences — Integrated Diagnostic Solutions)
Population_Description: Remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens (one per patient) collected at three sites (two in the United States, one in Canada) between January and August 2019; a single 30 µl aliquot was inoculated onto BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II and imaged on the BD Kiestra TLA System. 1,775 specimens enrolled, 1,593 evaluable; deidentified patient age and gender recorded but no clinical characteristics reported.
Age_Range: 3% of specimens from patients less than 20 years of age; 27% aged 20–59 years; 69% aged 60 years and over; no demographic information for 1%
Data_Source_Other: Digital agar plate images of BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II captured by the BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation System and managed in the Colony Information System (CIS)/Clindex; ground truth from laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Diagnosis / species identification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Laboratory scientist / microbiologist; Infection prevention and control team
Delivery_Platform: Instrument / device embedded; Laboratory information system (LIS) integrated
All_Models_Evaluated: MRSA App (BD Kiestra methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus Application) — the only model evaluated: sensitivity 98.15% (95% CI, 96.03, 99.32), specificity 96.69% (95% CI, 95.55, 97.60), concordance 96.98%, PPV 88.11%, NPV 99.52%. Internally it comprises four machine-learning models (zone CFU/non-CFU classification, plate growth status, mauve/non-mauve CFU classification, plate positivity) for which no per-model metrics are reported.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites (Total row, Table 1)
Specificity_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites (Total row, Table 1)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest level the paper's own evidence supports is external validation: this is the first evaluation of the pre-existing, sponsor-developed MRSA App, a locked commercial algorithm, applied without retraining to independent anterior nares specimens collected at three sites in two countries (two US, one Canada) and read against a blinded laboratory technologist reference standard, with sensitivity (98.15%) and specificity (96.69%) reported. No model development or training on the study data is described, and there is no prospective clinical impact evaluation, CDS integration or routine-use assessment of this cohort.
Reported_Limitations: Discrepant specimens were not available for repeat testing to confirm that discrepancies were not imaging artefacts, nor for confirmation of MRSA positivity by a different testing method; the study design allowed technologists at each site to choose one of two streaking patterns, so the higher false-positive count at Site 3 may reflect the pattern chosen, and de-identification prevented further analysis.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: False-positive App results carry the potential for unwarranted patient management: about one in ten MRSA-App-positive results could trigger isolation, topical or systemic antibiotics or other clinical attention although the patient is negative; in this study technologists were blinded to App results, and in real-world use all suspected positives would be reviewed by a technologist.
Reviewer_Notes: Laboratory-automation diagnostic accuracy study of an AI imaging application (BD Kiestra MRSA App) on chromogenic MRSA screening plates; no patient-level clinical or sociodemographic data beyond age band and gender. Two conventions had to be judged. (1) Validation/maturity: the paper reports no development or training data, so the multi-site evaluation of the pre-existing commercial algorithm is coded as external validation (Validation_Strategy 'External only', Clinical_Maturity_Level 3) rather than internal validation of the study's own dataset — flagged for team discussion. (2) Best_Performing_Model: a single index test is evaluated and no models are compared, so the NA checkbox is ticked. Reported artefact: the negative predictive value CI is printed in reverse order ('98.96, 98.78') in the results text. Sex was collected (gender stored in Clindex/CIS) but no sex distribution is reported.
Unresolved_Items: Whether a locked, sponsor-developed commercial application evaluated for the first time on independent multi-site specimens is coded as external validation (Validation_Strategy 'External only' / Clinical_Maturity_Level 3, as recorded here) or as internal validation of the study's own dataset (level 2); the MRSA App's training/development data are not reported anywhere in the paper.
Sample_Size: 1,593 evaluable specimens (1,775 enrolled, 166 excluded, 16 without a standard-of-care result removed)
Conflicts_of_Interest: S.M., J.L., D.M., C.O., J.-M.V. and K.B. are employees of the study sponsor (Becton, Dickinson and Company) and own BD shares; D.R. has received research support for this investigation and performed sponsored research with Abbott, Altona, BD, bioMerieux, Cepheid, Luminex, Hardy Diagnostics, HelixBind, Hologic, Qiagen, Q-Linea, Roche, Specific Diagnostics, Cleveland Diagnostics, Thermo Fisher and Vela Diagnostics, served as an advisor for Roche, Thermo Fisher, Luminex/DiaSorin and Seegene, received travel funds from Cepheid and owns equity in Next Gen Diagnostics; M.D. has received research support for this investigation; P.P. and C.E.G. have no conflicts; E.M. has received research support for this investigation and is a sponsored speaker for BD.
Inclusion_Criteria: Remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens collected at the three participating sites (standard of care at each facility); only one Eswab per patient was eligible for inclusion.
Exclusion_Criteria: Plates removed from the incubator at any point before completion of the imaging process, or specimens meeting routine laboratory rejection criteria; after enrolment, 166 specimens were excluded (inoculation outside QC-plate time span, missing incubation images, algorithm-detected issues such as a bead in the plate or failed image quality check, no truth collected) and 16 further cultures with no standard-of-care result were removed.
Data_Types_Used: Imaging; Other
Data_Source_Name: BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation (TLA) System with the BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II (CHROMagar); Colony Information System (CIS) and Clindex (BD Clinical Information system)
Dataset_Size: 1,593 specimens evaluated (from 1,775 enrolled; 166 excluded; 16 without SOC result)
Geographic_Representativeness: Three clinical laboratory sites: two in the United States (Illinois, Ohio) and one in Canada (Ontario) — a North American, high-income multi-site sample; representativeness of the wider population is not discussed.
Specimen_Type_Detail: remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens (one 30 µl aliquot inoculated onto BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection of MRSA from anterior nares surveillance specimens: agreement between the MRSA App's automated colorimetric interpretation of CHROMagar MRSA II plate images (mauve colony growth) and the reference standard of laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images, reported as sensitivity, specificity, concordance, PPV and NPV.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA). Enterococcus faecalis ATCC 29212 is named only as the negative quality-control organism.
Drug_Classes: Not modelled: the endpoint is presence/absence of MRSA (mauve colony growth) on chromogenic agar; no antimicrobial class outcome is modelled and no susceptibility testing was performed.
Specific_Antibiotics: Not tested: methicillin resistance is inferred from the chromogenic MRSA phenotype (mauve colonies); no susceptibility testing was performed.
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Mauve-pigmented (chromogenic) colony growth on BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II read from digital plate images = MRSA positive; plates are first assigned growth/no growth, and growing plates are assessed for chromogenic colony appearance signalling MRSA. The label is the laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images (standard of care / reference standard).
AI_Purpose: To automate the reading of chromogenic MRSA screening plates: the MRSA App uses digital plate images and conventional image processing plus a four-stage machine-learning pipeline to interpret colorimetric information (mauve colonies), detect MRSA growth and sort cultures into categories for batch reading, replacing manual reading of agar plate images.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (the MRSA App as a single index test, compared with the technologist reference standard; the App itself combines four machine-learning models — zone CFU/non-CFU classification, plate growth status, mauve/non-mauve CFU classification and plate positivity — with no per-model comparison)
Feature_Engineering: Areas of interest (pixel-value changes after incubation, i.e. CFUs or artefacts) are detected by conventional image processing; color, morphology, metrics and opacity are extracted from each zone and fed to an initial machine-learning model (CFU vs other), then plate-level metrics and descriptors of the detected CFU population feed a second model for growth status, with mauve/non-mauve classification and plate positivity in two further models.
Software_Libraries: R (R Core Team, 2020) version 4.0.2; MedCalc Software (v.22.021)
Other_Metrics: Concordance 96.98% (1,545/1,593); PPV 88.11% (95% CI, 84.62, 90.89); NPV 99.52% (95% CI, 98.96, 98.78 — as printed); 48 discrepant results (3.01%) with per-site discrepancy rates 0.8% (5/634), 2.7% (17/634) and 8% (26/325); 42 false positives and 6 false negatives; site-level sensitivities 99.56%, 91.30%, 98.00% and specificities 99.01%, 97.79%, 90.91%; chi-square tests across sites with P-values 0.0036, 0.0015, 0.0002, 0.0416, 0.9301NS and <0.0001.
Baseline_Method: Manual reading of the same digital agar plate images by two trained, blinded laboratory technologists at each site (with a third arbiter reader if consensus was not reached), used as the reference standard / standard of care.
Baseline_Performance: The technologist reading is the reference standard and is not scored separately; agreement with the MRSA App was 96.98% (1,545/1,593) with 42 App-only detections (false positives) and 6 technologist-only detections (false negatives).
External_Validation_Description: First evaluation of the pre-existing, sponsor-developed MRSA App, applied without retraining to anterior nares specimens collected independently at three clinical sites (two in the United States, one in Canada) and compared with a blinded laboratory technologist reference standard; no training or development dataset is reported in the paper.
Generalisability_Details: Authors argue that in real-world use, where technologists are not blinded to the App results, all suspected MRSA-positive plates would be reviewed by a technologist and the App's PPV would therefore likely be higher than the 88.11% measured here.
Maturity_Evidence: Multi-site diagnostic accuracy evaluation of the locked MRSA App against a blinded technologist reference standard on independent specimens (sensitivity 98.15%, specificity 96.69%); no model training on the study data, no prospective clinical impact evaluation, no CDS integration and no routine-use evidence reported for this cohort.
Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory BD Kiestra TLA workflow: CHROMagar MRSA II plates imaged after 22-24 h of incubation, sorted by the MRSA App into batch-reading categories for technologist review and confirmation, with results then entered into the laboratory information system for viewing by physicians and clinical staff in the electronic medical record.
End_User_Described: Laboratory technologists / medical laboratory technologists who read and interpret the plate images (with clinicians receiving the results); no other end user is specified.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The App sorts MRSA screening cultures into growth/no growth categories so technologists can rapidly review and confirm pigmented colonies; cultures without growth can be batch-reviewed in up to 20 plates before final results, reducing data entry; in European laboratories mauve colonies are technologist-reviewed before reporting, no-growth cultures are automatically released and non-mauve growth is batch reported.
Stewardship_Details: Not measured: the paper states only that faster reporting may support antimicrobial stewardship efforts, without assessing any stewardship outcome.
Barriers_List: False-positive App results (42/1,593; PPV 88.11%) would need technologist review and confirmation to avoid unwarranted isolation and antibiotics; discrepant specimens were unavailable for repeat testing to exclude imaging artefacts; site-to-site variation in performance (lower sensitivity at Site 2, lower specificity at Site 3) and the two-option streaking pattern that could not be analysed further after de-identification; no visual explanation for 28 App-only detections.
Facilitators_List: Laboratory staffing shortages and an ageing workforce; existing laboratory automation (Kiestra TLA, Copan WASPLab) already integrated in clinical microbiology laboratories; batch reading of no-growth cultures (up to 20 plates) and European auto-release of no-growth cultures reduce hands-on time, data entry and reporting delays.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 2 (digital agar plate images / microbiological colony features; laboratory plate-level metrics and CFU descriptors)
Limitation_Categories: Discrepant specimens not available for repeat testing or confirmation by another method; study design allowed two streaking patterns, a possible explanation for the higher FP rate at Site 3 that could not be investigated further because specimens were de-identified; unexplained App-only detections (28 cultures); higher FP than FN balance driven by sensitivity-prioritising algorithm tuning.
Data_Quality_Concerns: 166 enrolled specimens were excluded (inoculation outside the QC-plate time span, missing incubation images, algorithm-detected issues such as a bead in the plate or a failed image quality check, plates with no truth collected) and 16 further cultures lacked a standard-of-care result; discrepant specimens were not retained for repeat testing; diffuse mauve pigment in the agar at the inoculation site and colony mixtures may explain some App-only detections.
Reporting_Clarity: Methods, index test, reference standard and per-site 2x2 data (Table 1) are reported with 95% CIs, but the NPV confidence interval is printed in reverse order as 98.96, 98.78 and the NPV/PPV are given only for the total, not per site.
Page_References: pp. 1-2 (abstract, background, AI program overview); p. 3 (specimen collection, MRSA App algorithm, processing, plate reading); p. 4 (QC, statistics, results incl. PPV/NPV); pp. 5-6 (discussion, Table 1, workflow); p. 7 (limitations, conclusions, funding, contributions); p. 8 (affiliations, data availability, supplemental material, references).

Feature_Selection_Method: feature_importances attribute (tree-based models); absolute coefficient values (LR and linear SVM); SelectKBest with chi2 (non-linear SVM); absolute first-layer weights (Keras NN)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Random down-sampling of the majority class
Hyperparameter_Method: scikit-learn RandomizedSearchCV (for SVM and FFNN)
Software_Libraries: Scikit-learn 1.3.2; Keras 2.12.0; xgboost 1.7.6; lightgbm 4.1.0; catboost 1.2.2; fastp 0.23.4; BCFtools 1.18; SAMtools 1.18; statsmodels 0.14.0
Hardware_Details: Open Science Grid High Throughput Computing infrastructure
Other_Metrics: AUC-ROC; precision; recall; F1 score; accuracy; Tukey's HSD test for pairwise AUC differences
Baseline_Method: Logistic Regression (LR) as baseline for binary classification
Internal_Validation: five times 5-fold stratified cross-validation
External_Validation_Description: Independent external dataset from Uganda, Nigeria and Tanzania (up to 170 samples) with a severe class imbalance; models trained on England data evaluated on both the raw public dataset and a balanced (down-sampled) set.
Clinical_Insights: Identified marker genes/SNPs associated with AMR in E. coli, implicating membrane transport, rRNA methylation, DNA repair and cell wall synthesis in resistance development.
Generalisability_Details: Models trained on England WGS data showed promise there but the application to the highly imbalanced African dataset illuminated significant challenges; performance varied by antibiotic.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation performed on an independent African dataset (Uganda, Nigeria, Tanzania); no prospective evaluation or deployment reported.
Barriers_List: Limited availability of African WGS data (relatively small evaluation dataset); high class imbalance with underrepresented resistance classes; exclusive focus on SNPs; model performance specific to the datasets used.

Future_Directions: Integrating larger and more diverse datasets and maintaining a balance between dataset size and class distribution.

Novel_Predictors_Details: Identified key marker genes/SNPs potentially involved in AMR: CIP - rlmL, yehB, rrfA, yciQ, ygjK; AMP - rcsD, yjfI, tdcE, ugpB, ugpQ, ggt; CTX - ydbA, mltB, lomR, mppA, recD, glyS.
Limitation_Categories: Exclusive focus on SNPs; limited African WGS data (small dataset); high class imbalance; context-specific (non-generalizable) model performance.
Data_Quality_Concerns: High class imbalance in the African dataset; limited availability of African WGS data resulting in a small evaluation dataset.

Title: Analysis of Risk Factors for Multidrug-Resistant Organism (MDRO) Infections and Construction of a Risk Prediction Model in a Cancer Specialty Hospital

Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.

Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single nomogram model; no models are compared)

Title:
Emulation of a Target Trial to Estimate the Effect of Selective Serotonin 
Reuptake Inhibitors on the Development of Antimicrobial-Resistant 
Infections using Electronic Health Record Data and Causal Machine Learning
Study_Design_Other: Target trial emulation of a hypothetical randomised trial
Funder_Names: National Institutes of Health (National Institute on Aging, R33AG062884; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, R01AI141810)
Population_Description: Adult UF Health patients with a bacterial infection diagnosis and antimicrobial susceptibility test results, restricted to those with a diagnosis of mood, anxiety or stress-related disorder; 1,715 SSRI-treated and 6,618 control patients before matching, 1,696 per group after 1:1 propensity score matching
Age_Mean_Median: Mean 54.5 years (SD 17.5) in the SSRI group and 54.5 years (SD 17.1) in the non-SSRI group after matching; overall mean about 54.5 years
Age_Range: Adults only (≥18 years at the index date); exact age range not reported
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
Task_Type_Other: Causal survival analysis — conditional average treatment effect estimation for a right-censored time-to-event outcome
All_Models_Evaluated: Kaplan-Meier survival curves (log-rank p<0.001); Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for sex, age, race-ethnicity, Charlson comorbidity index and grouped zip code (adjusted HR for SSRI use 1.44, 95% CI 1.26-1.64); causal random survival forest (grf causal_survival_forest): average treatment effect -0.0499, standard error 0.0188
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were estimated and statistically evaluated only on the single-system UF Health matched cohort (Kaplan-Meier, adjusted Cox HR with 95% CI, causal survival forest ATE with SE); no external validation dataset, no prospective evaluation and no clinical integration is reported
Reported_Limitations: Cohort restricted to patients who had received antimicrobial susceptibility testing, mainly hospitalised patients; medication exposure captured only from the inpatient MAR so outpatient prescriptions may be missed (exposure misclassification); outcome misclassification when the relevant drug was not tested or testing occurred outside UF Health; residual confounding from unmeasured variables; bias from converted ICD codes; EHR missingness and inaccuracies; single health system and about half the patients from one county, limiting generalisability
Reviewer_Notes: Target trial emulation on UF Health EHR data with causal machine learning; outcome is a binary antimicrobial susceptibility test result (resistant to at least one antibiotic) analysed as time-to-event. No discrimination or classification metrics (accuracy, AUROC, sensitivity, specificity) are reported, so all *_Reported metric fields are answered No for the best-performing-model unit of analysis; the three analytic approaches are reported as concordant rather than ranked, so Best_Performing_Model_NA is TRUE.
Sample_Size: 3,392 patients after matching (1,696 SSRI users and 1,696 non-SSRI patients); 8,333 patients before matching (1,715 treated and 6,618 control)
Sex_Distribution: After matching: female 1,201 (70.8%) in the SSRI group and 1,197 (70.6%) in the non-SSRI group; before matching: 1,211 (70.6%) and 4,783 (72.3%); 'Over 70% of the population was female'
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients at UF Health who (1) had a previous bacterial infection greater than 90 days before enrolment, (2) had at least two years of medication EHR data, (3) had not previously been given sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram, citalopram, paroxetine or fluvoxamine, (4) had been diagnosed with mood, anxiety or stress-related disorder, and (5) did not have a bacterial infection at study initiation; each included patient also had a previous antimicrobial susceptibility test result or a diagnosis of bacterial infection more than 90 days before the index date
Exclusion_Criteria: No MAR Action containing the word 'GIVEN' for one of the SSRIs (patients may not have received the SSRI); fewer than two years of medication data before the index date; control-group patients whose last medication record or recorded death date preceded the index date; estimated age younger than 18 years at the index date; antimicrobial susceptibility test results or bacterial infection diagnostic codes within 30 days of the index date
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: University of Florida (UF) Health Integrated Data Repository (IDR)
Dataset_Size: 3,392 patients after matching (1,696 per group); 8,333 before matching (1,715 treated, 6,618 control)
Ethnicity_Details: After matching: Non-Hispanic White 1,137 (67.0%) SSRI vs 1,140 (67.2%) non-SSRI; Non-Hispanic Black 469 (27.7%) vs 470 (27.7%); Hispanic 51 (3.0%) vs 49 (2.9%); Other 39 (2.3%) vs 37 (2.2%)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single integrated academic health system (UF Health, North and Central Florida); about half of the patients came from the 326 grouped zip code (Alachua County area); the authors state the results may not be generalizable to other populations
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antimicrobial susceptibility test result of 'resistant' (including 'tentative interpretation: resistant' or 'non susceptible') to at least one antibiotic tested, from 30 to 1,825 days after the index date
Drug_Classes: SSRIs as the study exposure (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram, citalopram, paroxetine, fluvoxamine); the outcome is resistance to at least one antibiotic tested, with no antimicrobial class specified
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary: an antimicrobial susceptibility test result of 'resistant', 'tentative interpretation: resistant' or 'non susceptible' for at least one antibiotic tested, from 30 to 1,825 days after the index date
AI_Purpose: To estimate the causal effect of SSRI exposure on the incidence of antibiotic-resistant infection, using a target trial emulation framework and causal machine learning (causal survival forest) alongside conventional survival regression
Num_Models_Compared: 3 analytical approaches (univariable/multivariable survival regression, Cox proportional hazards model, causal random survival forest)
Feature_Engineering: All diagnostic codes converted to the ICD-10-CM revision; ICD-10 code sets used to define bacterial infection and mood/anxiety/stress-related disorders; index date defined as the first MAR mention of an SSRI (treated) or a randomly sampled time before study initiation (control)
Num_Features_Total: 5 covariates (sex, age, race-ethnicity, Charlson comorbidity index, three-digit zip code)
Software_Libraries: matchit (propensity score matching); grf (causal_survival_forest)
Other_Metrics: Log-rank test p-value less than 0.001; adjusted hazard ratio 1.44 (95% CI 1.26-1.64); average treatment effect -0.0499 (standard error 0.0188); Kaplan-Meier probabilities of not developing an antibiotic-resistant infection with 95% confidence intervals
Baseline_Method: Multivariable Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for sex, age, race-ethnicity, Charlson comorbidity index and grouped zip code (conventional regression comparator against the causal random survival forest)
Baseline_Performance: Adjusted hazard ratio 1.44 (95% CI 1.26-1.64) for SSRI users versus non-users
Clinical_Insights: The authors conclude that documented SSRI use is associated with a higher risk of antibiotic-resistant infection, framed as supporting prior in vitro findings and suggesting SSRI usage should be investigated as a possible driver of antimicrobial resistance
Generalisability_Details: Data come from one health system (UF Health) and about half of the patients came from one county (326 grouped zip code, Alachua County area); the authors state the results may not be generalizable to other populations
Maturity_Evidence: Retrospective single-system EHR cohort (2011-2023); all three analyses were fitted and evaluated on the same 1,696-per-group matched cohort, with no external validation cohort, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment reported
Barriers_List: Exposure measured only through the inpatient medication administration record, so outpatient SSRI use may be missed and patients misclassified into the control group; the outcome can be missed when the relevant drug was not tested or testing occurred outside UF Health; residual confounding from unmeasured variables; bias from converted ICD codes; EHR missingness and inaccuracies; single health system and one county, limiting generalisability
Future_Directions: Further studies in human patients are needed to examine the effects of different SSRIs (for example sertraline versus escitalopram), dosages and lengths of treatment, and to explore differences in infection type, organism and type of AMR
Novel_Predictors_Details: SSRI exposure (a non-antimicrobial drug class) as a newly documented risk factor for antibiotic-resistant infection in human EHR data, together with geographical (grouped zip code) differences in risk
Limitation_Categories: Restriction to patients who had antimicrobial susceptibility testing (mainly hospitalised); exposure measured from the inpatient MAR only; outcome and exposure misclassification; residual confounding; bias from converted ICD codes; EHR missingness and inaccuracies; single health system and one county limiting generalisability
Data_Quality_Concerns: EHR data are prone to missingness and inaccuracies; medication exposure captured only from the inpatient MAR; converted ICD codes may introduce bias; outcome may be missed when susceptibility testing was not performed for the relevant drug
Page_References: pp. 1-8 of the PDF (printed pages 997-1004); Table 1 p. 2; Table 2 p. 5; Table 3 p. 6; Figures 1-2 p. 3, Figure 3 p. 5

Title: Performance of Risk Models for Antimicrobial Resistance in Adult Patients With Sepsis
Funder_Names: National Institutes of Health / National Institute of General Medical Sciences (grant No. 1K08GM140310-01); Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital; Washington University Institute of Clinical and Translational Sciences grant No. UL1TR002345 from the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences of the National Institutes of Health
Population_Description: 39 893 adult patients with sepsis (85 238 sepsis episodes; 43 207 community-onset, 42 031 hospital-onset) admitted to 10 acute-care BJC hospitals in Missouri and Illinois, January 2016 to October 2021
Top_Predictive_Features: Top 10 features (SHAP values, gradient-boosting model), all episodes of community-onset sepsis: History of P aeruginosa; History of antibiotic administration; History of pneumonia due to P aeruginosa; Age; Albumin; History of resistance to multiple antibiotics; History of urinary tract infection; Pneumonia due to other GNB; BMI; ALT
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Deep learning model vs gradient-boosting model (XGBoost, dedicated to SHAP variable importance). Comorbidity/medical-history-only comparison: deep learning AUROC 0.81 (95% CI, 0.81-0.81) and AUPRC 0.30 (95% CI, 0.29-0.31); gradient boosting AUROC 0.76 (95% CI, 0.76-0.76) and AUPRC 0.23 (95% CI, 0.23-0.23)
Best_Performing_Model: Deep learning model (deep neural network with fully connected, recurrent neural network and transformer subnetworks) - highest AUROC vs gradient boosting (0.81 vs 0.76) in the comorbidity-only comparison
AUROC_Value: Deep learning model, community-onset sepsis: AUROC 0.84 (95% CI, 0.83-0.84) for RS episodes and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.79-0.83) for RR episodes
AUROC_Population_Set: Holdout testing dataset, community-onset sepsis episodes (RS and RR GNB isolates), 10 hospitals
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal validation: 80% of the data trained the models (70% training, 10% model selection) and 20% was held out for patient group-specific testing within the same 10 hospitals and period; no external or prospective validation, no CDS integration
Reported_Limitations: Limitations inherent to retrospective analyses based on EHR data; potential confounders not included (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices); a large study capturing difficult-to-extract variables not stored in structured data format is nearly impossible
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Widespread overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics (the unintended consequence of previous risk stratification tools derived at centres with high resistance prevalence), which may have detrimental effects at the population and patient levels; national study reporting only 0.9% of samples retrieved ARO GNB while 76% of those patients were flagged as candidates for double GNB coverage
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: The 3 example hospitals differ socioeconomically: an academic quaternary centre serving a socioeconomically diverse population, a suburban community hospital serving an affluent population, and a community-based hospital serving a socioeconomically disadvantaged population; model performance varied with local resistance prevalence rather than patient casemix, so the same patient subgroup falls into different risk categories depending on the institution
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Washington University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board approved the study and granted a waiver of consent due to the retrospective nature of the study; data sharing is via Supplement 2; no code or model sharing statement
Reviewer_Notes: Record built from the pypdf text layer. Main judgements: the paper evaluates 2 models (a deep learning model named as 'the main tool' and a gradient-boosting model dedicated to SHAP variable importance) and reports no single primary dataset - results are given separately for RS and RR isolates in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis, so Accuracy/Sensitivity/Specificity/Precision/F1 are answered No and AUROC/AUPRC are reported for the deep learning model with both onset settings named
Unresolved_Items: No model-level AUROC is printed for the hospital-onset model (only AUPRC 0.25 for RS and 0.16 for RR); the AUROC 0.81 (0.81-0.81) figure appears only in the comorbidity-subset comparison and does not state which dataset; the paper names no single primary dataset for the review's unit of analysis
Sample_Size: 39 893 patients with 85 238 sepsis episodes
Conflicts_of_Interest: Dr Vazquez Guillamet reported selling stocks in Carsima Therapeutics, Bionano Genomics, and Ocugen Inc in September 2023 outside the submitted work; Dr Fraser reported that their spouse is a former senior vice president/chief medical officer and now consulting for Cigna/Express Scripts; no other disclosures were reported
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients meeting the US CDC adult sepsis event criteria admitted to any of the 10 acute-care BJC hospitals between January 2016 to October 2021; inclusion combined presumed infection (blood cultures and 4 qualifying days of antibiotics) with concomitant organ dysfunction (any of vasopressor use, mechanical ventilation, increased creatinine or bilirubin levels, and thrombocytopenia)
Exclusion_Criteria: 148 patients excluded due to missing antimicrobial susceptibility results and 77 due to missing sex or race
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Electronic health record of the 10 acute-care BJC hospitals, greater St Louis region, Missouri and Illinois
Dataset_Size: 49 726 admissions and 85 238 sepsis episodes in the final dataset
Missing_Data_Method: Removed patients with any missing categorical feature (eg, sex and race); carried forward the last observation for missing laboratory results and vitals
Ethnicity_Details: Race and ethnicity: Black 9112 (22.8%), White 23 982 (60.1%), Other 6799 (17.0%) in the entire cohort
Geographic_Representativeness: Large and diverse dataset of patients across urban and rural areas of the greater St Louis region in Missouri and Illinois; 3 hospitals illustrated as examples of different patient casemixes, including a socioeconomically disadvantaged population
Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture specimen: Blood 1602 (13.7%), Urine 4575 (39.0%), Respiratory 2957 (25.2%), Other 2598 (22.1%)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: GNB antimicrobial resistance level in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis episodes, categorised as ceftriaxone-susceptible (SS), ceftriaxone-resistant but cefepime-susceptible (RS), and ceftriaxone- and cefepime-resistant (RR)
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (36.2% of RR isolates, community-onset), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (56.6% of RS isolates in community-onset; 58.3% in hospital-onset), Klebsiella spp; non-GNB organisms (eg, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, viruses) were labelled SS
Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefepime)
Specific_Antibiotics: ceftriaxone; cefepime
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility results documented in the EHR; ceftriaxone-susceptible (SS; negative cultures and non-GNB cultures also labelled SS), ceftriaxone-resistant but cefepime-susceptible (RS), and ceftriaxone- and cefepime-resistant (RR); the most resistant GNB microbe determined the category for polymicrobial cultures; intermediate isolates labelled susceptible; CLSI breakpoints based on minimal inhibitory concentration
AI_Purpose: To develop deep learning models based on artificial neural networks (separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis) that project levels of antimicrobial resistance in GNB, and to assess whether patient casemix and local prevalence rates of resistance explain the variable performance of a general risk stratification model across hospitals and patient subgroups
Feature_Engineering: All vitals and laboratory data points within 5 days of the culture timestamp were resampled and the mean value of every 4-hour window was used by the deep learning model; plausible ranges defined and implausible values excluded; shock defined as vasopressor or inotrope use within 24 hours of the culture timestamp; age, time since admission, vital signs and laboratory results treated as continuous; hospital, sex and race categorical; procedures, antibiotic administration, comorbidities and previous susceptible or resistant culture results binary; all input variables screened at the culture timestamp
Feature_Selection_Method: Laboratory value and vital sign features selected considering redundancy, collinearity, and availability in the EHR; gradient-boosting model with SHAP dedicated to variable importance for the first 10 features contributing to the model
Class_Imbalance_Method: Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) to oversample the RR and RS minority groups and focal loss to reweight the loss of the minority group
Hyperparameter_Method: Gradient boosting implemented with tuned tree depth and feature subsampling; deep learning implemented with tuned network width and depth and learning rate; a 10% random validation split of the training set used to monitor validation performance and terminate training before overfitting
Software_Libraries: PyTorch version 2.1; XGBoost version 2.0.0; scikit-learn version 1.3.0
Other_Metrics: AUPRC for RS and RR isolates in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis; SHAP values for feature importance; correlation (R) between AUPRC and RS/RR prevalence rates
Baseline_Method: Gradient-boosting model (XGBoost) compared with the deep learning model on the comorbidity and medical-history feature subset
Baseline_Performance: Gradient boosting: AUROC 0.76 (95% CI, 0.76-0.76); AUPRC 0.23 (95% CI, 0.23-0.23) (deep learning comparator: AUROC 0.81 [95% CI, 0.81-0.81]; AUPRC 0.30 [95% CI, 0.29-0.31])
Internal_Validation: 80/20 split: 70% training, 10% model selection, 20% holdout for patient group-specific testing (infections from the same patient exist only in either the training or the testing set); 10% random validation split of the training set to terminate training before overfitting; models tested separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis
Train_Test_Split: 80% train (70% for training and 10% for model selection); 20% holdout set for patient group-specific testing
External_Validation_Description: None - the general model was tested on holdout data from the same hospitals and period
Overfitting_Method: 10% random validation split of the training set used for both models to monitor validation performance during training and terminate training before overfitting; model brittleness (failure to generalise) addressed by developing a general model tested on same-hospital holdout data
Clinical_Insights: In community-onset sepsis, history of P aeruginosa infections and history of antibiotic administration were the strongest factors discriminating RS and RR from SS; history of antibiotic-resistant organisms and previous episodes of severe sepsis or septic shock were associated with RR. In hospital-onset sepsis, age and history of P aeruginosa infections were the most impactful factors; time since admission was associated with lower risk of SS and higher risk of RR. Vasopressor use and longitudinal data added minimal contributions.
Generalisability_Details: The results do not support widespread use of generalized models; model performance was associated with prevalence rates of resistant GNB and varied across hospitals and patient subgroups; future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates to accompany patient-level variables
Maturity_Evidence: Internal holdout testing only: 80/20 patient group-specific split, models trained on the whole training set and tested separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis, results reported without oversampling; performance varied widely across hospitals and subgroups and the authors conclude against widespread use of generalized models
Integration_Point: Not described for this model (research model evaluated on holdout data); the Epic Sepsis Model is described as integrated into the clinical EHR system as prior work
End_User_Described: Clinicians choosing between narrow- or broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics for patients with sepsis; risk stratification models that guide clinicians' empirical choices
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Prediction of antimicrobial resistance must occur at suspicion of infection to initiate empirical antibiotics, so all input variables were screened at the culture timestamp
Stewardship_Details: No stewardship outcome was measured; the authors state that future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates, and that the results argue against the use of generalized models for predicting resistant GNB etiologies in sepsis
Barriers_List: Difficult-to-extract variables such as nursing home residence are not usually stored in a structured data format, making a large study that captures them nearly impossible; study limitations inherent to retrospective EHR-based analyses; potential confounders not included (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices)
Facilitators_List: Model robustness against subgroup distribution heterogeneity may be improved using domain generalization approaches or group-fairness classification approaches, which the authors are considering for future work
Future_Directions: Future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates (warranting availability of microbiology data) to accompany patient-level variables; institutions are encouraged to develop their own risk stratification models to identify patients at risk for resistant GNB, similar to maintaining local antibiograms; domain generalization and group-fairness approaches are being considered
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) values from the gradient-boosting model, reported as mean impact on model output magnitude for the top 10 features
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective EHR-based analysis; unmeasured confounders (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices); difficult-to-extract variables not stored in structured format; no external or prospective validation; model performance not transferable across hospitals
Data_Quality_Concerns: Patients with any missing categorical feature (eg, sex and race) were removed; the last observation was carried forward for missing laboratory results and vitals; plausible ranges defined and implausible values excluded; missing antimicrobial susceptibility results handled by general logic rules for intrinsic resistance
Reporting_Clarity: Clear - STROBE reporting guideline and published recommendations for machine learning models followed; full feature list and preprocessing details in Supplement 1 (eTable, eFigures 1-2); all results reported with 95% CIs

Title: Enhancing Antibiotic Stewardship: A Machine Learning Approach to Predicting Antibiotic Resistance in Inpatient Care
