Title: Machine Learning-Led Optimization of Combination Therapy: Confronting the Public Health Threat of Extensively Drug Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria
Country_Countries: United States of America (Buffalo and Troy, New York; Nutley, New Jersey; San Diego, California)
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design_Other: In vitro hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) experiments providing the pharmacodynamic data for a mechanism-based mathematical model
Funder_Names: National Institutes of Health, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (R01AI165997; R01AI148560; L30AI164450)
Population_Description: Four clinical, extensively drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada) studied in 7-day in vitro hollow fiber infection model experiments; regimens simulated in a critically ill patient population using published human population PK models (no human participants)
Data_Source_Other: In vitro hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) data from previously performed studies (35 experiments, 1,056 samples) and previously published human population pharmacokinetic models for each agent
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance; Dose optimisation
Task_Type_Other: Genetic algorithm (GA)-led optimisation of multi-drug dosing regimens (dose, infusion duration, dosing interval, loading dose) against PK/PD/toxicodynamic end points; mechanism-based pharmacodynamic model fitting and Monte Carlo simulation
All_Models_Evaluated: Four GA fitness functions (F1-F4) tested across 13 optimisation end points: PD-only end points (F1, 10 2 CFU/mL at the 90th/80th/70th/60th prediction interval), polymyxin B TD-only end points (F2), and joint polymyxin B + aztreonam TD end points with two weighting schemes (F3 0.990/0.005/0.005; F4 0.90/0.05/0.05). Reported output is target attainment and regimen parameters (Table 1) - no accuracy, AUROC or error metric is reported for any optimisation scheme.
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest level supported: the mechanism-based PD model was internally qualified with visual predictive checks and the GA regimens were evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation only; no external validation, prospective evaluation, CDS integration or routine clinical use is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Only four XDR K. pneumoniae isolates / 35 HFIM experiments, so a larger, more representative panel of isolates is needed to match current XDR epidemiology; regimens were optimised on literature PK reports from monotherapy studies in critically ill patients, whereas co-administration augments exposure and optimal doses could therefore be lower.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: The GA 1:1 PD:TD weighting scheme had to be abandoned: it terminated early after 200 iterations with no change in the fitness function and produced a regimen that attained the polymyxin B AUC24,ss target of 100 mg·h/L but failed to produce bacterial killing. Toxicity targets (polymyxin B nephrotoxicity, aztreonam hepatotoxicity) also constrained the optimised regimens.
Reviewer_Notes: Prospective regimen-optimisation study, not a diagnostic model: no classification/discrimination metrics exist, so every *_Reported accuracy field is answered No rather than left blank. AI_Application_Type and Task_Type have no vocabulary entry for GA-based regimen optimisation, so 'Other' was used (with AI Predictive and Prognostic Models / AI Clinical Decision Support Systems ticked for the modelling and regimen-guidance aspects) and Needs_Team_Discussion is Yes.
Sample_Size: 4 clinical XDR K. pneumoniae isolates (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada); HFIM dataset of 35 experiments and 1,056 samples
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declared no competing interests for this work.
Inclusion_Criteria: Four clinical K. pneumoniae isolates from previously performed hollow fiber infection model studies (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada); no patient-level eligibility criteria are reported
Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype; Other
Data_Source_Name: Not a named repository: hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) experiments from previously performed studies plus published human population PK models for aztreonam, ceftazidime/avibactam and polymyxin B
Dataset_Size: 35 7-day HFIM experiments (1,056 samples) across 4 isolates; 13 GA optimisation end points each with a final population of 75 candidate regimens
Geographic_Representativeness: Four clinical XDR K. pneumoniae isolates only, so the authors state that a larger panel of isolates should be explored to properly generalise the results to current XDR epidemiology
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Bacterial killing of XDR K. pneumoniae by GA-optimised combination regimens: attainment of a bacterial concentration of 10 2 CFU/mL at 168 hours (assay limit of detection) in the HFIM, while keeping polymyxin B and aztreonam exposures within their toxicity limits
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (four clinical extensively drug-resistant isolates: ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada)
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (aztreonam, ceftazidime); beta-lactamase inhibitor (avibactam); polymyxins (polymyxin B)
Specific_Antibiotics: Aztreonam; ceftazidime; avibactam; polymyxin B
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Threshold definition, not a metric: the bacterial PD end point was a bacterial concentration of 10 2 CFU/mL at 168 hours (assay limit of detection, lower end of reported bacteraemia concentrations); the PK/TD end points were polymyxin B AUC24,ss = 100 mg/h/L and aztreonam AUCss = 1,336 mg/h/L, each evaluated at a prediction interval of simulated subjects
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: Use a genetic algorithm, driven by a mechanism-based PD model with human population PK, to optimise aztreonam + ceftazidime/avibactam +/- polymyxin B combination regimens de novo against joint efficacy and toxicity end points for XDR K. pneumoniae
Num_Models_Compared: No head-to-head comparison of predictive models: 4 GA fitness functions (F1-F4) across 13 optimisation end points, each with a final population of 75 candidate regimens
Feature_Engineering: Mechanism-based PD model translated to RxODE with HFIM PKs replaced by published human PopPK models; regimen inputs (dose, infusion time, doses per day, loading dose) rounded to the nearest milligram, 0.5 hours and integer value before GA evaluation
Software_Libraries: GA package in R (genetic algorithm); RxODE solved with the Livermore Solver for Ordinary Differential Equations
Other_Metrics: Regimen target attainment (10 2 CFU/mL at 168 h), median infusion duration 2 h (range 1.5-3 h), median dosing interval 9 h (range 6-12 h), mean aztreonam 6.18 vs 7.16 g/day, mean ceftazidime/avibactam 8.55 g/day (SD 1.45), mean polymyxin B 3.18 mg/kg/day (SD 1.05) producing AUC24,ss,avg 115 mg/h/L
Baseline_Method: Comparator regimens derived empirically over years of clinical use, and current FDA package labelling for each agent
Baseline_Performance: Optimised aztreonam daily dose 6.18 vs 7.16 g/day (with vs without an aztreonam TD end point) against FDA-labelled 6-8 g/day; optimised ceftazidime/avibactam dose exceeded the package label (mean 8.55 g/day); polymyxin B optimisation produced AUC24,ss,avg 93.5-115 mg/h/L against the 100 mg/h/L consensus target
Internal_Validation: Visual predictive checks used to internally qualify the mechanism-based PD model
Clinical_Insights: PD/TD weighting must be deferential to patient safety and clinical feasibility because missing an individual target carries consequences such as microbiological failure or drug toxicity; optimised regimens mirror empirically derived clinical dosing (prolonged beta-lactam infusion, higher avibactam exposure) and are proposed as a testing framework for new or special-population regimens
Generalisability_Details: Four XDR K. pneumoniae isolates only, so a larger and more representative panel of isolates is needed for the results to match current XDR epidemiology (strain types, virulence factors, resistance mechanisms); regimens rest on monotherapy PK data from critically ill patients
Maturity_Evidence: Internal qualification of the mechanism-based PD model by visual predictive checks and Monte Carlo evaluation of GA-optimised regimens; no external validation cohort, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment is reported
Integration_Point: Output of the optimised regimens (dose, infusion duration, dosing interval, loading dose) is proposed for clinical trial simulation and preclinical regimen design; not integrated into any clinical, EHR or LIS system
End_User_Described: Not named explicitly: the framework is aimed at preclinical drug development and at regimen design for special patient populations, i.e. researchers and prescribers in critically ill patients
Barriers_List: Multiple PK end points must be met simultaneously for combination therapy and target attainment multiplies geometrically with each added drug, making optimisation experimentally intractable; choice of PD/TD weighting affects the search; PK variability between drugs; the 1:1 weighting scheme failed to explore the parameter space
Facilitators_List: GA-led regimen design can be integrated into preclinical drug development to produce testable regimens, avoid pre-existing notions of a 'best' schedule, reduce the number of animal experiments, and hypothesise alternative regimens for special patient populations with altered PK
Future_Directions: Expand the isolate panel to a representative sample of the most resistant isolates (by national prevalence of strain types, virulence factors and resistance mechanisms) so the results generalise to current XDR K. pneumoniae epidemiology; apply GA-led regimen design to new drugs and to special patient populations
Feature_Interactions_Method: Mechanism-based model interaction terms: avibactam reduces the aztreonam KC50 by up to 99.3%, and polymyxin B kills aztreonam-induced persister cells
Limitation_Categories: Limited isolate panel and generalisability; reliance on historical monotherapy PK data; modelling assumptions (persister cell subpopulation, two-subpopulation structure)
Data_Quality_Concerns: Regimens were optimised on prior literature PK reports in critically ill patients all studied in monotherapy; co-administration of aztreonam and ceftazidime/avibactam augments exposure, so optimised doses could be lower than reported
Reporting_Clarity: Model, GA implementation (13 end points, population size 75, weightings) and optimised regimen parameters are reported in detail, but only PK/PD target attainment is reported - no accuracy-type performance statistics, no confidence intervals, no calibration

Title: Development and validation of machine learning models to predict MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission by using electronic health record data
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Population_Description: ICU patients (adults, ICU stay ≥24 h) from PLAGH-ICU (n=3,536) and MIMIC-IV (n=34,923) who underwent microbial culture within 24 h of ICU admission; outcome is MDRO colonization or infection.
Top_Predictive_Features: PLAGH-ICU (via SHAP values): C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), serum urea, duration of pre-ICU hospital stay, interleukin-6 (IL-6), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: LR, KNN, SVC, RF, XGBoost, MLP, and a stacking ensemble. In temporal validation the ensemble models performed best: PLAGH-ICU AUROC 0.786 [0.748, 0.825]; MIMIC-IV AUROC 0.744 [0.723, 0.766]. By AUROC, Random Forest, XGBoost and Ensemble outperformed the other algorithms.
Best_Performing_Model: Ensemble model
AUROC_Population_Set: Best-performing ensemble model on PLAGH-ICU temporal validation set
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation performed: PLAGH-ICU model assessed on MIMIC-IV (AUROC 0.638) and MIMIC-IV model on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615); therefore maturity level 3 (external validation).
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design requiring prospective validation; low precision (positive predictive value) at thresholds ensuring higher recall, entailing potential high costs if applied clinically; models built from specific institutions may not be directly applicable elsewhere; feature importance indicates correlation, not causality.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Low positive predictive value at high-recall thresholds could entail high costs if applied clinically at this stage.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Implementation challenges include data access, privacy concerns, hardware and software integration, physician adoption, and regulatory compliance.
Sample_Size: 3,536 patients (PLAGH-ICU)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Sex_Distribution: PLAGH-ICU Table 1: male n (%) — non-MDRO 1,980 (63.6), MDRO 301 (71.2)
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients who underwent microbial culture within 24 h of ICU admission; aged ≥18 years; ICU stay ≥24 h.
Exclusion_Criteria: Age <18 years; ICU stay <24 h; MDRO detected within 14 days prior to ICU admission; positive MDRO within 1 day of ICU admission.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: PLAGH-ICU; MIMIC-IV version 2.2
Dataset_Size: 3,536 patients (PLAGH-ICU); 34,923 patients (MIMIC-IV)
Missing_Data_Method: Variables with >30% missing excluded; cases with >20% missing lab values excluded; Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) for the remaining missing data.
Geographic_Representativeness: Two centres: an ICU of the (Chinese) PLA General Hospital and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (USA), the latter via the MIMIC-IV database.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Body fluid samples (not further specified)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission (binary outcome).
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (incl. MRSA), Enterococcus spp., Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter spp.
Drug_Classes: three or more classes of antimicrobial agents (not enumerated)
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDRO = bacteria resistant to three or more classes of antimicrobial agents; MRSA directly categorized as MDRO; outcome is a binary MDRO colonization/infection label.
AI_Purpose: Early detection of patients at risk of MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission, to curb MDRO proliferation and support empirical pharmacotherapy.
Num_Models_Compared: 7 (6 base algorithms + stacking ensemble)
Feature_Engineering: Min-max normalization before training LR, KNN, SVC and MLP models; Spearman correlation-based clustering to remove collinear features; MICE imputation; top-25 feature distillation.
Feature_Selection_Method: Spearman's rank correlation for stratified clustering (collinearity removal), then Random Forest permutation feature importance ranking; top 25 features retained.
Num_Features_Total: 25 (retained for the final prediction model)
Hyperparameter_Method: Bayesian optimization with 5-fold cross-validation
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, shap (Python); dplyr, ggplot2, pROC (R)
Other_Metrics: Brier score, calibration curve intercept and slope, decision curve analysis (standardized net benefit).
Baseline_Method: Logistic Regression (LR)
Internal_Validation: Temporal validation within each dataset (data 2017-2019, after training on 2008-2016); 5-fold cross-validation used for hyperparameter tuning.
External_Validation_Description: PLAGH-ICU model assessed on MIMIC-IV (peak AUROC 0.638 [0.628, 0.648]); MIMIC-IV model assessed on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615 [0.585, 0.646]).
Clinical_Insights: Interpretability allows clinicians to identify high-risk patients, understand individual risk profiles, and tailor treatment plans.
Data_Repository: MIMIC-IV via PhysioNet (physionet.org/content/mimiciv/2.2/); other data from the corresponding author on request
Generalisability_Details: Models show significant variance in feature selection and performance across institutions; collecting data from various hospitals/regions could enhance generalizability; unit-specific MDRO early-warning models may be preferable.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation performed in both directions: PLAGH-ICU model on MIMIC-IV (AUROC 0.638) and MIMIC-IV model on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615) — sets maturity at level 3.
Integration_Point: ICU-admission screening / risk stratification; future CDSS integration
End_User_Described: Clinicians (ICU)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Deployment with real-time data integration via EHR-compatible interfaces; models incorporated into a CDSS delivering alerts and recommendations.
Barriers_List: Data access, privacy concerns, hardware and software integration, physician adoption, regulatory compliance; limited feature-target correlations in early ICU EHR data; poor cross-institution transferability.
Facilitators_List: Models are easily adaptable to hospital EHR systems and use routinely available EHR data.
Future_Directions: Deployment in clinical settings with real-time data integration; integration into a CDSS; establishing a monitoring framework to continuously assess and enhance model performance.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP values
Novel_Predictors_Details: Shorter pre-ICU hospital stays in PLAGH-ICU surprisingly correlated with increased MDRO risk (possibly reflecting resistant-bacteria carriage among patients transferred from other hospitals or community-acquired MDRO).
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design; need for prospective validation; low precision (PPV) / potential clinical cost; limited cross-institution generalizability; feature importance reflects correlation not causality.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing data handled by excluding variables with >30% missing and cases with >20% missing lab values, then MICE imputation.

Title: Machine learning algorithms to predict colistin-induced nephrotoxicity from electronic health records in patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infection
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Ministry of Education
Population_Description: 1392 patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative (MDRGN) infection receiving their first intravenous colistin at three Taipei Medical University hospitals (TMUH, SHH, WFH), Taiwan, 2011-2020; adults (>=18 y) with >=2 d of colistin, no chronic dialysis and available serum creatinine records
Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP feature importance (CAT-SVM-SMOTE): days of colistin use, cumulative dose, daily dose, latest C-reactive protein, and baseline haemoglobin
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: 15 models (CatBoost, LGB, RF x SVM-SMOTE, SMOTE, SMOTETL, Tomek and original data) compared by sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, MCC, AUROC and AUPRC on the temporal validation set (heatmap, Supplementary Table S11). Best RFE-estimated F1: CatBoost 0.603 (48 features), LGB 0.610 (46 features), RF 0.585 (16 features). Best model CAT-SVM-SMOTE: AUROC 0.823, AUPRC 0.737, sensitivity 0.860, F1 0.740, MCC 0.533
Best_Performing_Model: CAT-SVM-SMOTE (CatBoost with SVM-SMOTE resampling) - decided by the highest AUROC (0.823) and AUPRC (0.737), together with the highest sensitivity (0.860), F1 (0.740) and MCC (0.533) on the temporal validation set
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Temporal validation cohort (2018-2020; 402 patients)
AUROC_Population_Set: Temporal validation cohort (2018-2020; 402 patients)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The reported performance of the best model comes from a temporally separate validation cohort (2018-2020, n=402) distinct from the derivation cohort (2011-2017), i.e. TRIPOD type 3 temporal/external validation; no prospective or independent multi-centre external test is reported
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design limits applicability; multiple healthcare datasets needed to generalise; newer AKI biomarkers (cystatin C, NGAL, IL-18) not assessed; features with >25% missing data discarded may have introduced bias; covariate shift between the two cohorts
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: High-sensitivity predictions may elevate false positives, but the authors argue the benefits outweigh misidentifying false negatives
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Vulnerable patients developing AKI despite low colistin doses are identified (14 of 17 patients with very low daily doses were AKI-positive), but no equity analysis by demographic group is reported
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Only ethics approval is described: Joint IRB approval with a waiver of patient consent for de-identified registry data; no data-sharing or model-governance plan, and no regulatory clearance
Sample_Size: 1392 patients (989 in the derivation cohort and 402 in the temporal validation cohort)
Conflicts_of_Interest: Declared none: "The authors bear all of the responsibility for the data in this article and have no conflicts of interest to declare."
Inclusion_Criteria: Admission to TMU Hospital (TMUH), Shuang Ho Hospital (SHH) or Wan Fang Hospital (WFH) with a first intravenous colistin course between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2020; a patient needing more than two courses after a cured episode with an interval >90 d was treated as a new subject for the second course
Exclusion_Criteria: Pregnancy, age <18 y, colistin period <2 d, chronic dialysis, or no serum creatinine (SCr) records
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: Taipei Medical University Clinical Research Database (TMUCRD)
Dataset_Size: 1392 patients (989 derivation / 402 temporal validation); 77 candidate features reduced by RFE to 48 (CatBoost), 46 (LGB) and 16 (RF)
Missing_Data_Method: Features with a missing rate above 25% were discarded; remaining missing values imputed by Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE)
Geographic_Representativeness: Three hospitals in one academic health system in Taiwan (single country, single health-system database); generalisability to other geographies and ethnic populations is stated as untested
Specimen_Type_Detail: No microbiological specimens analysed - blood/laboratory measurements from the EHR (serum creatinine and eGFR slope, creatinine clearance, WBC, CRP, haemoglobin, BUN, sodium, potassium)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Colistin-induced nephrotoxicity (acute kidney injury) in patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infection, defined by the KDIGO criteria
Pathogens: Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative (MDRGN) organisms; individual species are not named in the text
Drug_Classes: Polymyxins (colistin); concomitant nephrotoxic drugs including aminoglycosides and vancomycin
Specific_Antibiotics: Colistin (colistimethate sodium); aminoglycoside; vancomycin
AMR_Outcome_Definition: KDIGO definition of colistin-induced AKI: serum creatinine increase of 0.3 mg/dL from the baseline value within 48 h, or a >=1.5-fold increase within 7 d
AI_Purpose: To construct and compare 15 machine learning models (CatBoost, LGB, RF under four resampling strategies plus original data) that early predict colistin-induced AKI in MDRGN-infected patients, and to interpret the best model with SHAP
Num_Models_Compared: 15 (three algorithms x four resampling strategies plus the original dataset)
Feature_Engineering: New features engineered: creatinine clearance by the Cockcroft-Gault equation and eGFR by the MDRD formula; features with >25% missing rate discarded; remaining missing values imputed by MICE
Feature_Selection_Method: Recursive feature elimination (RFE) with 5-fold cross-validation of the training set
Num_Features_Total: 77 candidate features
Class_Imbalance_Method: SMOTE, SVM-SMOTE, Tomek links and SMOTETL (SMOTE + Tomek link); the best model used SVM-SMOTE
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over 36 (CatBoost), 5940 (LGB) and 3520 (RF) combinations, combined with resampling in a pipeline to maximise the F1 score
Software_Libraries: matplotlib.pyplot (AUROC and AUPRC curves); CatBoost, LightGBM and random forest implementations (library names not stated)
Other_Metrics: AUPRC 0.737; MCC 0.533; hazard ratio for high- vs low-risk AKI group 24.79 (95% CI 14.32-42.92, P<0.005); multivariate logistic regression odds ratios (CBA dose/kg 2.113, CKD 1.614, longer course 0.733, other pathogens 0.583)
Baseline_Method: Models built on the original data without resampling (and Tomek under-sampling), compared against SMOTE/SVM-SMOTE/SMOTETL models; multivariate logistic regression as a traditional comparator
Baseline_Performance: Models without resampling had lower sensitivity, F1 and MCC than the resampling models; multivariate logistic regression: CBA dose per kg/day OR 2.113, CKD OR 1.614, longer course length OR 0.733, other pathogens OR 0.583
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation of the training set used for recursive feature elimination and grid-search hyperparameter tuning
Train_Test_Split: Derivation cohort 2011-2017 (training) vs temporal validation cohort 2018-2020, with a standard 7:3 proportion for data splitting
External_Validation_Description: Temporal validation cohort of 402 patients treated in 2018-2020 at the same three hospitals (a separate time period from the 2011-2017 derivation cohort), not a geographically independent dataset
Overfitting_Method: No formal overfitting assessment reported (no calibration or learning curves); the authors only note CatBoost's ordered boosting has a lower rate of overfitting
Clinical_Insights: A cutoff colistin dose of 4.0 mg/kg body weight/d identifies patients at higher AKI risk; days of colistin use, cumulative dose and daily dose are the most important features; CKD interacts with dose/BUN so vulnerable patients develop AKI even at low doses
Generalisability_Details: Single retrospective health-system dataset; external validation with different ethnic population data and prospective online studies are required to strengthen generality and real-world applicability
Maturity_Evidence: Models were developed on the 2011-2017 derivation cohort with 5-fold cross-validation and then compared in an independent temporal validation cohort (2018-2020), where CAT-SVM-SMOTE reached AUROC 0.823; no prospective evaluation or deployment is reported
Integration_Point: Not described - no clinical system integration is reported; the model is proposed only as a preliminary evaluation tool for clinicians
End_User_Described: Physicians / clinicians treating patients on colistin
Barriers_List: Retrospective design; results need multiple healthcare datasets; absence of newer AKI biomarkers; discarding features with >25% missing data; covariate shift between the two cohorts; no external validation in different ethnic populations or prospectively
Facilitators_List: Explainable ML (SHAP) gives individualised, patient-specific information to support dose adjustment, kidney function monitoring and identification of concurrent nephrotoxins
Future_Directions: Validation with different ethnic population data and prospective studies; determining whether modifying dose adjustment for renal impairment and the upper limit of colistin dose per weight could reduce AKI risk
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP values (mean absolute SHAP importance), with summary, force, dependency and decision plots
Novel_Predictors_Details: The interaction of colistin dose with CKD and BUN, and a cutoff of 4.0 mg/kg body weight/d for higher AKI risk - including vulnerable patients who developed AKI at very low doses (0.71 +/- 0.30 mg/kg/d)

Dataset_Size: 345,748 bacterial specimens; 10,227 S. aureus isolates (5,872 MRSA, 4,355 MSSA); 2,848 SCCmec type IV isolates used for PVL prediction

Facilitators_List: Analysis of MALDI-TOF MS spectra already generated for species identification (no extra test); automated hierarchical workflow replacing PCR; web interface with per-step confidence; webinars, training and feedback collection for adoption.
Future_Directions: Proteomic experiments to link discriminative m/z features to proteins and to integrate additional biomarkers; further clinical validation of the impact on mortality.

Pathogens: Enterococcus (ERV) is the target pathogen; Enterobacterales CRE, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, SARM and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia appear as prior-colonisation covariate organisms
Num_Pathogens: 1 target pathogen (Enterococcus, ERV); 5 further organisms appear only as prior-colonisation covariates (Enterobacterales CRE, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, SARM, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia)
Drug_Classes: Glycopeptides (Vancomycin, the target drug); prior-exposure variables for third generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, B lactams and antifungal agents
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin (VANCOMYCIN, target drug of the MICROBIOLOGYEVENTS table); previous exposure to third generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluorquinolones, aminoglycosides, b_lactam and antifungal agents
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; VRE
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary susceptibility label: 'Susceptibility: sensitive or resistant' (attribute culture_susceptibility) for the VANCOMYCIN antibiotic, with the target phenomenon being an Enterococcus strain resistant to vancomycin (ERV)
AI_Purpose: Mine diverse top-k antibiotic-resistance phenotypes (subgroup lists) from a real MIMIC-III use case, to give clinical experts multiple and diverse explanations of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus patterns and support decision-making
Num_Models_Compared: 2 phenotyping algorithms compared (EDSLM vs SSD++); Random Forest and Logistic Regression were additionally fitted (with and without phenotype attributes) for the statistical validation
Feature_Engineering: Two-stage pipeline: SQL query on MIMIC-III (PostgreSQL) creating previous-admission binary features, then preprocessing with (1) deletion of duplicated instances and attributes, (2) removal of empty or single-valued attributes, (3) treatment of missing values, (4) attribute discretization and (5) correlation analysis (Pearson coefficient, threshold 0.8)
Feature_Selection_Method: No explicit feature-selection step: all 32 mining-view attributes are used; a Pearson correlation analysis with a threshold of 0.8 is applied during preprocessing, and the overlap strategy places correlated attributes in different subgroup lists
Num_Features_Total: 44 attributes in the initial query dataset; 32 attributes in the final mining view
Num_Features_Selected: 32 attributes (all mining-view attributes); subgroups are limited to a maximum depth of 4 selectors
Class_Imbalance_Method: Subsampling of negative instances: from 8918 negatives to 1872 negatives to match the 1872 positive instances, giving a balanced mining view of 3744 instances
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid over 9 values of beta (0.0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.65, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0) and 8 values of max_positive_overlap / max_negative_overlap (0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.5, 0.6), with k = 3 and sl_max_size = 10 fixed, giving 576 executions; model selection by quality (Eq. 4) and coverage (Eq. 5)
Software_Libraries: pandas 2.0.3, scikit-learn 1.3.0, matplotlib 3.7.2, numpy 1.24.3 (pipeline); pingouin 0.5.5 (McNemar's test); subgroups Python library (EDSLM implementation); RuleList library (SSD++)
Other_Metrics: Quality of the phenotypes (Eq. 3 and Eq. 4, based on the WRAcc quality measure of the subgroups) and coverage (Eq. 5) are the measures computed for every execution; overlap between phenotypes (Table 8) and McNemar's test p-values (Table 7) are additionally reported
Baseline_Method: SSD++ algorithm (RuleList library) applied to the same dataset as an alternative phenotyping approach; Random Forest and Logistic Regression fitted without the phenotype attributes (model 1) as the baseline against which model 2 (with phenotype attributes) is compared
Baseline_Performance: SSD++ phenotype: quality 0.061, covering 1030 of 1872 positive (55%), 1019 of 1872 negative (54%) and 2049 of the total instances (55%); Random Forest model 1 accuracy 0.73; Logistic Regression model 1 accuracy 0.66
Internal_Validation: 70% of the mining-view instances for training and 30% for testing, with McNemar's test (pingouin 0.5.5) comparing classification models with and without phenotype attributes (Table 7)
Clinical_Insights: The ERV phenotypes are dominated by general subgroups: patients with ERV in 'SWAB' cultures from surgical ICUs and in urine cultures with previous vancomycin exposure; a more specific subgroup has previous ERV colonisation and organ transplantation; further subgroups describe patients who are adults, largely women, and who do not die
Data_Repository: GitHub (query of stage 1 and source code of stage 2): https://github.com/antoniolopezmc/Discovering-multiple-antibiotic-resistance-phenotypes-using-diverse-top-k-subgroup-list-discovery; source data: MIMIC-III database
Generalisability_Details: The authors note that MIMIC-III data for clinical problems are solely focused on ICUs, temporally displaced (admissions 2001–2012) and not all relevant data are available in tabular format, while the extracted phenotypes remain interpretable
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: 70/30 train-test split of the balanced mining view with McNemar's test on predictive capacity; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment
Integration_Point: Not reported — the algorithm is delivered as the open-source subgroups Python library; no clinical system integration point is described
End_User_Described: Clinical experts / clinicians interpreting the phenotypes (and researchers using the subgroups library)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Phenotypes could be mined in different scenarios for decision-making, e.g. using patient data at hospital admission to carry out colonisation studies, or using microbiological diagnostic data to predict the growth of multiresistant bacteria
Barriers_List: Performance (the algorithm must repeatedly explore the collection of candidate subgroups) and the fact that it only accepts nominal attributes; also limited availability of MIMIC-III data (ICU-focused, temporally displaced, not all relevant data in tabular format)
Facilitators_List: Multiple and diverse explanations of the same dataset; an overlapping strategy improving diversity in terms of coverage; a deletion refinement strategy improving diversity in terms of descriptions; only subgroups covering at least one positive instance are added; the candidate subgroup collection can be filtered a-priori, improving legibility of results
Future_Directions: Apply the proposal to other clinical problems and datasets (e.g. drug repurposing); design algorithms that mine diverse top-k subgroup lists without previously generating candidate subgroups; explore other measures to assess diverse top-k phenotypes; adapt the approach to other subgroup models (subgroup sets, truly unordered rule sets); add support for numerical attributes; extend to a multiclass setting
Predictor_Categories_Count: 7 (clinical; microbiological; pharmacological; healthcare utilisation; laboratory; sociodemographic; temporal)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Minimum Description Length compression gain (Eq. 1) combined with the positive/negative overlap factor (Eq. 2) decides which subgroup is added to a phenotype; the WRAcc quality measure is used by VLSD when mining the candidate subgroups
Feature_Interactions_Method: Subgroups are conjunctive patterns: a pattern is a set of selectors forming a conjunction of conditions (up to a maximum depth of 4 selectors); phenotypes chain subgroups as else-if rules
Limitation_Categories: Performance / scalability (repeated exploration of the candidate subgroup collection); attribute type (only nominal attributes accepted); data limitations of MIMIC-III (ICU-only, temporally displaced, not all relevant data in tabular format)
Data_Quality_Concerns: MIMIC-III data for clinical problems are solely focused on ICUs, are temporally displaced and not all relevant data are available in tabular format; duplicates handled per CLSI M39-A4 and missing values treated during preprocessing
Reporting_Clarity: Clear reporting of dataset sizes, preprocessing steps, hyperparameter grid, quality/coverage values and statistical tests; the imputation method behind 'treatment of missing values' is not specified

Title: Machine learning-based evaluation of risk factors for carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae dissemination in neonatal units
Journal_Source: mSystems (American Society for Microbiology), vol. 10, issue 10, October 2025
Funder_Names: National Natural Science Foundation of China (32170003, 32370099, 82202465); Research project of Pudong New Area Health Commission (PW2023D-03); Natural Science Foundation of Jiangsu Province (BK20211311); Suzhou Science and Technology Innovations Project in Health Care (SKY2021013); Suzhou Top-Notch Talent Groups (ZXD2022003); National Health Commission (ECCUAEAR-2024-10)
Population_Description: 58 neonates admitted to a paediatric teaching hospital (Shanghai Children's Medical Center, 56.9% NICU, 12.1% CICU, 31.0% neonatal unit) with carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates; 53.4% premature; median age 4.11 days; 25.9% congenital heart disease, 19% necrotizing enterocolitis
Top_Predictive_Features: Random-forest permutation importance (regression): carbapenemase-carrying plasmids 0.233 ± 0.006; bacterial genotypes 0.212 ± 0.005; carbapenemase genes 0.127 ± 0.006; healthcare groups (HGs) 0.114 ± 0.006; hospital wards 0.112 ± 0.008. Classification model: 21 accessory genes with ≥0.01 impact (incl. gtfA and apxIB, pentose transport/metabolism cluster, chaperone-usher fimbriae cluster)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Infection prevention and control team; Surveillance analyst / public health
All_Models_Evaluated: RandomForestRegressor (random forest regression on pairwise isolate time intervals; 100 trees, max depth 12; mean squared error 0.86 with fivefold cross-validation); RandomForestClassifier (outbreak-associated genotype ST433/ST14-C1/ST14-C2 from accessory genes; accuracy 100%)
Best_Performing_Model: RandomForestClassifier model (100% accuracy predicting outbreak-associated genotypes); the RandomForestRegressor reached a mean squared error of 0.86
Accuracy_Population_Set: Outbreak-associated genotype classification (ST433, ST14-C1, ST14-C2) of the 64 CRKP isolates, using 7,371 accessory genes
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Random forest models developed and evaluated with fivefold cross-validation and grid-search hyperparameter tuning; no external or prospective validation and no deployment
Reported_Limitations: CRKP isolates from neonates only; single paediatric hospital; NICU environment and carbapenem-susceptible isolates could not be sampled retrospectively; relatively small number of isolates affecting robustness/generalisability; findings viewed as preliminary
Ethical_Governance_Risks: None reported; study approved by the hospital IRB with informed consent waived because it focused on bacteria and not patients
Reviewer_Notes: Unit of analysis: the models developed here (RandomForestRegressor for isolate time intervals, MSE 0.86; RandomForestClassifier for outbreak-associated genotypes, accuracy 100%). Judgement calls: Selection_Bias_Discussed coded Yes (the authors discuss their inability to sample NICU environments/reservoirs); Data_Source coded Hospital / clinic registry for the retrospective clinical records plus sequenced isolates; Prediction metrics other than MSE/accuracy are not reported.
Sample_Size: 64 CRKP isolates from 58 neonates (65 isolates from 59 neonates collected, one excluded)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Infants aged ≤28 days; infection symptoms and positive culture for K. pneumoniae in clinical samples; complete clinical records; K. pneumoniae isolates resistant to one or more carbapenems; only one isolate kept per sample
Exclusion_Criteria: One isolate (HB021691) and one further CRKP isolate were excluded for discrepancies between Illumina and Nanopore sequencing results (suspected sample contamination / inconsistency), leaving 64 isolates from 58 neonates
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Shanghai Children's Medical Center (SCMC) CRKP isolate collection; EnteroBase; GenBank; Genome Sequence Archive (PRJCA012323, CRA008499, CRA016970)
Dataset_Size: 2,080 pairwise comparisons among 64 CRKP isolates; pan-genome of 11,226 genes (7,371 accessory genes used by the classifier)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single paediatric teaching hospital in Shanghai, China; not geographically representative (authors call for multi-centre studies)
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood (37.5%), sputum (31.3%), and urine (10.9%)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) persistence and dissemination/outbreaks in neonatal units: clonal spread, healthcare-group transmission and plasmid-mediated persistence
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (carbapenem-resistant CRKP; 21 sequence types including ST14, ST433 and ST11, with clones ST14-C1 and ST14-C2)
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems
Specific_Antibiotics: imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Carbapenem resistance defined as K. pneumoniae with an inhibition zone diameter not exceeding 19 mm (disk diffusion); carbapenemase genes blaNDM-1, blaIMP-4, blaKPC-2 etc. were used as features
AI_Purpose: Use two random forest models to identify and rank the risk factors driving CRKP persistence and dissemination in neonatal units (regression on pairwise isolate isolation-time intervals; classification of outbreak-associated genotypes from accessory genes)
Feature_Engineering: Model inputs: bacterial genotypes (STs and sub-ST clones), plasmid content, carbapenemase genes/ARGs, healthcare groups and hospital wards; target: time differences between isolates (regression) and outbreak-associated genotype (classification) from an accessory-gene presence/absence matrix
Feature_Selection_Method: Not reported (all 7,371 accessory genes used as classifier features); permutation importance used to rank/interpret features
Num_Features_Total: 11,226 pan-genome genes; 7,371 accessory genes used as classifier features
Num_Features_Selected: 21 genes with at least a 0.01 impact score
Hyperparameter_Method: GridSearchCV over n_estimators, max_features and max_depth with fivefold cross-validation; final model 100 trees and maximum depth 12
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn (RandomForestRegressor, RandomForestClassifier, GridSearchCV, permutation_importance)
Other_Metrics: Mean squared error (MSE) 0.86 (fivefold cross-validation); model explained 86% of the variance in isolation times; permutation importance values; significance expressed in sigma (1,000 permutations, P < 0.01 after Bonferroni adjustment)
Internal_Validation: Fivefold cross-validation (with grid-search hyperparameter tuning)
Train_Test_Split: A data split was used but proportions are not reported; cross-validation used to ensure robustness
Overfitting_Method: Fivefold cross-validation and grid-search hyperparameter tuning to reduce overfitting and improve model stability
Clinical_Insights: Accessory genes enriched in outbreak-associated isolates (gtfA/apxIB surface polysaccharide synthesis and RTX toxin secretion; pentose transport and metabolism; chaperone-usher fimbriae) are proposed to enhance adhesion, biofilm formation, nutrient-limited survival and immune evasion, supporting plasmid surveillance as an early warning system
Data_Repository: Genome Sequence Archive (GSA) in National Genomics Data Center, China National Center for Bioinformatics/Beijing Institute of Genomics (PRJCA012323; CRA008499, CRA016970); EnteroBase; GenBank
Generalisability_Details: Authors note the surprisingly small number of isolates impairs robustness and generalisability of the machine-learning analysis and call for larger, more diverse data sets and multi-centre studies
Maturity_Evidence: Fivefold cross-validation and grid-search hyperparameter tuning of both random forest models; no external validation, prospective evaluation or integration into a decision-support system is reported
Barriers_List: Lack of long-term surveillance hindering evaluation of introduction/spread in ICUs; single neonatal population; no retrospective sampling of NICU environments or susceptible isolates; small isolate number limiting robustness of the machine-learning analysis
Future_Directions: Multi-centre studies combining environmental surveillance and genomic data; larger and more diverse data sets to validate and strengthen conclusions; surveillance of pre-outbreak plasmids in neonatal and NICU units as an early warning system
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Permutation importance (permutation_importance function); error bars indicate standard variations in permutations
Novel_Predictors_Details: Carbapenemase-carrying plasmids are highlighted as the previously overlooked most significant factor for long-term persistence (Importance 0.233 ± 0.006), and 21 accessory genes (gtfA, apxIB, pentose metabolism, chaperone-usher fimbriae) classify outbreak genotypes
Limitation_Categories: Population/setting: neonates only, single paediatric hospital; sampling: no environmental or carbapenem-susceptible isolates sampled retrospectively; statistical: small number of isolates, machine-learning findings preliminary and requiring larger, more diverse data sets
Data_Quality_Concerns: One isolate excluded because Illumina and Nanopore results disagreed (suspected sample contamination) and one further isolate excluded for the same reason; no isolates excluded for poor sequencing quality
Reporting_Clarity: Models, hyperparameters and validation are described explicitly, but metric reporting is limited to mean squared error and accuracy
Page_References: PDF pages 1-18 (mSystems vol. 10, issue 10, article e00909-25); methods pp. 2-4; results pp. 4-12; discussion pp. 13-15

Title: Integrating Machine Learning with MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry for Rapid and Accurate Antimicrobial Resistance Detection in Clinical Pathogens

Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: ANID Chile, FONDECYT Iniciación en Investigación No. 11220897
Population_Description: 2229 MALDI-TOF mass spectra of clinical bacterial and fungal isolates, focusing on S. aureus (n=377), E. coli (n=256), K. pneumoniae (n=187) from the Regional Hospital of Talca, Chile.
Top_Predictive_Features: S. aureus-oxacillin: ions 3890, 5670, 2450 Da; E. coli-ciprofloxacin: ion 5890 Da (resistant), peaks 5230, 3850, 9225 (susceptible); K. pneumoniae-ciprofloxacin: absence of m/z 6590. Method: SHAP (TreeExplainer).

All_Models_Evaluated: SVM, RF, LR, CatBoost, TL evaluated by 10-fold CV; best CatBoost (S. aureus-oxacillin AUROC 0.86/F1 0.61; E. coli-cipro AUROC 0.91/F1 0.78; K. pneumoniae-cipro AUROC 0.73/F1 0.78).
Best_Performing_Model: CatBoost (AUROC 0.91 for E. coli-ciprofloxacin)
AUROC_Population_Set: E. coli ciproﬂoxacin (10-fold CV)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation on a single hospital dataset (Regional Hospital of Talca); no external or prospective validation.

Sample_Size: 2229 mass spectra
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conﬂicts of interest.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: Regional Hospital of Talca; VITEK MS (BioMérieux)
Dataset_Size: 2229 mass spectra
Geographic_Representativeness: Single site — Regional Hospital of Talca, Chile; authors note need for validation across diverse clinical and geographical contexts.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistance classification: oxacillin resistance in S. aureus; ciprofloxacin resistance in E. coli and K. pneumoniae.

Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Resistance phenotype determined by disk diffusion AST (Kirby-Bauer) per CLSI M100; binary resistant/susceptible label.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)

Num_Models_Compared: 5 (SVM, RF, LR, CatBoost, transfer learning)
Feature_Engineering: Spectral pre-processing: normalization, peak selection 2000-10000 Da, binning with 5 Da bin size to fixed-length vectors; RFECV for dimensionality reduction.
Feature_Selection_Method: Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation (RFECV)
Class_Imbalance_Method: AUPRC as optimization metric for imbalanced data; decision threshold calibration; SMOTE evaluated separately

Software_Libraries: scikit-learn; Skopt
Other_Metrics: Balanced accuracy (E. coli CatBoost 0.81); AUPRC (E. coli CatBoost 0.91)

Baseline_Performance: RF second-best: AUROC 0.86, AUPRC 0.68, balanced accuracy 0.74, F1 0.56 (S. aureus-oxacillin)
Internal_Validation: 10-fold stratiﬁed cross-validation
Overfitting_Method: 10-fold cross-validation
Clinical_Insights: SHAP identified resistance-associated spectral biomarkers (e.g. ion 3890 Da linked to SCCmec type II in S. aureus; ST131-associated peaks in E. coli), supporting early diagnosis.

Title: Clinical scoring model for predicting cefotaxime-resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia: development and validation based on portal of entry
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Population_Description: Adult patients (aged ≥18 years) with K. pneumoniae bacteraemia: 358 patients enrolled, 256 in the derivation cohort (March 2018-December 2019) and 102 in the temporal validation cohort (January-August 2020).
Age_Mean_Median: Mean 70.85 ± 11.55 years (all patients, Table 1); median updated CCI 2 (0-4)
Age_Range: Adults aged ≥18 years (lower limit only; no upper limit reported)
Top_Predictive_Features: Age ≥65 years; hospital-acquired infection; previous antimicrobial use within 90d; updated CCI ≥3 points (1 point each, ranked by multivariable adjusted odds ratio)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Single model evaluated: four-component clinical scoring model from forward stepwise binary logistic regression. Derivation cohort AUC 0.761 (95% CI 0.690-0.832), sensitivity 73.6%, specificity 67.5%, PPV 37.1%, NPV 90.7% at cut-off ≥2; temporal validation cohort AUC 0.781 (95% CI 0.690-0.902), sensitivity 75.0%, specificity 69.5%, PPV 37.5%, NPV 91.9% at cut-off ≥2. No comparator model evaluated.
Best_Performing_Model: Four-component clinical scoring model (points-based score derived from the logistic regression model) - the only model under study
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Derivation cohort (primary dataset), cut-off score ≥2
Specificity_Population_Set: Derivation cohort (primary dataset), cut-off score ≥2
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Derivation cohort (primary dataset), cut-off score ≥2
AUROC_Population_Set: Derivation cohort (primary dataset)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Temporal validation only, performed in the same single centre as the derivation cohort; the authors state that more extensive external validation is still needed.
Reported_Limitations: Single-centre derivation with same-centre validation (generalisability and regional cut-off differences; external validation needed); model can only be applied after bacterial identification, so the time to adjust antimicrobials may be little shortened; the study shows diagnostic value only and does not demonstrate reduced mortality.
Sample_Size: 256 patients in the derivation cohort (primary dataset); 102 patients in the temporal validation cohort
Conflicts_of_Interest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).
Sex_Distribution: Male 161 (62.9%) of 256 in the derivation cohort (Table 1)
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients (aged ≥18 years) with K. pneumoniae bacteraemia (derivation and validation cohorts)
Exclusion_Criteria: Polymicrobial bacteraemia; carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae bacteraemia (derivation cohort)
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 358 patients in total (256 derivation cohort, 102 validation cohort)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single tertiary-care hospital in Changwon, Republic of Korea (760 beds); the authors note that prevalence of resistance varies by centre and region, so the optimal cut-off may differ elsewhere.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood cultures: two sets (aerobic and anaerobic) drawn via a peripheral vein or central venous catheter
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Cefotaxime resistance (binary susceptible/resistant) in patients with Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteraemia
Drug_Classes: Third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime); extended-spectrum beta-lactamase / AmpC-mediated resistance; carbapenems discussed as the broad-spectrum alternative
Specific_Antibiotics: Cefotaxime
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Antimicrobial susceptibility (including cefotaxime) determined by the Vitek II automated system and defined by the CLSI M100S16:2018 guidelines
AI_Purpose: To evaluate clinical factors associated with cefotaxime resistance in K. pneumoniae bacteraemia, to model a simple clinical scoring system predicting cefotaxime resistance, and to analyse resistance rates by portal of entry and validate the score.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single scoring model; no comparator model evaluated)
Feature_Engineering: Continuous clinical variables converted to binary variables using the Youden index (age at 65 years, updated CCI at 3 points) before multivariable analysis; each retained factor given one point to build a zero-to-four-point score.
Feature_Selection_Method: Univariable screening at p<.15 plus clinically meaningful variables, then forward stepwise binary logistic regression (variables with zero frequency excluded)
Software_Libraries: SPSS version 25.0 for Windows; R software version 4.2.1
Other_Metrics: Positive likelihood ratio 2.26 (95% CI 1.75-2.92) and negative likelihood ratio 0.39 (95% CI 0.25-0.62) at cut-off ≥2; weighted accuracy analysis comparing cut-off scores 2 and 1 across resistance prevalences.
Internal_Validation: Temporal split: separate validation cohort collected January-August 2020 at the same centre (n=102)
Train_Test_Split: Derivation cohort March 2018-December 2019 (n=256) versus temporal validation cohort January-August 2020 (n=102)
Clinical_Insights: In this centre 45 of 138 (32.6%) derivation-cohort patients with cefotaxime-susceptible K. pneumoniae bacteraemia and a model score ≤1 had nevertheless received anti-pseudomonas penicillin, a fourth-generation cephalosporin or a carbapenem - suggesting the score could reduce unnecessarily broad empirical therapy.
Generalisability_Details: Single centre in the Republic of Korea; resistance prevalence differs by centre and region so the optimal cut-off may change, and more extensive external validation in larger multicentre studies is needed.
Maturity_Evidence: Temporal validation in a separate later cohort at the same centre gave AUC 0.781 (95% CI 0.690-0.902); no external validation and no prospective evaluation were performed.
Integration_Point: After bacterial identification (e.g. by MALDI-TOF MS) and before antimicrobial susceptibility results are available, to inform empirical antimicrobial choice
End_User_Described: Clinicians choosing empirical antimicrobial therapy; antimicrobial stewardship programmes
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The score applies only after the species has been identified (e.g. by MALDI-TOF MS), so any reduction in the time to adjust antimicrobials may be limited; it is intended to support empirical prescribing before susceptibility results return.
Stewardship_Details: 45 of 138 (32.6%) patients predicted susceptible (score ≤1) received anti-pseudomonas penicillin, fourth-generation cephalosporin or carbapenem, suggesting about one-third could receive narrower empirical therapy.
Barriers_List: The score can only be applied after bacterial identification, limiting the time saving; single-centre derivation and same-centre validation limit generalisability; prevalence-dependent cut-off values.
Facilitators_List: Simplicity: four routinely available clinical variables, one point each, easy to apply at the bedside.
Future_Directions: More extensive external validation and larger multicentre studies; prospective evaluation of whether applying the model reduces mortality; adapting cut-off values to local resistance prevalence.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 (clinical, sociodemographic, pharmacological/antimicrobial exposure, healthcare utilisation, behavioural)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Adjusted odds ratios from forward stepwise binary logistic regression; the four retained factors had similar adjusted ORs (2.67 to 3.62) and were therefore weighted equally at one point each.
Limitation_Categories: Single-centre derivation and same-centre validation; limited generalisability / need for external validation and multicentre studies; only applicable after species identification, limiting time savings; diagnostic value only, no demonstrated mortality reduction.
Page_References: Article pp. 112-120 (Journal of Chemotherapy 37:2); model development and diagnostic performance pp. 113-114; Table 1 p. 115; Table 3 p. 117; limitations p. 118

Title: Artificial intelligence for screening drug resistance in tuberculosis

Specificity_Population_Set: All FL- and SL-LPA strips across validation

Title: Predicting resistance as indicator for need to switch from first-line antiretroviral therapy among patients with elevated viral loads: development of a risk score algorithm
Country_Countries: Multi-country: nine countries enrolled in the PEARLS trial (A5175); author affiliations include the United States of America (North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts), Malawi, South Africa, India and Brazil
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Randomised controlled trial
Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (UM1 AI068634, UM1 AI068636, UM1 AI106701); Boehringer Ingelheim Pharmaceuticals Inc., Bristol-Myers Squibb, Gilead Sciences and Viiv Healthcare/GlaxoSmithKline (study drug; Gilead also funded purchase of study drug); SER supported by F30 MH098731 and T32 GM008719
Population_Description: 290 participants of the PEARLS (ACTG A5175) Phase IV open-label randomised trial who had at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml after week 16 while on an NNRTI-based first-line regimen (from 1045 analysed participants, 305 with an elevated VL and 15 excluded for unavailable resistance results); 53 % male, age 19-65 years
Top_Predictive_Features: Ranked by weighted predictor score (2 x beta coefficient, rounded) in the best model, Model 1: VL at time of first VL >=1000 copies/ml of 10,001-100,000 (score 4) > time on therapy <7 months (3) > BMI >25.0 kg/m2, treatment initiation VL >100,000 copies/ml and VL >100,000 copies/ml (2 each) > age <=30 (1). Model 2 additionally retains screening CD4 <100 cells/mm3 (score 2) and Model 3 retains ever missed medications (score 1)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Three multiple logistic regression risk-score models (full and reduced): Model 1 (treatment initiation VL and CD4 eligible) reduced AUROC 0.8165, full 0.842; Model 2 (initiation VL excluded) reduced AUROC 0.7981, full 0.819; Model 3 (initiation VL and CD4 excluded, n = 260) reduced AUROC 0.7937, full 0.801. Risk-score (weighted) versions: Model 1 AUROC 0.813 (p = 0.69), Model 2 0.797 (p = 0.91), Model 3 0.802 (p = 0.57). Sensitivity analyses in resource-limited-settings-only population: AUROC 0.823 (Model 1), 0.812 (Model 2), 0.804 (Model 3); Models 4-9 re-categorised therapy duration, compared by AIC
Best_Performing_Model: Reduced Model 1 (multiple logistic regression including treatment initiation VL and CD4; AUROC 0.8165)
Sensitivity_Value: 28.0 % (weighted risk score cutoff >=9, Model 1, unrestricted population)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Weighted risk score cutoff >=9, unrestricted population (resource-limited settings and non-resource-limited settings), Model 1, n = 290
Specificity_Value: 96.7 % (weighted risk score cutoff >=9, Model 1, unrestricted population)
Specificity_Population_Set: Weighted risk score cutoff >=9, unrestricted population (resource-limited settings and non-resource-limited settings), Model 1, n = 290
AUROC_Population_Set: Primary analysis, all study sites, n = 290 (reduced Model 1 on treatment initiation VL and CD4)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model developed and internally validated only (1000 bootstrap samples with replacement) on the trial dataset; performance assessed for Models 1-3 at risk-score cutoffs, with a sensitivity analysis restricted to resource-limited settings; no external or prospective validation performed - the authors state that these benefits must still be externally validated prospectively
Reported_Limitations: Controlled-trial population may not be representative of larger ART populations; frequent virological monitoring (every 8 weeks) unlikely in the intended settings; >12 months used as the referent therapy-duration category; all participants on efavirenz-based first-line regimens, so resistance patterns and predictors may not apply to other regimens; changing WHO CD4 eligibility guidelines; lower resistance prevalence than other sub-Saharan African cohorts; possible misclassification of resistance at low-level viraemia
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Premature switching to second-line therapy (false positives) occurs even at specificities >98 % and has significant person- and system-wide consequences: for patients, lost potential life years from remaining on first-line therapy; for the health system, drug costs 6-10 times those of first-line therapy. Conversely, missing resistant patients risks accumulation and transmission of resistant viral strains
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Trade-offs may vary by population: providers may be more willing to risk false positives in HIV-infected pregnant women because viral suppression at delivery prevents vertical transmission; acceptable true positive:false positive ratios may also differ with anticipated time-to-referral
Reviewer_Notes: Antiretroviral (HIV) drug resistance rather than bacterial AMR; the record codes it with the closest available vocabulary and flags the mapping choices in _notes. Model performance figures were read from the narrative text and Tables 2-3, which the text layer reproduces; the Additional file 1 supplementary tables (S1-S3) are not in the text layer
Unresolved_Items: Whether Provider_Facing_Applications should include 'Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)' when the model predicts resistance from clinical and demographic variables rather than from genotype or spectra; whether a modelled switching estimate in a hypothetical 10,000-patient cohort counts as stewardship impact; whether the paper's population estimates are healthcare costs 'reported'
Sample_Size: 290 participants with at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml (final sample of the primary analysis); Model 3 used n = 260
Conflicts_of_Interest: The author(s) declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Post-hoc analysis of de-identified PEARLS (A5175) data restricted to participants initiated on NNRTI-based regimens (lamivudine/zidovudine/efavirenz or emtricitabine/tenofovir/efavirenz) with at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml at any point after week 16 of enrolment
Exclusion_Criteria: Excluded from PEARLS: CD4 count >300 cells/mm3, previous ART exposure (except women given ART for prevention of mother-to-child transmission), pregnancy, acute illness or clinical instability. In this analysis, participants with two sequential visits with VL >=1000 copies/ml but no resistance test, and those without available resistance results at the time of confirmed elevated VL (n = 15), were excluded
Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: PEARLS trial (Prospective Evaluation of Antiretrovirals in Resource-Limited Settings), Adult AIDS Clinical Trials Group A5175, NCT00084136
Dataset_Size: 1045 participants analysed; 305 with at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml after week 16; 15 excluded for unavailable resistance results; final sample 290
Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case/data-availability exclusion: participants with two sequential elevated VLs but no resistance test were excluded (15 participants dropped for unavailable resistance results); resistance testing was not done for participants who resuppressed and these were classified as not needing ART change; no imputation reported
Geographic_Representativeness: Participants from all PEARLS study sites with a sensitivity analysis restricted to those enrolled from resource-limited settings; the authors caution that trial participants may not be representative of larger ART populations
Specimen_Type_Detail: Plasma HIV-1 RNA (Roche Amplicor Monitor assay [v1.5]) every eight weeks; stored specimens genotyped retrospectively for resistance
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Need for ART change (i.e. antiretroviral resistance) among participants with the first VL >=1000 copies/ml, from an algorithm combining resuppression and genotypic resistance: resuppression - no ART change needed; no resuppression and no resistance - no ART change needed; no resuppression and resistance - ART change needed
Drug_Classes: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTI); protease inhibitors excluded (PI class reserved for second-line therapy)
Specific_Antibiotics: Lamivudine/zidovudine/efavirenz or emtricitabine/tenofovir/efavirenz (first-line NNRTI-based regimens; also abbreviated 3TC/ZDV BID + EFV QHS and FTC/TDF/EFV QHS)
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Participants with NRTI or NNRTI resistance mutations, defined by 2014 International AIDS Society guidelines (excluding mutation 101P), were classified as resistant; resistance to protease inhibitors was not included; baseline and acquired resistance were not distinguished
AI_Purpose: Develop a risk score algorithm that predicts the need for ART change (resistance) among people with a single elevated viral load, so that providers in resource-limited settings can switch patients to second-line therapy without confirmatory VL testing
Feature_Engineering: Predictors collapsed into discrete categorical variables for point-of-care use; four categorisations of time on treatment tested and the one with the lowest AIC selected as the reference model; full models included all variables with bivariate p-value <0.5; variables with low frequency, extreme collinearity or insufficient detail for clinical implementation excluded
Feature_Selection_Method: Backward elimination in multiple logistic regression: starting with the largest p-value, variables removed one at a time until <=5 remained regardless of p-value; full models contained all variables with bivariate p <0.5
Num_Features_Total: 10 (full Model 1); 9 (full Model 2); 8 (full Model 3)
Software_Libraries: Stata statistical software, Version 13.0 (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX); no machine-learning libraries named
Other_Metrics: AUROC for the models and for the derived weighted risk scores; sensitivity and specificity at each cutoff; Hosmer-Lemeshow calibration p-values; AIC for therapy-duration categorisation; likelihood-ratio tests between successive models; unadjusted prevalence odds ratios with 95 % CI; number of true and false positives in a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 ART patients at varying resistance prevalence
Baseline_Method: Reduced logistic-regression Models 1-3 compared against each other (Models 2 and 3 exclude treatment-initiation VL and/or CD4 as eligible predictors); AUROC equality tested by chi-squared test; AIC used to choose the therapy-duration categorisation
Baseline_Performance: Reduced Model 2 AUROC 0.7981 and reduced Model 3 AUROC 0.7937 versus reduced Model 1 AUROC 0.8165; differences not statistically significant (p = 0.23 and p = 0.22)
Internal_Validation: 1000 bootstrap samples with replacement, assessed over 1000 replications
Clinical_Insights: In the best model, need for ART change was directly associated with higher treatment-initiation VL and higher VL at the first elevated measure, and inversely with treatment duration; age <30 and BMI >25.0 kg/m2 also predicted need for change; screening CD4 <100 cells/mm3 (Model 2) and ever missed medications (Model 3) were additionally retained
Generalisability_Details: The authors argue PEARLS' broad inclusion criteria improve generalizability, that participants were recruited largely from resource-limited settings and the risk score performed well in that subgroup, but caution that trial participants may not represent larger ART populations and that findings may not apply to non-efavirenz-based regimens
Maturity_Evidence: Development and internal validation with 1000 bootstrap samples on 290 trial participants; performance at risk-score cutoffs >=9 with a high-specificity threshold; sensitivity analysis restricted to resource-limited settings; no external or prospective validation reported
Integration_Point: Point-of-care use in ART clinics in resource-limited settings, based only on predictors available at the clinic, applied at the time of the first VL >=1000 copies/ml to decide immediate switch to second-line therapy instead of confirmatory testing
End_User_Described: Providers (clinicians) in ART clinics in resource-limited settings
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The risk score sits inside the WHO viral-load monitoring strategy: instead of the confirmatory test 3-6 months after an initial VL >1000 copies/ml, patients exceeding the algorithm threshold are switched immediately to second-line therapy; those below the threshold have confirmatory VL testing before any switch decision
Stewardship_Details: No stewardship impact was measured: the paper only models, in a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 ART patients, how many would be switched immediately (Model 1 correctly identifying 700 and misclassifying 248 at ~25 % resistance prevalence; 1540 true positives and 149 false positives at 55 % prevalence)
Barriers_List: False positives cause premature second-line switching with significant person- and system-wide consequences (lost potential life years; drug costs 6-10 times first-line therapy); low sensitivity (~15-30 %) is accepted but means misses rely on confirmatory testing; resistance may be misclassified at low-level viraemia (<1000 copies/ml); frequent 8-weekly monitoring in the trial is unlikely in the intended settings; changing WHO CD4 eligibility could dampen efficiency gains
Facilitators_List: Only readily available, point-of-care predictors used; a limited number of categorical variables (five) to keep the score manageable; high specificity minimises false positives; may avoid confirmatory VL tests and so save laboratory costs and reduce transmission of resistant virus
Future_Directions: Prospective external validation and evaluation of the effect of the risk score on health outcomes and resource utilisation; modelling the consequences of delayed second-line initiation versus premature switching to understand threshold trade-offs; alternative cost-saving monitoring strategies such as pooled specimens and targeted VL testing
Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 categories of potential predictors in the paper's own list (demographics; clinical diagnoses; immunological markers/CD4; self-reported and provider-assessed ART adherence; therapy duration); 7 coded predictor categories ticked above (clinical, microbiological, pharmacological, laboratory, behavioural, sociodemographic, temporal)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Weighted risk score: predictor score = two times the beta coefficient rounded to the nearest integer
Limitation_Categories: Trial population representativeness; frequent monitoring in the trial versus intended settings; referent category of therapy duration; efavirenz-based regimens only; changing WHO CD4 eligibility guidelines; lower resistance prevalence than other cohorts; misclassification of resistance at low-level viraemia
Data_Quality_Concerns: Resistance results unavailable for 15 participants with two sequential elevated VLs (excluded); resistance testing not performed for participants who resuppressed; frequent study-driven monitoring (every 8 weeks) unlikely in the intended settings; adherence self-reported and provider-assessed; resistance may be present at low-level viraemia below the 1000 copies/ml threshold
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: model development, candidate predictors, full and reduced model AUROCs, risk-score weights, sensitivity/specificity at defined cutoffs and calibration tests are all reported; no code or model repository link

Clinical_Insights: Methanobrevibacter smithii, Clostridium leptum and Bacteroides dorei were consistently associated with reduced AR event risk (protective commensals supporting gut microbial resilience); ARG classes for lincosamides, macrolides and streptogramins were negatively associated with AR events
Data_Repository: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (BioProject IDs PRJNA352060, PRJNA526551, PRJNA1124986, PRJNA1129514, PRJNA1128111)

End_User_Described: Clinicians - the authors state the findings offer valuable predictors for clinical decision-making and potential infection risk stratification

CV_Folds: Cross-validation reported by ClinProTools but the number of folds is not stated

Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is rapid, cost-effective and easy to use and is already established in clinical laboratories; it is applied directly to routine protein fingerprints without additional assays
Future_Directions: Larger sample sizes and more advanced machine learning techniques to improve algorithm sensitivity and specificity; broader validation with additional strains; further mass spectrometry and algorithm optimisation

Data_Quality_Concerns: Slime-type colonies gave poor mass spectrometry scores and were associated with misidentification/classification failure; sample preparation method and protein purity/concentration affect direct mass spectrometry accuracy

Title: Screening swabs surpass traditional risk factors as predictors of MRSA bacteremia
Population_Description: 376 adult patients with S. aureus bacteremia, 100 (26.6%) MRSA
Top_Predictive_Features: MRSA screening swab (30-Day and Ever-Positive criteria) ranked highest by random-forest importance
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forests (variable importance by mean increase in accuracy and Gini index); Lasso logistic regression (ORs: 30-Day 10.6 [5.08-19.2], Ever-Positive 8.26 [5.23-15.8])
Best_Performing_Model: Random forests
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Retrospective algorithm development validated only by internal 10-fold cross-validation; not externally or prospectively validated
Reported_Limitations: Small numbers per comorbidity (mitigated with CCI); retrospective and therefore hypothesis-generating; institution screens nares only (loss of sensitivity for other body sites)
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Vancomycin overuse harms cited as the motivation: nephrotoxicity, longer hospitalisation, cost, increased mortality
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethics approval obtained; patient consent waived as retrospective with no intervention; dataset release only on request with REB approval
Sample_Size: 376 patients (100 MRSA)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: All consecutive adult S. aureus bacteremia (April 2010 - April 2015) at McGill University Health Center
Exclusion_Criteria: Only the first positive blood culture per patient included; repeat positive cultures excluded
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 376 patients
Geographic_Representativeness: Single health centre spanning two hospitals in Montréal, Canada
Specimen_Type_Detail: Nares MRSA screening swabs; blood cultures for S. aureus bacteremia
Primary_AMR_Outcome: MRSA vs MSSA bacteremia (methicillin resistance among S. aureus blood isolates)
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (methicillin); glycopeptides (vancomycin) and beta-lactams as therapy discussed
Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin; vancomycin; beta-lactams
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary MRSA vs MSSA classification among S. aureus blood-culture isolates
AI_Purpose: Predict MRSA bacteremia in S. aureus bloodstream infection to guide empiric anti-MRSA (vancomycin) therapy
Feature_Engineering: Input variables: MRSA colonization status (30-Day and Ever-Positive), age, sex, previous admissions, and the Charlson Comorbidity Index
Feature_Selection_Method: Random forests and Lasso with 10-fold cross validation and the 1SE rule
Hyperparameter_Method: 10-fold cross validation with the 1SE rule (Lasso lambda selection)
Software_Libraries: glmnet, randomForest
Other_Metrics: Lasso logistic regression odds ratios; random-forest variable importance (mean increase in accuracy, mean decrease in Gini); PPV and NPV as functions of prevalence
Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross validation (Lasso, 1SE rule)
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: MRSA colonization swab is the only independent predictor of MRSA bacteremia among patient-level factors
Generalisability_Details: Local prevalence of methicillin resistance and nosocomial MRSA outbreak status shape how colonization status factors into the vancomycin decision
Maturity_Evidence: Internal 10-fold cross-validation only; retrospective derivation with no external or prospective validation
Integration_Point: Clinical decision to initiate empiric anti-MRSA (vancomycin) therapy
End_User_Described: Clinicians deciding on empiric vancomycin in patients with S. aureus bacteremia
Clinical_Workflow_Details: MRSA colonization status informs the empiric vancomycin decision for stable patients with S. aureus bacteremia
Future_Directions: Prospective studies to demonstrate reduced vancomycin overuse, increased early targeted beta-lactam therapy, and improved patient outcomes
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest: mean increase in accuracy and mean decrease in Gini
Novel_Predictors_Details: MRSA colonization swab identified as an independent marker of MRSA infection, surpassing traditional risk factors
Limitation_Categories: Small sample per individual comorbidity; retrospective design; nares-only MRSA screening
