Title: Genomic prediction of tuberculosis drug-resistance: benchmarking existing databases and prediction algorithms
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Funder_Names: NUS Graduate School of Integrative Sciences and Engineering
Population_Description: 6746 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates compiled from the PATRIC and ReSeqTB databases and 10 other studies (total 6756 samples across the three databases)
Data_Source_Other: Publicly available genomic databases (PATRIC, ReSeqTB) and literature-based studies (LitRev set)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Four tools benchmarked (TBProfiler, MyKrobe, KVarQ, PhyResSE), each with empirical sensitivity and specificity per anti-TB drug (Table 1). For INH (n=4840): TBProfiler sens 0.92/spec 0.94, MyKrobe 0.91/0.98, KVarQ 0.89/0.98, PhyResSE 0.91/0.97.
Best_Performing_Model: TBProfiler (highest sensitivity across most of the 14 drugs; decided on sensitivity)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: INH (isoniazid), 4840 isolates
Specificity_Population_Set: INH (isoniazid), 4840 isolates
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The four tools were benchmarked/validated on external isolates from three databases (PATRIC, ReSeqTB, LitRev) not used in their training — external validation
Reported_Limitations: Low sensitivity in detecting resistance to ETO, PAS, PTO and PZA; overfitting risk of the recalibrated performance; sample sizes lowest for several drugs; considerable uncertainty in the misclassification-rate estimates
Sample_Size: 6746 isolates (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests
Inclusion_Criteria: LitRev set: (1) isolates from clinical samples; (2) at least 10 samples per study; (3) DST on at least four of the five first-line drugs; (4) at least one drug-resistant TB isolate per study
Exclusion_Criteria: Samples with poor sequencing quality and discordant DST phenotypes were excluded
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: PATRIC; ReSeqTB; LitRev
Dataset_Size: 6756 samples total (PATRIC 5035; ReSeqTB 3568; LitRev 5471)
Missing_Data_Method: Samples with no-call or discordant predictions treated as missing; poor sequencing quality and discordant DST samples excluded
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates from different parts of the world, compiled from the PATRIC, ReSeqTB databases and 10 other studies
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary drug-resistance status (resistant vs susceptible) per anti-TB drug predicted from WGS and compared against conventional DST phenotypes as gold standard
Drug_Classes: First-line agents (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin); second-line injectables (amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin); oral second-line (ethionamide, prothionamide, p-aminosalicylic acid); fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin, amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin, ethionamide, prothionamide, p-aminosalicylic acid, ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible status per drug (Yj=1 resistant, 0 susceptible, NA if no call), compared against reported DST phenotypes
AI_Purpose: To benchmark the sensitivity and specificity of four bioinformatics tools for predicting TB drug resistance from WGS data and to identify probable DST phenotyping errors in public TB databases
Feature_Engineering: No feature engineering by the study; the tools use curated panels of resistance-associated genetic mutations
Feature_Selection_Method: Curated mutation panels associated with drug resistance (per tool)
Software_Libraries: TBProfiler v0.3.2; MyKrobe v0.5.6-0-gbd7923a-dirty; KvarQ v0.12.3a1; PhyResSE (metaphyresse.v7, SNP catalogue version 29)
Hardware_Details: High-performance computing clusters of the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health, National University of Singapore
Other_Metrics: Misclassification rates of DST phenotypes per drug and database; DST credibility scores; rate of non-utilizable data
Train_Test_Split: Samples used in tool training were omitted from evaluation
External_Validation_Description: Isolates from the PATRIC, ReSeqTB and LitRev databases
Overfitting_Method: Recalibrated accuracy treated as upper bound; unadjusted accuracy as lower bound
Generalisability_Details: WGS-based drug-resistance prediction faces infrastructural limitations to adoption in resource-poor settings
Maturity_Evidence: Tools benchmarked on external isolates from three databases (PATRIC, ReSeqTB, LitRev) not used in tool training
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiologists; physicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: WGS-based drug-resistance profiling guiding antibiotic prescription, in place of conventional DST
Barriers_List: Infrastructural limitations to WGS adoption in resource-poor settings; time and biosafety requirements of conventional DST
Facilitators_List: Speed of WGS-based resistance profiling relative to conventional DST
Future_Directions: Clearer understanding of genetic biomarkers of drug resistance and more powerful algorithms to capture resistance intricacies across multiple drugs
Limitation_Categories: Overfitting risk of recalibrated performance; low sensitivity for ETO, PAS, PTO and PZA; small sample sizes for several drugs; uncertainty in estimated misclassification rates; assumption of independent software outputs
Data_Quality_Concerns: Conventional DST phenotypes assumed error-free but containing errors; discordant DST results across databases; samples with poor sequencing quality; samples with no-call or discordant predictions treated as missing

Title: A Decision Tree Using Patient Characteristics to Predict Resistance to Commonly Used Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics in Children With Gram-Negative Bloodstream Infections
Journal_Source: Journal of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (awards T32-A1052071, K23-AI127935, K24AI141580)
Population_Description: Children with gram-negative bloodstream infections cared for at a tertiary care pediatric hospital (Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh); 689 episodes among 387 patients and 638 hospital admissions, June 2009 to June 2015
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Hospital / clinic registry; Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: In order of discriminatory potential: (1) prior carbapenem treatment for >=7 days, (2) prior culture with CPT resistance within 6 months, (3) intestinal transplantation, (4) >=7 prior gram-negative bloodstream infection episodes, (5) age >=3 years; importance determined by recursive partitioning (Gini splitting index)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Decision tree (recursive partitioning, rpart in R): sensitivity 46%, specificity 91%, AUC 0.70 (leave-one-out cross-validated); PPV 69%, NPV 78%. Multivariable logistic regression model (generalized estimating equations): adjusted odds ratios only, eg prior carbapenem within 6 months OR 2.74 (95% CI 1.54-4.88).
Best_Performing_Model: Decision tree (recursive partitioning; rpart in R) - the only predictive model developed and evaluated, with its discrimination (AUC 0.70) and classification metrics reported
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Leave-one-out cross-validated classification of patients as high risk of BSA-resistant infection
Specificity_Population_Set: Leave-one-out cross-validated classification of patients as high risk of BSA-resistant infection
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Whole cohort; prevalence of BSA-resistant bloodstream infection 31%
AUROC_Population_Set: Leave-one-out cross-validated model (pre-cross-validation value 0.68)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation only (leave-one-out cross-validation); the tree was developed and validated on the same data set and the authors state it needs wider validation before clinical practice.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design and no outpatient data, with possible misclassification or missing data; infections may have been missed if cultures were obtained elsewhere; single tertiary pediatric centre; additional risk factors not captured; too few carbapenem-resistant infections to model CPT and carbapenem resistance separately; the same data set was used to develop and validate the tree; limited generalisability to other infection types or colonization.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Misclassification may lead to undertreatment (close to 50% of high-risk BSA-resistant episodes classified as low risk) or overtreatment (9% classified as high risk).
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not discussed; the cohort is described only by race, sex and age.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Institutional Review Board approved the study with a waiver of informed consent; no further ethical or governance risks are discussed.
Sample_Size: 689 episodes of gram-negative bloodstream infection (387 patients; 638 hospital admissions)
Conflicts_of_Interest: P. D. T. received an investigator-initiated research grant from Merck, unrelated to the present work; A. M. M. reports consulting for Becton Dickinson for work unrelated to this project; all other authors report no potential conflicts.
Inclusion_Criteria: All patients admitted to CHP from June 2009 through June 2015 with at least 1 blood culture, from a peripheral or a central catheter source, in which gram-negative bacteria grew.
Exclusion_Criteria: Not admitted to hospital or insufficient antibiotic susceptibility information available; uniformly susceptible respiratory pathogens (eg, Haemophilus influenzae); pathogens primarily associated with gastroenteritis (eg, Salmonella and Shigella species); organisms intrinsically resistant to cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam (eg, Burkholderia cepacia complex and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia).
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: CHP microbiology database; CHP data warehouse
Dataset_Size: 689 episodes of gram-negative bloodstream infection; 387 patients; 638 hospital admissions
Missing_Data_Method: Manual chart review
Geographic_Representativeness: Single tertiary care pediatric hospital serving Western Pennsylvania; the authors note most complex cases in the region are managed at this hospital.
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood culture from a peripheral or a central catheter source
Primary_AMR_Outcome: BSA resistance: bloodstream infection with a gram-negative organism nonsusceptible to cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem or imipenem-cilastatin, or meeting criteria for ESBL production
Pathogens: Klebsiella species, Escherichia species, Enterobacter species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia species, Acinetobacter species, Citrobacter species, Proteus mirabilis, Morganella morganii, Achromobacter species, other gram-negative organisms (Chryseobacterium meningosepticum/Flavobacterium, Pantoea agglomerans, Aeromonas hydrophila)
Num_Pathogens: 11 categories in Table 1 (13+ species named, including the 'other gram-negative organisms' footnote)
Drug_Classes: Broad-spectrum antibiotics: cefepime and piperacillin-tazobactam, carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin); ESBL production
Specific_Antibiotics: cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin
AMR_Outcome_Definition: BSA resistance defined as a culture that (1) was nonsusceptible to cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem or imipenem-cilastatin or (2) met criteria for ESBL production; chosen a priori over conventional MDRGN definitions.
AI_Purpose: Develop a user-friendly clinical decision aid (decision tree) to predict the risk of resistance to commonly prescribed broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics in children with gram-negative bloodstream infections
Num_Models_Compared: 1 predictive model developed (decision tree); a multivariable logistic regression model was also fitted and its results compared with the tree
Feature_Engineering: Continuous variables retained with cutoffs generated by the tree; number of prior admissions converted into ordinal categories; days of antibiotic exposure within 6 months dichotomized at >=7 days
Feature_Selection_Method: All predictor variables assessed for contribution to discrimination; splits chosen by the Gini splitting index in recursive partitioning
Software_Libraries: rpart (Recursive Partitioning and Regression Trees); Stata 14.0 for the descriptive and regression analyses
Other_Metrics: Positive predictive value 69%; negative predictive value 78%; prevalence of BSA-resistant bloodstream infection 31%
Baseline_Method: Multivariable logistic regression fitted with generalized estimating equations (exchangeable correlation structure within patient, robust variance estimate)
Baseline_Performance: Adjusted odds ratios: intestinal transplantation 2.73 (95% CI 1.62-4.59); prior culture with a CPT-resistant organism within 6 months 1.94 (1.18-3.19); number of prior gram-negative bloodstream infections 1.07 (1.01-1.13); prior carbapenem within 6 months 2.74 (1.54-4.88)
Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation
Train_Test_Split: None reported; the same data set was used to develop and validate the tree
Overfitting_Method: Leave-one-out cross-validation; the authors acknowledge the tree may perform differently in a different cohort of patients
Clinical_Insights: Recent carbapenem therapy, a prior resistant culture, intestinal transplantation, >=7 prior gram-negative bloodstream infection episodes and age >=3 years raise the risk of a resistant infection; findings are congruent with clinical intuition and with the regression model
Generalisability_Details: The findings may not be generalizable to other types of infections or colonization status, and the tree needs validation in diverse patient populations; in a lower-prevalence setting (eg, community hospitals) the positive predictive value would decrease.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation by leave-one-out cross-validation only; the data set was used to both develop and validate the tree; no external validation performed
Integration_Point: At the time Gram stains from positive blood cultures indicate gram-negative organisms, before organism or susceptibility data are available
End_User_Described: clinicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Two hypothetical scenarios illustrate use: patient A (10-year-old with prior cefepime-resistant E. coli urinary infection and piperacillin-tazobactam treatment) categorized as high risk, warranting broader empiric therapy; patient B (2-year-old on chemotherapy, no prior carbapenem, 2 prior susceptible episodes) considered lower risk, with empiric cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam reasonable.
Barriers_List: Suboptimal sensitivity (46%): clinical judgment and deviations from tree predictions are needed when misclassification could be detrimental; a proportion of resistant infections classified as low risk are not foreseeable
Facilitators_List: Decision trees incorporate complex interactions, account for collinearity, generate easy-to-use cutoff values for continuous variables, and avoid requiring computation of a composite score at the time of use
Future_Directions: Refine prediction algorithms for individual patients' risk of antibiotic resistance and assess the potential impact on patient management
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Recursive partitioning: the variable that best minimized misclassification by the Gini splitting index was used to split the data
Feature_Interactions_Method: Recursive partitioning tree splits (incorporating complex interactions and collinearity)
Limitation_Categories: Design and data: retrospective, no outpatient data, possible misclassification/missing data, infections may have been missed; Setting: single tertiary center; Modelling: same data set used for development and validation, too few carbapenem-resistant isolates for a staged model, need for wider validation; Generalisability: other infection types or colonization
Data_Quality_Concerns: Possible misclassification or missing data from the retrospective design without outpatient data; bloodstream infections may not have been captured if cultures were obtained at an outside facility
